# Plan — restaurant-modules

Six modules on two branches, both named `feature/restaurant-modules`: the backend at
`../OkamAPI-modules` (ASP.NET Core 8, one test project, Testcontainers SQL Server) and this repo, the
frontend (Nuxt 2.17 / Vue 2.7, one app, file-based routing under `pages/`, Jest 26). This repo is the
doc authority because the backend checkout is one of roughly eighty worktrees and no plan there would
be reliably findable.

Probe sources are relative to this repo. Backend sources are reached as `../OkamAPI-modules/…`, which
assumes the two checkouts stay siblings under `~/okam`; if that stops being true the probes fail and
their facts go `unconf` rather than lying, which is the intended failure.

**Which world these facts were read from — measured, not assumed** (added 2026-08-02). The paragraph
above assumes the sibling checkouts stand in this plan's world, and until today nothing checked it.
The assumption protects against a source that is *absent*; nothing protected against one that is
*present and foreign*, and a foreign source produces green rather than red.

The six world facts that answer this are carried in the body of `F-PROBE-ROOT-WRONG-WORLD`, and
deliberately not here: the served projection renders entities, not this header, so a fact stated
in these paragraphs is a fact nobody reading the page can see.

These six spans exist so the served page states its own provenance. It re-projects `plan.md` on every
request, so it can never be staler than this file — which means the only way it shows something false
is if this file does, and the world these facts came from was the one thing this file never said.

Two structural facts govern everything below. First, **this repo has no browser-level test framework
at all** — no Playwright, no Cypress, nothing that drives a page — so no capability in the six modules
can be shown to work by anything except a person opening it.

**Correction, 2026-07-31:** the first of those two facts stopped being true while this plan was being
written. `lane/fe-playwright` merged at `ce77727`, so `test/e2e/` and a browser harness are on the
branch, and ten journeys have driven a real browser — against a Node fixture, never against the live
.NET backend. The paragraph above is left standing because it is why the plan is shaped as it is; read
it as history, not as the state of the repo. Second, **no committed artifact anywhere
records a backend suite run**; the numbers that circulate in commit messages were measured on lane
branches, never at either branch tip.

**Correction, 2026-08-01:** the second fact stopped being true too. `L-MRG-WASTE` ran the full SQL tier
from a clean detached worktree and committed the artifact: `artifacts/tests/50b85657/RUN.md`, **568/568
with 0 skipped**, every outcome read individually out of the `.trx` rather than inferred from the
summary, diffed set-against-set at +11/-0. It is one lane's tip rather than the branch tip, so it does
not discharge the whole debt — but the claim that *nothing* records a backend run no longer holds, and
Docker being down was the reason it had not.

**And again, wider, the same evening:** `L-DOWNLOAD-PDF-WIRE` ran the **whole assembly** at the SQL
tier — **4903 passed / 2 failed / 12 skipped of 4917**, in 45 minutes. Both failures were **proved
pre-existing** by reproducing them at its base in a throwaway worktree: the concurrent-acknowledgement
race that `F-WF-ACK-DUP` already describes, and an Events settlement cancel. So the branch now has a
whole-assembly SQL number for the first time, and it is honest about the two reds rather than reporting
around them. Together those two facts are why almost every landed lane below
sits at `built-unverified`, and why `L-JOURNEY-HARNESS` is the most load-bearing open item here.

**Standing procedure, ruled by Sven 2026-08-03.** Blockers and conflicts do not go to him one at a time.
**Fable reads the whole set, designs a resolution path with an order and a reason for that order, and the
path is then executed.** That is the standard for the rest of this plan, not a one-off.

The reason it is worth a rule: today alone, three things were found that **no single lane could see** — two
sibling lanes hoisting one predicate to different homes, two lanes committing different runs to one receipt
path, and a migration stack whose depth was wrong four times running. Each was invisible from inside the
lane that caused it and obvious from above. A per-item review cannot find that class; only reading the set
can.

## Features

### Feature FT-WORKFORCE — a manager runs the week and can hand an inspector a personalliste
state: built-unverified
needs: L-WF-PERSONNEL, L-WF-INBOX, L-WF-BASIS, L-WF-SUPPLEMENTS, L-WF-IDREG, F-WF-NOCORRECTION, F-WF-NO-INVITE, F-WF-CLOCK-UNLINKED, F-WF-PUSH-SILENT, F-PERSONALLISTE-PRINT, F-WF-BLIND-BIND
owner: @sven
exit: a manager walks plan, publish, punch, decide a request and open the personalliste in a browser and the walk is captured under artifacts/journeys/, AND the kodeoversikt for that business day can be produced

Six admin screens exist and are linked: `workforce-schedule`, `workforce-requests`, `workforce-roster`,
`workforce-rates`, `workforce-personnel-list`, plus the worker's own `workforce-me` in a separate nav
group. Six, not seven. The backend's own manifest records twelve Workforce journeys verified green at
service level and four blocked on unbuilt features (shift exchange, the timesheet tail).

**How to read every walkthrough in this plan.** Each capability below carries one of three
grounding words, and nothing is written that could not be placed in one of them:

- `driven` — a real browser opened the real app, walked this exact path, and asserted what
  appeared on screen. The specs live under `test/e2e/journeys/`.
- `reachable` — the page exists, is routed, and carries a control that calls this endpoint,
  established by reading the source. Nobody has driven it, so the copy, the states and the failure
  handling are unproven.
- `no door` — the backend supports it and no shipped surface reaches it. Live code behind a door
  nobody can open. Written down because it looks like a feature in a demo and is not one.

**Two things qualify every `driven` claim, everywhere below.** First, the journeys start the real
Nuxt app and point it at a throwaway Node fixture, `test/e2e/fixture/api-server.js` — **not the
live .NET backend**. The fixture holds parts of the contract on purpose: an `Idempotency-Key` on
every Workforce mutation, `If-Match` compared against the current draft checksum answering a typed
`409 workforce.stale-revision`, and a bearer token everywhere except the anonymous guest routes.
Its own header states the rest plainly — "it is not a model of the backend. It holds no
shift-overlap rule, no wage engine, no capability matrix." So `driven` proves the pages, the
client wiring, the state handling, the money formatting, the refusal wording and the security
posture: that a person can perform the flow and reads the truth while doing it. It does not prove
the .NET backend answers the same way, and nobody has yet driven these screens against a live API.
Second, `lane only` on a walkthrough means the code sits on an unmerged lane. **Measured 2026-08-03: there are none left** — the seventh was hand-ported to the integration branch, and the other six had been landed weeks earlier by `L-FE-JOURNEYS-MERGE` with their marks never cleared. Separately, and not the same thing, **15 journey specs exist on lane branches and not on integration** — those are in-flight lanes rather than stale bookkeeping. Merge state is a
different question from grounding and is marked separately, never as a fourth tier.

Neither is a substitute for a capture. No journey has left a committed artifact behind, which is
what `F-NO-BROWSER-EVIDENCE` records and what `L-JOURNEY-HARNESS` has to end. A journey that ran
and left nothing behind is a claim, not evidence.

**Who does what.** Manager: builds and publishes the week, runs the roster, issues sign-in codes.
Worker: claims a code, reads their own shifts, asks for time off. Payroll: rates, attendance, hours
export.

**Walkthrough — publishing a week.** `driven` · `merged`
(`test/e2e/journeys/workforce-schedule-publish.spec.js`)

- **1.** Open `/admin/workforce-schedule` signed out → bounced to `/admin?redirect=…`; it remembers where
  you were going.
- **2.** Sign in as the manager → lands back on the schedule, titled **Vaktplan**.
- **3.** Read the week's state → the badge says there is no plan, which is **not** the same as an empty
  week, and exactly one button is offered: **Opprett utkast**.
- **4.** Click it → toast **Utkast opprettet**, badge flips to **Utkast**, a revision number appears.
- **5.** Add a shift on an employee's row — times, unpaid break, note, role → toast **Vakten er lagt
  inn**, and the shift lands on the grid with a cost chip the server priced.
- **6.** Click **Valider** → a validation panel opens with rule results; badge flips to **Validert**.
- **7.** Click **Publiser** → the toast reads **Publisert til …** with the server's recipient count, not
  the page's. The view switches to **Publisert**.
- **8.** Try to edit the published week → there is nothing to click. The **+** buttons and the publish
  button are **gone**, not greyed out, and the shift is still on screen. "Cannot edit" is not
  "nothing here".

**Walkthrough — a worker is refused, and given their own page.** `driven` · `merged`
(`test/e2e/journeys/admin-refusal-worker.spec.js`)

- **1.** Sign in at `/admin` as a real account that administers no store → the sidebar has no **Vaktplan**
  link and no store selector. It does have **Min side**.
- **2.** Type `/admin/workforce-schedule` into the address bar anyway → redirected to `/registrer`, and
  none of the schedule is left mounted behind it: no grid, no draft button.
- **3.** Go to `/admin/workforce-me` → it renders. This is the boundary: every route that page calls
  resolves the caller from their own token, so the person the shell bounces everywhere else is
  exactly this page's reader.

**Walkthrough — getting a new hire signed in.** `driven`
(`test/e2e/journeys/workforce-invitation-onboarding.spec.js`)

- **1.** On `/admin/workforce-roster`, open a new hire → the panel reads **Ingen innlogging** and states
  up front what it cannot do: there is no way to withdraw a code, only to reissue one, which kills
  the previous.
- **2.** Click **Lag invitasjonskode** → a handover card replaces the button. The code is shown **once**,
  with its expiry, the sentence **Vi har ikke sendt koden noe sted**, and the address the worker
  must go to: `/workforce/join`.
- **3.** Publish a week containing that person's shift → the toast confirms publication.
- **4.** As the worker, open `/workforce/join`, paste the code **before** signing in, then sign in → the
  sign-in happens in place, nothing navigates, and the pasted code survives. It was never in the
  URL, the store, or session storage.
- **5.** Claim → **Du er inne**, with the engagement's existing grants printed on the receipt. A claim
  never widens what you can do.
- **6.** Click through to my shifts → `/admin/workforce-me` shows the published shift, and back on the
  roster the person now reads **har koblet en innlogging**.

**Reachable, undriven.**

- `/admin/workforce-personnel-list` — personalliste for a chosen day, with day-stepping and a
  first-class **print** button, because § 8-5-6 requires it on paper immediately.
- `/admin/workforce-rates` — rate timeline per role and per person, planned-versus-clocked
  attendance, and an hours export.
- `/admin/workforce-requests` — inbox of staff time-off and shift requests.

**Where Workforce stops.**

- **There is no punch clock in this app** · `no door`. The backend has
  `POST workforce/pos/clock-events` and no frontend client calls it — `utils/workforce/` carries no
  POS client at all. The attendance table **reads** clocked minutes; nothing in the web app can clock
  anyone in or out. That would have to come from a POS terminal. **This Feature's own `exit:` above
  names a punch step, so the exit as written cannot be walked in a browser today** — either the walk
  drops the punch or a surface has to exist for it.
- **Workforce is the one module with no config gate.** The other five ship dark behind an
  `appsettings.json` section or a per-store flag; here, access is by capability grant per
  engagement, so there is no switch to flip and no deployment where the module is simply absent.
- **Attendance counts published shifts only.** A week still in draft contributes zero planned
  minutes, so every variance in it reads as pure overtime and unclocked draft shifts are invisible.
  The table says so in prose above the rows.
- **You cannot list or revoke invitation codes** · `no door`. The controller binds no list route and
  no revoke verb, though a `Revoked` state is declared and written by nothing. A manager cannot see
  whether a code is live, or pull one back that went to the wrong person; reissuing is the only
  mitigation, and the panel says so.
- **The invitation flow is not on the merged branch.** `pages/workforce/join.vue` exists only on
  `lane/fe-wf-onboard`. On `feature/restaurant-modules` as it stands, a venue can build a complete
  roster of people who can never sign in. `F-WF-NO-INVITE` records this — note that the flag's body
  says the endpoints "have no UI anywhere", which that lane has since made false: the UI exists and
  is unmerged.
- **Driving found the schedule's three pivots rendering each other's grids.** A `v-else` bound to
  the wrong chain: the employees pivot drew the month grid underneath the week grid and complained
  about weeks nobody asked for, and the roles pivot of an editable week drew an instruction
  **instead of** a schedule. Invisible to a green component suite, because it is a property of the assembled
  page. Fixed on `lane/fe-wf-onboard`, so it is live at the branch tip today.

### Feature FT-MARGIN — a venue costs a plate and freezes a week
state: built-unverified
needs: L-MARGIN-STATEMENT, L-MARGIN-SUPPLIER, F-MRG-STATEMENT-UNATTRIBUTED
owner: @sven
exit: a chef enters an ingredient, a supplier price and a recipe, then opens, costs, freezes and corrects one week in a browser, captured under artifacts/journeys/

Four screens: `margin-recipes`, `margin-suppliers`, `margin-price-imports`, `margin-statements`. The
backend journey manifest reports every intended Margin workflow reachable at the API level, including
statement reconciliation and the CSV export.

**Grounding.** `driven` below means a browser walk against the throwaway Node fixture in
`test/e2e/fixture/`, never the live .NET backend. FT-WORKFORCE carries the three grounding words
and what the fixture does and does not prove; the same qualification governs every claim here.

**Who does what.** Chef or owner: ingredients, recipes, versions, and linking a recipe to the dish
it is sold as. Whoever does the books: opens the week, enters purchase spend, finalises. PowerUser:
rebuilds the sales projection when it lags.

**Walkthrough — a recipe becomes a margin.** `driven`
(`test/e2e/journeys/margin-recipe-to-margin.spec.js`)

- **1.** Open `/admin/margin-recipes`, **Oppskrifter og kostpris** → no blocker panel, which is the only
  signal separating "this module is off for this store" from "the read failed".
- **2.** Add two ingredients from the starter library → the count reads back. An empty store cannot author
  anything, so the backend ships a bootstrap set.
- **3.** Name a recipe, give it a yield and a portion count, add two lines, click **Lagre og regn ut** →
  batch cost, per-portion cost and per-line costs appear, badge **Utkast v1**. The page does no
  arithmetic; every figure is one field off the wire.
- **4.** Look for a margin → it says nobody sells this yet, which is a fact about your setup rather than
  an empty table.
- **5.** Try to save a product link with no product chosen → **En rad mangler produkt**, refused in the
  browser; nothing was sent.
- **6.** Pick a product already linked to another recipe → the server refuses it: a product can **bare
  være aktivt koblet til én oppskrift**.
- **7.** Link it to a free product instead → two margin rows appear and both withhold. Plate cost and
  contribution are a **dash**, each naming its reason, **ingen aktiv versjon**. A dash, not a zero:
  the menu margin only ever costs the version active right now.
- **8.** Click **Aktiver utkastet** → badge becomes **Aktiv v1** and the table fills in, one row per price
  basis. Two rows, because eat-in and take-away carry different VAT, and a food-cost ratio without
  its basis is not a number.

**Walkthrough — a week reconciled and frozen.** `driven`
(`test/e2e/journeys/margin-statement-week.spec.js`)

- **1.** Open `/admin/margin-statements`, **Ukentlig marginoppgjør**, and pick a mid-week date → refused,
  and **not** snapped silently to a week you did not choose: it offers the Monday and draws no create
  button until you take it.
- **2.** Accept the Monday and open the settlement → badge reads **Ikke beregnet**, which is its own
  state. Net, theoretical and every ratio show a dash rather than the three zeros the columns
  actually hold.
- **3.** Try to open the same week twice → the create button is replaced by a link to the statement that
  already exists.
- **4.** Add the week's purchase spend with a date, a supplier and an amount → the row echoes the amount
  back before saving, fed from the parsed figure, so a mis-parse shows up before anything is
  written.
- **5.** Recalculate → net, theoretical, actual, covered, uncovered, both ratios, the gap and the coverage
  all render, with the time the calculation ran.
- **6.** Read the coverage panel → two uncovered buckets, including open-price sales, frequently the
  single biggest reason a week's coverage is short.
- **7.** Finalise → badge **Låst**, and **every mutating control disappears**: recalculate, finalise,
  add-spend, the amount, date and supplier fields, opening and closing stock. Not disabled; absent.
  The frozen spend line and the figures stay on screen.
- **8.** Click **Åpne en retting**, the one action a frozen week has → revision 2 opens uncalculated,
  naming revision 1 as its predecessor. Forward-only; there is no un-finalise.

**Reachable, undriven.**

- `/admin/margin-suppliers` — suppliers, their items, and a price timeline per item: the data every
  plate cost is built from.
- `/admin/margin-price-imports` — bulk supplier price import batches with summaries.

**Where Margin stops.**

- **No store has Margin turned on.** `Margin:EnabledStoreIds` is an empty list in `appsettings.json`.
  On top of that, `PriceImport` and `Statements` are separately false, so the weekly settlement
  surface and the price importer stay dark even once a store is enabled.
- **The money in both walkthroughs is the fixture's.** What is proven is that the right field
  reaches the right cell through a real currency formatter and that the page invents nothing.
  Whether the live backend computes the same plate cost for that recipe has not been driven.
- **Projection repair is PowerUser-only.** A store admin meets a 403 from the role filter before the
  module gate, so the rebuild control is not drawn for them at all.
- **Driving found two different coverage figures answering to the same test hook** on the statement
  screen — on the module whose entire purpose is that its figures agree. They are legitimately
  different numbers: one frozen at the last calculation, one recomputed at read time. Fixed on
  `lane/fe-journeys`, so it is live at the branch tip today.
- **A week can be frozen while the projector is behind,** and the lag panel that would say so renders
  only for power users. `F-MRG-FINALIZE-LAG` holds it; nothing in the walkthrough above would reveal
  it, because the fixture has no projector to lag.

### Feature FT-EVENTS — a private booking runs from public enquiry to a settled statement
state: built-unverified
needs: L-EV-GUEST, L-EV-VAT, L-EV-RAILS, L-EV-DIETARY, F-EV-ACCEPT-UNGATED, F-EV-INQUIRY-UNGATED, F-EV-NO-GUEST-ORIGIN, F-EV-GUESTLINK-FORK, F-EV-CALLBACK
owner: @sven
exit: a host takes one booking from the public enquiry page through a paid Vipps deposit to a settled statement in a browser, captured under artifacts/journeys/, AND the run sheet prints a recorded dietary requirement

**One** admin page, `events-pipeline` — not four; the pipeline and the journey panel are components
composed into it. Three public guest pages exist: `/events/inquiry/:store`, `/events/proposal/:token`,
`/events/deposit/:token`.

**Grounding.** `driven` below means a browser walk against the throwaway Node fixture in
`test/e2e/fixture/`, never the live .NET backend — FT-WORKFORCE carries the three grounding words
and what that does and does not prove.

**Who does what.** Guest or organiser: sends the enquiry, reads and accepts the offer, pays the
deposit. Events coordinator: runs the pipeline — propose, deposit, service, settle. Accounts:
settlement lines, reconcile, close.

**Walkthrough — a guest accepts an offer.** `driven` · `merged`
(`test/e2e/journeys/events-guest-proposal.spec.js`)

- **1.** Open `/events/proposal/<token>` — no sign-in, no admin shell → the offer renders.
- **2.** Read the figures → four independent money columns, in the **proposal's** currency and never the
  site's. The page invents no "total to pay".
- **3.** Read the offer lines and the venue's terms → the terms render as plain text, not markup. They are
  venue-authored copy on a public page.
- **4.** Press **Godta tilbudet** with no name and email → refused locally. Nothing was sent, so no
  receipt could exist naming nobody.
- **5.** Enter a name and email and accept → a receipt naming the proposal version, the moment in the
  reader's own timezone, and the content hash the server settled at send and re-verified at
  acceptance.
- **6.** Look for the accept and decline buttons → gone, but the offer is still rendered. The answering is
  over; the evidence is not withdrawn.
- **7.** Reload while watching the network → **no Authorization header on any request**. Venue staff open
  these links too, and a page riding their admin token would answer differently for them than for
  the guest.

**The coordinator's pipeline.** `reachable` · undriven

`/admin/events-pipeline` is the largest single screen in this repo. Filter by status and date range,
then drive one event the whole way: intake (title, date, start and end time, planned guest count,
contact name, email and phone, company), proposal (build a version with lines, send it to the guest,
or mark the enquiry lost), deposit (issue one, or cancel one), service (start service, generate a run
sheet, close the event), settlement (add settlement lines, reconcile, close the settlement),
cancellation with a refund, and delivery (see guest links that failed to send, and requeue them).
Every one of those controls exists on the page and calls the events client; none has been driven by a
browser. One detail worth showing a colleague: when the server refuses an action, this page prints
the status the server actually holds **and** the transitions legal from it, verbatim. The screen keeps
no copy of the state machine.

**Reachable, undriven.**

- `/events/inquiry/:store` — public enquiry form with local validation and a stated refusal if the
  store is unknown.
- `/events/deposit/:token` — shows the amount and one sentence per deposit state, then hands off to
  the payment provider by link. The page itself takes no money.

**Where Events stops.**

- **No guest link is emailed.** `Events:DispatchEnabled` is `false` in `appsettings.json`, so the
  outbox never drains and proposals and deposit links have to be relayed by hand. The pipeline page
  is honest about it on screen: it prints the queued count beside the notice, because with delivery
  stopped an empty failure list would otherwise read as "all clear".
- **The mail path itself is real.** Unlike Growth, `EventsEmailNotificationDelivery` is written and
  bound in DI, and the hosted dispatch service is inert until the flag is set. A config flip, not
  missing code.
- **The coordinator's pipeline is unproven.** Every stage action on the largest screen here is
  undriven. It is the widest gap in this plan between "built" and "shown working".
- **The deposit has not been driven end to end.** This Feature's `exit:` names a paid Vipps deposit;
  what has been driven stops at the guest's acceptance, and the deposit page only hands off by link.
  `F-EV-CALLBACK` is the reason that gap matters rather than merely being untested: one lost callback
  releases the guest's authorized hold and no instrument retries.

### Feature FT-MEALS — a company's lunch accounts reach a statement an accountant accepts
state: built-unverified
needs: L-MEALS-WRITE, L-MEALS-CLAIM, L-MEALS-RACE, L-MEALS-EMPREF, L-MEALS-FUNDED, F-UTLKVIT-SALE-ROW, F-XZ-CREDIT-UNSPEC, F-MEALS-EIGHTH-READ, F-MEALS-LEVER-INERT, F-MEALS-NO-SQL-ON-REQUOTE
owner: @sven
exit: an invited employee claims a membership, places a funded order a company budget pays for, and the month reaches a finalized statement line naming that employee, captured under artifacts/journeys/

Two admin screens (`meals-agreements`, `meals-companies`) and one public page, `/meals/join`, which the
brief did not have. The funded-order half of the loop cannot be started from any client today.

**Grounding.** `driven` below means a browser walk against the throwaway Node fixture in
`test/e2e/fixture/`, never the live .NET backend — FT-WORKFORCE carries the three grounding words
and what that does and does not prove.

**Who does what.** Concierge (an Okam PowerUser): company, agreement, programme, policy,
invitations. Not a store admin — the forms are not drawn for one. Employee: turns a pasted code into
a membership. Company admin: holds authority over the account afterwards.

**Walkthrough — standing a pilot up.** `driven`
(`test/e2e/journeys/meals-admin-setup.spec.js`)

**Correction, 2026-08-04.** This and the guest-claim walk below were marked `driven` **before either had
ever been run here** — both specs were committed at `ddc27fa`, but no artifact and no ledger line existed
anywhere in this checkout. The word rested on a branch nobody was on. `L-JOURNEY-MEALS` has since walked
both green at `e34977a`, so the classification is now earned rather than assumed — which is precisely why
the gap was worth writing down instead of quietly closing.

- **1.** Open `/admin/meals-companies`, **Bedriftskontoer** → before anything else, the top of the page
  states the step this surface **cannot** perform: standing a programme up does not make a lunch
  buyable.
- **2.** Create the company with an org.nr and a market, keeping "make me the admin" ticked → the corridor
  panel appears and the new company is selected. Naming somebody else here would create an account
  you could then read nothing of.
- **3.** Sign the agreement → it reads **Aktiv** with an agreement reference. Currency is not a field: it
  is part of the agreement's identity and comes from the venue's market.
- **4.** Create the programme → one row, and the policy column reads **Ingen** rather than a zero.
- **5.** Issue its first policy — a per-period limit, a timezone, a start — and publish it → version 1,
  and the panel warns first that no route can read a policy version back. A programme carries only
  its latest version **number**.
- **6.** Create an invitation with neither email nor phone → **E-post eller telefon må fylles ut**, refused
  before anything is sent.
- **7.** Try with both an email and a phone → the server refuses, and the message says whether anything was
  saved: **Ingenting ble lagret**. Exactly one channel is what makes the intended recipient
  identifiable.
- **8.** Leave just the email and create → the token appears, **once**. The panel names the claim page's
  address, `/meals/join`, separately: the credential and the destination travel as two things.
- **9.** Dismiss the card with **Jeg har gitt koden videre** → the list shows the contact and never the
  code. The server stores a hash; no route can produce the plaintext again.

**Walkthrough — an employee claims their code.** `driven`
(`test/e2e/journeys/meals-guest-claim.spec.js`) The refusals are the valuable part here, and they are
why this page is a security boundary rather than a form.

- **1.** Open `/meals/join` with no code and continue → refused locally. The paste field is the primary way
  in, because what reaches an employee is a bare string in a message.
- **2.** Paste an unknown code → asked to sign in first. There is no anonymous preview and the page does
  not pretend there is one.
- **3.** Sign in as someone who was not invited → **Vi kjenner ikke igjen denne koden**, naming **both**
  possibilities — a bad code, or the module being switched off — and saying in as many words that it
  cannot tell which, because the server gives it nothing to distinguish them.
- **4.** Try a code somebody already used → **Koden er allerede brukt**, with the branch that matters:
  **Var det deg, er du med fra før**. No retry is offered, because pressing again cannot help.
- **5.** Try a valid code belonging to a different person → **Invitasjonen hører til en annen konto**, with
  a way to come back as somebody else, and **the whole rendered page contains none of that person's
  email, phone or name**. It also says out loud that it is withholding, so a reader does not conclude
  the page is broken and go asking someone to read the invitation out to them.
- **6.** Switch account and sign in as the right person → the held code survives without a reload. The
  preview names the company, and names what it cannot tell you: there is no allowance, venue or
  inviter on the wire.
- **7.** Claim → **Du er med i …**, with the membership reference you will have to quote if you ever query
  a line on your employer's bill.

**Reachable, undriven.**

- `/admin/meals-agreements` — the venue's own directory of company agreements: which companies have a
  live corridor here.

**Where Meals stops.**

- **Nothing is ever sent. There is no outbox at all** — no mail, no SMS. The invitation token comes
  back on the create response and reaches a human only because another human copies and relays it.
  Dismiss the card and the plaintext exists nowhere. This is a design decision rather than an
  oversight, and it does not scale past a pilot.
- **No employee can buy a funded lunch** · `no door`. `Features:Meals:Ordering` is false, and
  flipping it would not help: no cart or checkout code in this repo references Meals funding, and the
  funding path needs a reservation token nothing in the estate sends. This is the module's headline
  promise and it is not reachable. `F-MEALS-UNFUNDED` and `L-MEALS-FUNDED` carry it, and
  `D-SPEC-L-MEALS-FUNDED` has since ruled that the funded checkout is bound in ConsumerWeb — so it
  will not become reachable from this repo at all.
- **Ordering, Projection and Statements are not per-store levers.** They are deliberately kept out of
  the operator catalog because they are money-path: a company may fund a checkout only once its
  billing terms are signed, and no generic toggle can enforce that. They need config plus a dedicated
  enablement flow that has not landed. So: no allocations and no monthly bill.
- **The claim page does not work at the branch tip.** It read the sign-in token in `created()`, which
  Vue runs before the session is restored from local storage in `mounted()`, so both invitee routes
  answered 401 on every load and every invited employee was told they were signed out. The page
  rendered a plausible sentence, and the only place the truth existed was the network log. Fixed on
  `lane/fe-journeys` and unmerged — so `L-MEALS-CLAIM` has landed over a capability that does not
  work on the branch it landed on.
- **You cannot read a policy back, or list company accounts** · `no door`. Both routes are absent. A
  concierge can supersede a policy they cannot see.
- **A member is a bare identifier on every statement line, permanently.** There is no employee
  reference field, so the membership id is what appears on the employer's bill, and it cannot be
  corrected afterwards — which is why the concierge has to tick an acknowledgement before issuing an
  invitation. `F-MEALS-INVITE` and `D-MEALS-EMPREF` hold this open, and the first invitation is the
  deadline.
- **The Meals admin screens carry no test hooks.** Every other module's surfaces do, so the journey
  has to find controls by CSS class and Norwegian label text: renaming a label breaks a test that
  should only break when the product does.
- **Whether any of this can be switched on at all is unsettled.** `L-MEALS-GATE` records that
  `Configure<MealsFeatureSettings>` is called nowhere, so the host gate reads false in every
  deployment whatever `appsettings.json` says, and `F-MEALS-LEVER-OPAQUE` records that the per-store
  lever lights four routes while the other 25 answer only to the host section. Treat "flip
  `Features:Meals:Module`" as a claim those two have to make true, not as a step a colleague could
  take today.

### Feature FT-TRAINING — a course becomes evidence somebody holds
state: built-unverified
needs: L-TRAIN-FIXES
owner: @sven
exit: a manager authors a course, assigns it, a worker passes the quiz, and the completion is readable as evidence in a browser, captured under artifacts/journeys/

One admin screen, `training-courses`. Seven entities exist: course, version, assignment, completion,
certificate, audit event, idempotency record. The internal-control wave (onboarding tracks, checklists,
deviations) has no tables, no services and no routes; that is `H-TRAIN-IK`, not a gap in this Feature.

**Grounding.** `driven` below means a browser walk against the throwaway Node fixture in
`test/e2e/fixture/`, never the live .NET backend — FT-WORKFORCE carries the three grounding words
and what that does and does not prove.

**Who does what.** Manager: authors courses, publishes versions, assigns them, files completions.
Staff: the subjects of the record — there is no self-service surface in this wave. Inspector: the
reason the ledger is append-only.

**Walkthrough — a course becomes evidence.** `driven`
(`test/e2e/journeys/training-course-to-evidence.spec.js`)

- **1.** Open `/admin/training-courses`, **Opplæring** → the context zone and the flag family are shown,
  because a flag being off on a visible store is the one refusal a client could not have predicted
  from a read.
- **2.** Author a course with a category and a competency key → one course row carrying the key. A course
  without one teaches something and confers nothing, which is a real choice, and why the field is
  optional.
- **3.** Cut a draft version with content and a pass threshold of 80 → the row reads **Utkast · 80**. The
  quiz is deliberately not authored, and the panel says why: it is one of three inputs to the content
  hash, so a schema guessed today would be minted permanently into every completion.
- **4.** Publish it → **Publisert**, with a content hash. The publish control is **gone**, not disabled — a
  published version is immutable and no server path would accept a change.
- **5.** Assign it to a person with a due date → only published versions are offered in the picker, and the
  person is chosen from the Workforce roster, a different module read purely to suggest.
- **6.** Type a non-GUID as a person reference → refused in the browser, and submit is disabled. A non-GUID
  would hit model binding and return a framework error this page could not have explained to anyone.
- **7.** Use a well-formed GUID that names nobody → the server refuses: it **peker ikke på en kjent person**.
  Nothing was filed.
- **8.** File a score of 55 against the threshold of 80 → the row comes back **Ikke bestått**, **and the
  screen never decided that**. There is no pass checkbox to contradict the server with; the verdict
  is the server's, graded against the threshold frozen into that exact version, and the row is
  stamped with the version hash.
- **9.** File a retake of 90 → two rows now, **55 Ikke bestått** and **90 Bestått**. The first survives. The
  ledger is append-only; a surface that replaced it would be destroying statutory evidence.
- **10.** Look up what the person holds → the competency key, with the panel stating this is **possession,
  never a verdict**. An absent key means "no fact recorded", not "not qualified".

**Where Training stops.**

- **The publish button cannot be clicked with a mouse on a 1280px laptop.** Found by driving, then
  measured: the six-column versions table overflows its grid track and its last cell lands underneath
  the next column, which paints over it. Asking the browser what sits at the button's own centre
  returns the right-hand column. It is reachable by keyboard, which is the only reason this is not a
  total block. The fix is one line of layout — let the table scroll inside its column. The journey
  refused to fake the click, because forcing one would have fired at the covering element and proved
  nothing; it dispatched the event directly while recording that the path a real user takes is broken.

  **Closed 2026-08-04 at `28548f96` — and the diagnosis above was right about the cause and one number
  short.** The table's min-content width is 607px, growing to **635px** once a published row carries a real
  hash and timestamp, against a ~488px `auto-fit` track; a table never shrinks below min-content, so it
  escapes and the later-painted neighbour wins the hit test. Fixed with `.trn-table-scroll{overflow-x:auto}`
  across all **seven** tracked Training tables, and proved by an A/B inside a single browser run that
  neutralised the fix at runtime so both arms shared one browser, fixture and page state: **eight of ten
  cells flip FAILS → LANDS over five widths × two table states, and the two that already landed still
  land** — so the failure did not merely move to 1024 or 1440. Real pointer clicks, no `force` and no
  `dispatchEvent`. Mutation-proved: restoring `overflow: visible` reds the journey with the diagnosed cause
  verbatim.

  **Residue, stated rather than smoothed:** at 1024 and 1280 the button is reachable **only after scrolling
  the table sideways**; from 1366 up it sits in plain view. Narrowing the table to fit 1280 unscrolled is a
  design call the lane declined to make alone. A sibling table, `assignment-revoke`, had the same overflow
  with a different consequence — nothing covered it in the last column, so it forced a **page-level**
  horizontal scrollbar at 1024–1440; fixed too. And `TrainingEvidenceDocument.vue`, another lane's untracked
  file, carries an unwrapped `.trn-table` and needs the same one-line wrap.
- **Five of the seven declared flags gate nothing.** `training.onboarding`, `training.checklists`,
  `training.deviations`, `training.competency-seam` and `training.reminders` change the outcome of no
  request, and are deliberately withheld from the operator catalog for exactly that reason: a flag an
  operator can flip while nothing reads it is a lever that lies. Only `training.setup` and
  `training.assignments` do anything.
- **All seven default off for every store,** so the module is invisible until someone flips a flag per
  store, and the "off" answer is a plain 404 indistinguishable from a store that does not exist.
- **No certificate vault surface exists** · `no door`. `training-courses.vue` is the only Training
  page in the app — courses, versions, assignments, completions and holdings on one screen.
  Certificate storage and expiry are named in the flag documentation, and no screen uploads or reads
  one.
- **The inspector evidence pack has no route** · `no door`. `F-TRAIN-NO-EVIDENCE` records it: the
  projection, its golden pack and a probe pinning the absent surface all exist; only the endpoint does
  not. A competency register whose evidence cannot be produced for an inspector is a binder with no
  pages.
- **Training never evaluates a role requirement.** It records what people hold. Deciding whether that
  is enough to work a shift is not something this module does.
- **Nobody takes a quiz.** This Feature's `exit:` and `L-TRAIN-FIXES`'s both name a worker passing a
  quiz. What has been driven is a manager filing a score against a threshold, and there is no staff
  self-service surface in this wave to take one from — so both exits, as written, name a step no
  shipped screen offers.

### Feature FT-GROWTH — only a guest who consented is contacted, and they can leave
state: built-unverified
needs: L-GROWTH-HONESTY, L-GROWTH-GUEST, L-GROWTH-PREFCENTRE, L-GROWTH-MAIL, F-TRAIN-EVIDENCE-SERVICE-UNCENSUSED, F-JOURNAL-FINALIZE-INDEX-DROPPED, F-EV-CONCURRENCY-GUARD-UNTESTED, F-MRG-WASTE-PANEL-CALLS-NOTHING, F-MEALS-SUPERSEDE-BYPASSES-AUTHORITY, F-PLAN-NOT-IN-GIT, F-INTEGRATION-BRANCHES-UNCOMPOSED, F-MEALS-FUNDING-AUTHORITY-COLLISION, F-EXIT-PREFIX-IS-A-STAMP, F-BACKEND-FACTS-OFF-BRANCH, F-WF-TWO-ADMINS-TWO-ENGAGEMENTS, F-POS-TENDER-WIRE-REINTRODUCES-TWO, F-ROLLBACK-LEAVES-TRACKED-STATE, F-GR-PROVIDER-ACCOUNT-UNGATED, F-GR-UNCONFIRMED-EMAIL, F-CONFIRM-BRUTEFORCE, F-GR-DISPATCH-UNATTRIBUTED, F-GR-FALSE-EVIDENCE, F-GR-HEALTH-DEAF, F-GR-NEWSLETTER-CROSS
owner: @sven
exit: a guest subscribes from the public page, receives a real double-opt-in mail from the ruled provider, confirms, then withdraws from the preference centre at the deployed origins, captured under artifacts/journeys/

One admin screen (`growth-newsletter`) and four public pages (`/subscribe/:store`, `/subscribe/confirm`,
`/preferences/communications`, `/preferences/unsubscribe`). Note that `poweruser-growth` is Okam's own
internal sales dashboard and is not part of this module.

**Grounding.** `driven` below means a browser walk against the throwaway Node fixture in
`test/e2e/fixture/`, never the live .NET backend — FT-WORKFORCE carries the three grounding words
and what that does and does not prove.

**Who does what.** Guest: subscribes, confirms, unsubscribes. Marketing operator: drafts,
test-sends, approves, dispatches. PowerUser: consent register, privacy requests, delivery health.

**Walkthrough — a guest joins the newsletter.** `driven`
(`test/e2e/journeys/growth-guest-consent.spec.js`)

**Correction, 2026-08-04 — this `driven` is unverifiable in this checkout.** A Fable review of
`L-JOURNEY-GROWTH` searched for the artifact and found **none anywhere**: the spec exists, the walk it
claims has produced no evidence here. `driven` therefore rests on a run nobody can point at. Either that
journey is re-run to regenerate its capture, or the word is withdrawn — and until one of those happens the
right reading of this line is *a spec exists*, not *a walk was made*.

**Same correction, one line worse.** `growth-newsletter-send-gate` is recorded elsewhere as stale; it is
**a failed run** — artifact at `31fc45d`, `backendServed: 0`, and the run itself ended in a login timeout.
Stale-green and failed are different states, and the more alarming one was the one not written down.

- **1.** Open `/subscribe/:store`, **Meld deg på nyhetsbrevet** → the tick box is present and **unticked**.
  There is no pre-selection anywhere on the page.
- **2.** Read the label beside the tick → it is the server's own sentence, **character for character**, and
  beside it the consent version and locale the page will record. Text and version arrive in one
  response precisely so that a page cannot display one version and post another.
- **3.** Switch the page to English → a notice appears explaining that the consent register holds only
  Norwegian, and the consent sentence itself **does not move**. Translating it here would show a
  sentence different from the one on the receipt.
- **4.** Type an email and submit **without** ticking → **zero requests leave the browser**, counted from the
  browser's own network log, and the form states why. A box that was unticked but posted anyway
  would be worse than a pre-ticked one, because the receipt would exist.
- **5.** Tick it and submit → exactly one request, carrying **no Authorization header**.
- **6.** Read the acknowledgment → **Vi har tatt imot forespørselen**, and nothing more. It does not echo
  the address, does not claim a mail was sent, and does not say you are subscribed, because the
  endpoint answers identically whether the address is new, pending or already verified. Varying
  would make it an address-existence oracle. The form is replaced rather than left beside it.
- **7.** Open the same page for a venue with the module off → no form at all, and it does **not** tell the
  guest their link is wrong, because a dark store and a store that does not exist are deliberately
  the same answer.

**The operator's send flow.** `reachable` · undriven

`/admin/growth-newsletter` runs draft → test send → approval → gate → dispatch → run outcome. Two
things on it are worth showing a colleague, and neither has been driven. **The gate fails closed**:
"we could not read consent" never renders as "consent is absent", and neither ever renders as
"consent is granted", and an un-computed audience shows a dash rather than a zero — because a wrong
number in the permissive direction is a lawful-basis breach, not a display bug. **The approval screen
admits it is not informed**: it cannot show the newsletter body, so rather than implying the reviewer
saw what they approved, it says so and names the route that does show it.

**Reachable, undriven.** `/subscribe/confirm` and `/preferences/unsubscribe`.

**Where Growth stops.**

- **No mail leaves the process, and this is not a flag.** The mail provider interface is bound to a
  deterministic fake in `Program.cs`. The transactional sender carries no SMTP dependency at all — the
  code's own comment is that the anonymous subscribe endpoint is **provably incapable** of sending real
  mail until the provider is promoted. `F-GROWTH-FAKE-MAIL` records it.
- **So the signup does not complete** · `no door`. No double-opt-in confirmation arrives, which means
  `/subscribe/confirm` cannot be reached by a real guest and no subscription is ever verified. The
  signup page is honest — it never claims a mail was sent — but a demonstration that stops at the
  acknowledgment is the whole of it.
- **A real adapter exists, and it is not a one-line swap.** `GrowthSmtpMailProvider` is written over
  the platform's MailKit sender and registered as a concrete type nothing resolves. `L-GROWTH-MAIL`
  records what it costs: it answers only submit, the three bulk capabilities throw, and the dispatch
  reconciler swallows that and parks every uncertain delivery for review. `D-MAIL` has since been
  ruled toward postmark, so the promotion that lands is that provider's adapter, not this one.
- **The privacy resolutions record deliveries that never happened.** The Art. 15 export and the
  Art. 17 completion notice both terminate in the fake, and the resolution record is written marked
  delivered regardless. `F-GR-FALSE-EVIDENCE` holds it, and it is worse than the delivery gap itself:
  as deployed, these are false entries in the evidence a regulator would be shown.
- **Consent wording exists in Norwegian only.** An English-speaking guest is shown Norwegian and told
  why.
- **One-click unsubscribe is a deployment property no endpoint reports.** It is an explicit input to
  the send gate, and "unknown" blocks a send exactly as "absent" does.
- **The preference centre is undriven and unreachable from the deployed origins.**
  `/preferences/communications` is the fourth public page this Feature names and no walkthrough
  covers it; `F-PREF-UNREACHABLE` and `D-PREF-ORIGIN` hold why a guest cannot take themselves out of
  a mailing list from where the pages are actually served.

This is the instrument the whole plan is missing. There is no Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO or any
other browser driver in this repo — the Jest suites all mount components in jsdom. Until something can
drive a real page against a real backend, C5 makes every module capability unverifiable, and the sixteen
landed lanes above stay `built-unverified` no matter how much more code lands.

Scope is one harness plus one exemplar capture, not six. The remaining captures are `L-JOURNEY-PLAN`'s
output, because what a capture must assert per module is not knowable before the harness exists.

### Lane L-ACCT-UIDX — the accounting day cannot post twice on a chain-built database
state: open
class: sql
gate: D-ACCT-TIMING
owner: agent
dir: ../OkamAPI-modules
exit: fact:acct.uidx is present AND a database built by replaying the migration chain refuses a second row for one store and date
agent: acct-uidx
needs: F-SQL-HEADROOM

The model declares a unique index on store and date; no migration in the chain creates it. Two details
make this more than a one-liner: the snapshot already carries the index, so `dotnet ef migrations add`
emits an empty diff and the migration has to be hand-authored; and the date column is still
`nvarchar(max)` on a chain-built database, which SQL Server refuses as an index key, so it has to be
narrowed first and any existing duplicate pairs removed before the index can be created.

### Lane L-GROWTH-MAIL — a confirmation mail leaves the process
state: verified
class: suite
gate: D-MAIL
owner: agent
dir: ../OkamAPI-modules

agent: L-GROWTH-MAIL
evidence: artifacts/journeys/growth-doi-postmark-sandbox.json

The mail boundary is bound to the in-memory fake. A real adapter does exist — an SMTP one over the
platform's MailKit mailer — and is registered as a concrete type nothing resolves, but it answers only
submit; the three bulk capabilities throw, and the dispatch reconciler swallows that and parks every
uncertain delivery for review. Promoting it is therefore a transactional-only fix, which is part of
what `D-MAIL` has to rule.

### Lane L-GROWTH-PREFCENTRE — a guest completes a withdrawal at the deployed origins
state: open
class: suite
gate: D-PREF-ORIGIN
owner: agent
dir: ../OkamAPI-modules
exit: a withdrawal completes from the deployed consumer origin against the deployed API origin, captured under artifacts/journeys/, AND the session cookie is accepted by the browser in that capture
agent: prefcentre
needs: D-PREFCENTRE-DEPLOY, L-PREFCENTRE-DEPLOY-EXEC

The mechanism is not the one in the brief: `AllowCredentials` is never called anywhere, so ASP.NET Core
does not throw at startup. The default policy answers with a wildcard origin and no credentials header,
while the client sends credentials on the four session calls, so the browser rejects the session-opening
call as a network error before the cookie matters. The cookie is separately `SameSite=Strict` on a
different registrable site from the page, so it would not attach even if CORS were fixed. Both have to
move, or the API has to be served same-site.

### Lane L-WOLT-SYNC — the never-registered background service is registered or deleted
state: built-unverified

agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-WOLT-SYNC/evidence.md

**Exit amended by the clerk after Sven ruled, and the reason is on the record.** This lane was authored
before `D-WOLT` was decided. Its original exit required `fact:wolt.sync.host` **present** *or* the class
**gone** — and the ruling is `leave-as-is`: **neither register it nor delete it.** So both disjuncts were
forbidden by the decision the lane is gated on, and dispatching it would have sent an agent at a wall it
could not pass.

Amending an **undispatched** lane's exit to match a ruling made after it was authored is not laundering a
contract — no agent has been sent against it. **Rewriting the exit of a lane that has already reported
would be**, and this plan has declined to do that elsewhere.

**What `leave-as-is` actually leaves to do is named in its own `con`:** *"dead code that writes to someone
else's system stays in the tree, and the next reader has to rediscover that it has never run."* That
rediscovery is the remaining cost, and it is payable — make the tree say it, at the class and at the
sweep entry, and make an accidental registration red rather than silent. Turning it loose on a third
party is exactly what the ruling refused, so the check matters more here than the comment.

`git log -S` across all refs finds no commit in history that ever added a hosted-service registration for
`WoltMenuSyncBackgroundService`. It has never run in any deployment. Registering it starts live
eight-minutely menu pushes to Wolt for every store with enabled configuration and pending changes, with
no dry run and no per-store opt-out — which is why this is a ruling and not a one-line commit.

Sixteen candidates against roughly a hundred and fifty specified. Onboarding is the module's own stated
kill risk and this is the cheapest lever against it. The curation content itself needs an owner ruling.


**Built on 2026-08-05: sixteen rows to a hundred and fifty, with the yield column deliberately empty and the
file now saying why.** The starter file was **not on the integration tip** — the tip still carried the old
collection initializer and no file at all — so the lane cut from the tip and cherry-picked the mechanism,
which applied clean because that branch was behind rather than divergent. The original sixteen are carried
over **with their values untouched**, reordered only so the list reads as a kitchen reads it.

**The reason the yields stay at zero is now written where the next author will meet it.** A yield exists in
this product on exactly one thing — a recipe *component* — so an ingredient has none of its own, a curated
fraction cannot follow it into the recipes that use it, and the editor has no control for one. **Writing `1`
everywhere would be worse than leaving them blank**, because it asserts that nothing is lost about a hundred
and fifty ingredients nobody has ruled on. The order that would make filling them worth doing is recorded:
store a default on the ingredient, give the recipe line a control that pre-fills from it, and only then ask a
cook for numbers that are per-venue more often than not.

**One new pin, and it exists because the old ones could not catch this.** The existing counters hold the file
to a number **the file itself declares**, so deleting rows and lowering the count with them stays green —
exactly how a library quietly returns to a sample. Proved non-vacuous: cutting the file to twenty rows *and
matching the counter* left the new pin as the **only** red.

**C5 is not met, and the lane named the reason to look rather than claiming otherwise.** The ingredient panel
renders every candidate as a flat chip with **no search, no grouping and no cap**. At sixteen that was a
helpful row; **at a hundred and fifty it is a wall above the create form** — and the file's category grouping
**does not survive the wire**, because the API returns a flat list.

two containers it had **no slot for**. They were created and removed by the harness, and nothing it did not
create was touched. **A test filter can claim a container slot silently** — that is the operational lesson.

reason it lost: the flag-setting endpoint authorizes on store-admin, so cataloguing these would hand **a
pilot venue's own admin the switch that arms issuance of billing documents the module records as
un-withdrawable.**

So the first half becomes the opposite change: the surface must **say the flags are deployment
configuration** instead of reporting an effective value that implies a lever exists. The screens already
name the gap, which the brief called mitigation rather than a fix — under this ruling naming it *is* the
fix, provided it says the right thing.

The second half is untouched and independent: the CORS policy exposes one header, so `fetch` cannot read
the export's content hash or filename, and **the determinism the export exists for is uncheckable by the
client that downloads it.** One string on the policy.

### Lane L-TRAIN-DISCLOSURE — a person can see who read their training record
state: built-unverified
class: suite
owner: agent
dir: ../OkamAPI-modules
exit: the disclosure events recorded against a person are readable through a route, with the read itself recorded, shown at the wire tier under an authorization matrix
agent: train-disclosure
evidence: OkamAPI-modules 06b8b582 (lane/train-disclosure) + Web-modules 2d3488c; artifacts/tests/L-TRAIN-DISCLOSURE/after.trx

Every read of a person's training file appends a disclosure event keyed to that person, and **no route
returns it** — so "who has looked at my record" is captured and unreadable, including by its subject.
That is the same shape the evidence rows were in before the inspector read landed: a fact the system
holds and nobody can be shown.

The register's whole claim is that it can produce evidence on demand. A disclosure log that cannot be
produced is the part of that claim that is not yet true.

**Built, and what it refused is the better half of the lane.**

**No name resolution.** The ledger stores a minimised actor reference and **that is exactly what is handed
over.** Resolving it would be **a disclosure about the reader, made to the person the log is about, that
nobody authorised** — and not this lane's to authorise. A person sees when, how many distinct people, and
**whether one of them was themselves.**

**No store-wide feed** — one person at a time, because **the same query with nobody named is a surveillance
report.** And **the subject branch cannot name anyone**: asking about another person falls through to the
admin gate.

**Its two readers were decided with a reason:** the subject, resolved **from the token and never from the

deleted.**

Found by the lane that guarded the two named release paths. The reconciliation worker's own release has

expiry sweep for that store, leaving every remaining strand unreleased for that run.

It is also, as that lane pointed out, the rival that makes the core-facing race real in the first place:
the sweep is what a guest's release is racing against.

**Sharpened by that lane on hand-back:** this is not simply a fourth instance of the shape. The caller's
loop has **no catch at all**, so one lost race abandons every remaining strand in that store for the
whole run — a worse blast radius than the guest-facing defect it fixed, even though nothing here ever
reaches a guest.

**Built, and it re-proved the killed run's claim rather than trusting it** — captured frame by frame that
the exception escapes to a foreach **with no try at all**, so the remaining stores died with the store.

**Two things the brief did not say, both found by its own mutants.** Removing the detach is **worse than
untidy**: the un-detached loser re-fails **every later strand's save**, so the sweep degrades wholesale
rather than losing one. And an **honest negative** — deleting the explicit rollback leaves all four pins
green, because disposal rolls back anyway. **It refused to claim that as a reddened line.**

Its discriminating mutant is the one that matters: **hoisting the containment from the strand to the loop
reds four pins**, with the isolation pin reading *expected 2, actual 0* — which is what separates this
lane from a plain try/catch.

**It tested masking both ways with the sibling lane**: its own mutant reds its pins and leaves theirs
green, and theirs reds theirs and leaves its own green.

**An arithmetic correction for whoever merges:** another lane reported a base total that implies 4358; this
one **measured 4357**. Compute merged totals from the measured base, not from lane totals.

And a pre-existing gap it flagged rather than papered over: **the hosted loop discards the entire sweep
tally.** Rather than add a fourth number nobody reads, it paid the visibility this fix owed with the
worker's own warning line.

agent: MODAL-LAND
evidence: artifacts/journeys/modal-scroll-lock.playwright.json

`L-MODAL-SCROLLLOCK` cannot be verified and `L-MODAL-SEVEN` cannot be merged, and it is the same
cause: **the journey artifact each names lives on its own unmerged lane branch.** The exit asks for a
capture under `artifacts/journeys/` and there is no such file here — `modal-scroll-lock.playwright.json`
is on `lane/modal-scrolllock @ 178c895`, and `modal-estate-scroll-lock.playwright.json` on
`lane/modal-seven @ 839d377`, which is itself built on top of the first.

`L-MODAL-SEVEN`'s own report asked for this in terms: *off lane/modal-scrolllock, UNMERGED — must land
with or after it.* So the order is fixed and not a judgement call.

Land scrolllock first, then seven, then run the frontend suite at the merged tip. The seven lane
already had to correct one assertion in its sibling's test when it moved `atoms/Modal` onto the shared
mixin, so the two suites have met each other on a branch but never at a tip. If the merged tip is red,
say so and stop — do not repair a conflict by deleting an assertion.

Local commits only. Nothing is pushed.

**Built. Both artifacts are on the integration branch and the deadlock is cleared** — the scroll-lock lane
is now **verified** on its own capture.

**Its method avoided the hazard rather than surviving it.** It did both merges in an **isolated worktree**
cut from the branch tip and then fast-forwarded the shared checkout, **so no merge commit was ever built in
the integration checkout and the index-sweep hazard could not fire** — the same hazard that swallowed six
of one lane's files earlier today. The diff against the old tip is **exactly the two lanes' forty-three
paths and nothing else.**

**The conflicts were precisely the shared multi-lane fixture files**, and both were purely additive — each
side appending in the same region. It **kept both sides, restored nothing from a snapshot, and deleted no
assertion.**

**And it re-ran both browser journeys**, on ports outside the band every other lane has used, **because its
hand-merge of the fixture server is code the unit suite never exercises.** A first attempt failed on a cold
compile timeout; it diagnosed that as **not a product defect** and the warm re-run passed.

**One finding worth keeping:** the journeys directory is **gitignored**, with a comment saying such files
are a record of a run and deliberately not committed — **and both modal lanes force-added theirs anyway.**
That is why the exit was satisfiable only by a merge, and why a suite run dirties them.

`EventsDepositPaymentPortAdapter.Initiate` sends **no `FallBack`**. The only caller that sets it is
checkout. Vipps eCom v2 requires `merchantInfo.fallBack`, so a live initiate is either refused or the
paying guest is stranded with no way back.

**It is faked in every test**, which is why no suite can see it — the deposit port fake and the
scripted Vipps service both accept the call happily. Only a live harness run decides this one.

**The fix is built and proven as far as this machine allows, on `lane/ev-vipps-fallback`** — the fallback
is now composed from the configured guest origin and the deposit token, **sharing shape and origin
validation with the outbox mail path so the two cannot drift.**

It deliberately did **not** resolve the origin from the caller: a deposit is issued by the **venue's
admin**, so live money would have pointed the guest at whichever origin staff happened to be logged in
from. With no origin configured the initiate **refuses before the provider call**, because a Vipps order is
money on the guest's card and cannot be un-made.

**It nearly retired a security check and caught itself.** Its first shape moved the token behind a
parameter, which red a credential-composition sweep whose exemption keys on a member read in the same
statement. **Deleting the now-stale entry would have gone green while silently ending the check.** It
restructured instead so both composition sites stay visible and declared, and mutation-proved the rule
still fires.

Its mutation record is the clean demonstration of what the brief warned about: removing the field from the
adapter reds five tests, and nulling it in the real service reds **only** the serialized-body test — the
doubles are blind, exactly as briefed.

One correction: **two** callers already set the field, not one.

### Lane L-GR-WITHDRAW-ORIGIN — a guest can withdraw from a real newsletter link
state: verified
class: node
pts: 1
needs: D-SPEC-L-GR-WITHDRAW-ORIGIN
exit: a browser at the deployed preference-centre URL shows the session cookie attached on the preferences read, answering 200, recorded in lanes/L-GR-WITHDRAW-ORIGIN/RUNS-2.md
agent: gr-withdraw-origin
evidence: lanes/L-GR-WITHDRAW-ORIGIN/RUNS-2.md

Two independent breaks, either one fatal. The session cookie is `SameSite=Strict` while the pages are
served from one site and the API from another — and `azurewebsites.net` is a public suffix, so those
are different **sites** and a Strict cookie is never attached. Separately the default CORS policy uses
`AllowAnyOrigin`, which a browser refuses to combine with credentialed requests, so the preflight
fails before the cookie matters.

**Both frontend files already state this defect in their own headers.** It is a topology fix, not a
config value — and it needs a decision on which topology, so surface the options rather than picking
one silently.

**Returned fail-spec, and it found a third topology that beats both the ones offered** — see the decision.
It confirmed the second break **against the live deployed API**: a preflight to the real host answers with
a wildcard origin and **no allow-credentials header at all.** And it established the exit was unreachable
for a reason nobody had noticed: **the deployed preference centre answers 404, because the Growth guest
surface is unshipped.**

The Events binding is split, and the split matters: **the cookie half does not bind Events**, whose guest
client sends no credentials and carries its token in the URL. **The CORS half does** — so under the
recommended topology the Events guest origin must sit under the same domain, or this exact problem reopens
there later.

### Lane L-GR-TESTSEND-GUARD — test-send stops being an unattributed path to any address
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a wire test proves a test-send to an arbitrary address is refused or attributed, and reds if the attribution is removed
agent: gr-testsend-guard
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-gr-testsend @ 5719fc96 · WebApi.Tests/Growth/GrowthTestSendBindingTests.cs · Growth 460/0/1 (SqlServer excluded, no slot held)

The dispatch chain is genuinely tight — consent snapshot plus a final per-recipient re-check with
evidence receipts, and no send path bypasses approval. **Test-send is the exception.** It does no
consent check, does not verify the address belongs to the admin, and — alone among Growth writes —
passes no user id, so the submission names nobody.

With a real provider bound that is a working path around markedsføringsloven § 15.

**Built, and it corrected the finding in a way that matters.** *Unattributed* is the weaker half of the
defect than it reads: the estate had already established, in a test of its own, that the store gate
refuses a principal with no identity while the actor resolver accepts every principal that has one. **So
the caller was always identifiable — the controller simply discarded the identity.** The audit trail
named nobody; the path was never anonymously reachable.

That has a practical edge the lane drew out: **a wire test asserting a 401 for an unattributed caller
cannot be driven**, and one that appears to be is measuring a substituted gate. It wrote no such test.

**It chose both remedies, and bound the address to the actor** — which is what makes attribution
load-bearing rather than decorative. The submission is composed from the account address, **never from
the request**, so a later softening of the comparison cannot widen who actually receives mail.

Three judgement calls behind that, each argued: a consented-contact rule would have been **worse than the
hole**, because test-send skips the dispatch service's final per-recipient re-check and would reach a
guest who had since withdrawn; the check sits **after** the ownership load, so a cross-tenant probe still
answers not-found rather than becoming an existence oracle; and the lookup is deny-closed, so an admin who
signed up by phone cannot test-send at all — **a real functional consequence, and the honest one**, since
there is no address the platform can prove is theirs.

Nothing asserts that a mail was sent — the fake provider accepts everything and has no failure mode. The
pins assert the refusal, that **the provider was never called**, and the recipient the service composed.

### Lane L-GR-POSTMARK-WEBHOOK — delivery truth stops being frozen at zero
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a genuine Postmark delivery and bounce payload replayed against the webhook route lands a receipt and moves a delivery to delivered or failed, pinned by a wire test
agent: gr-postmark-webhook
evidence: lane/gr-postmark-webhook 5b895dc4 (worktree ../wt-gr-postmark) — Wire/GrowthPostmarkWebhookWireTests 8/8, Growth/GrowthPostmarkEventReaderTests 38/38, Growth non-SQL 544/0, Wire+Modules 377/0

The webhook route requires a timestamp-bound HMAC signature. **Postmark does not sign webhooks**, and
the verifier fails closed by its own design. So on the ruled provider, delivered, failed and opened
stay frozen at zero forever and bounce suppressions never ingest.

The authentication mechanism that replaces the signature is a ruling, not a coding choice — it relaxes
an invariant deliberately chosen. Name the options; do not pick one.

**Built, and the brief understated the gap — authentication was one of two blockers.** The ingestion
service parsed only three fields, **a shape no real provider sends**, so even an event that somehow
authenticated was refused as malformed. That second half needed no ruling at all, and is now built and
proven against genuine payloads.

The reader picks its body shape from the **verified account's** provider key, never from the route
segment — so a Postmark body offered against a non-Postmark account is refused, and that is pinned. A new
ignored outcome answers 202 without a receipt, because a 4xx makes Postmark redeliver forever.

**Two mappings are decisions rather than translations, and it said so.** Only four bounce classes defer
and two suppress; the other sixteen — auto-responder, address change, DMARC — move nothing, because a
channel-global suppression **silences a real person on every store**. And a subscription change acts only
on a recipient-origin manual suppression, because a hard bounce arrives as **both** a bounce and a
subscription change, and acting on both writes two suppression rows that a later lift has to find all of.

**It did not decide the authentication**, as instructed: three options with a pro and con each, no
default shipped, and the signature path left untouched — pinned by a genuine payload with no credential
answering 401 and writing nothing.

**Its honest limit is stated on the suite rather than buried:** the payloads are genuine Postmark, the
credential is today's HMAC through the single authenticated seam. **The payload is real; the credential is
a stand-in.**

### Lane L-MRG-PRICE-CORRECTION — a frozen week can be repriced when a later price already exists
state: open
class: suite
pts: 2

exit: a week frozen on a wrong price, where a later price already exists on that item, reaches a corrected revision whose theoretical cost differs — asserted in a backend test
agent: mrg-price-correction

The correction path works, contrary to what the plan claimed — but only while the wrong price is still
the newest row on that item's timeline. Prices supersede forward only, so **the moment this week's
price is typed before last week's error is noticed, every instant covering the frozen week is refused
and the correction reproduces the identical wrong cost forever.**

There is a second, bounded case: a price effective exactly at Monday midnight cannot be re-priced at
that instant, so the earliest correction leaves Monday itself on the wrong price silently.

**Blocked on a ruling — and it turned the whole finding into executable tests first**, which is what makes
the ruling answerable rather than theoretical. Five tests, green, covering the control that works today,
the hole, and the midnight case: **once a later price exists, all seven of the week's midnights refuse, and
the correction revision still opens, recomputes and finalizes — at exactly the wrong figure.**

**Two corrections to the finding.** It is **two different uncoded refusals**, not one. And **the "bounded"
midnight case is the ordinary one** — a weekly price list and a statement week both start on a Monday, so
the exact-instant refusal usually fires first.

**Its falsification is the right shape:** equalising the two prices reds the control, and deleting the
supersede-forward guard from production source **reds exactly the two hole tests and only those two.**

It chose between the two shapes with reasons and named what the other would have cost — see the decision
beside this lane — then **stopped at the one column that has nowhere to live.**

The PDF generator returns null on a non-2xx answer from the renderer, and **all six call sites
dereference it**. So a renderer outage is not a handled failure — it is a 500 carrying a null-reference

Pre-existing, found while building the wire seam, and deliberately not touched there because it was

**Built — and the count was six of twelve, with two more one hop away.** The lane drove **each route to a

content to attach the report. **Eight live routes, not six.** Both extra ones fixed and pinned, each
red-proved with the real fault inside the service.

**Its rejected alternative is the reasoning worth keeping.** Deriving the new exception from the existing
base type would have been **one word and zero new code**, since all eight already catch it — **and it
answers 400.** A well-formed request told *bad request* **gives a client no reason to retry and fires no
alert.** It mapped to 502 instead, copying a shape the repository already uses.

**And it distinguished two callers that look alike.** The bulk runs notify and skip; the payout send
**deliberately does not catch**, because continuing would **mail an empty report and then set the flag that
stops a retry.**

**Containment held and was proven, not promised:** the production renderer runs in the host's own path over
a transport handing it a genuine non-2xx, **nothing was removed from the quarantine list, and no client was
exempted inside the deny filter.** One route is pinned at the service tier precisely because its seam is
quarantined.

**On the committed key, it did the careful thing:** the assertion reads the value **by reflection off the
production type**, so the lane **does not commit it a second time** — and the receipt was scanned to confirm
neither key nor host appears. **Rotation stays the owner's.**

Its delta is **exactly the tests added**, measured on its own worktree before any edit.

rule in its own file does it. The sidebar has worked exactly this way all along, which is why it has
never printed down the side of a kitchen sheet. So no body class, no vue-meta, no unscoped rule, and the
Swiss market class was never at risk. **The estate-wide body-class question stays open — it just no
longer blocks this.**

Its best moment was deleting its own work: it asserted the sheet's first line sat above a height
threshold, reasoning a banner above must push the sheet down. Measured, the topmost text is **56 points
with the banner and without it** — the banner takes the top of the page and displaces the sheet onto
later lines rather than moving it down. **No threshold could have discriminated the defect from the
fix.** It replaced the assertion with which line comes first, and recorded the reasoning so it is not
re-derived wrongly.

Its absence assertion carries three positive controls, and it hard-requires the PDF reader rather than
degrading to the screen — because this journey's only claim is about the artifact, so a silent
downgrade would report evidence it never gathered.

Left for the § 8-5-6 lane: `workforce-personnel-list.vue:358` carries the same rule on the **inert**
body-class path and is now redundant.

The page reads only the selected revision's state; the backend rules — proven by that lane's own test —

### Lane L-MRG-WASTE-500 — an unknown ingredient stops being an unhandled 500
state: verified
class: suite

exit: a waste entry naming a nonexistent or foreign ingredient answers a coded refusal, and a cross-tenant create is pinned, recorded in /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-mrgwaste500/artifacts/tests/L-MRG-WASTE-500/RUN.md
agent: mrg-waste-500
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-mrgwaste500/artifacts/tests/L-MRG-WASTE-500/RUN.md

The service never verifies the ingredient exists in the store, so the composite key refuses at save and
the controller — which catches only its own problem types — lets it out as a 500.

**Isolation itself holds** and the review verified it: the key carries the store id and the ingredient id
is globally unique, so nothing leaks into any response. The defect is the failure *shape* — the exact
500-on-operator-input that the same file spends code avoiding elsewhere.

The tenant sweep never tries one store creating with another's ingredient id, which is why nobody saw it.

**Built, verified by injection at two layers.** A throwaway probe ran against the **unmodified base
binary**, at the service and again **through the controller action itself**, and caught the exception
coming *out of* the action — neither type the action catches, **so it reached the middleware as an
unhandled 500.** Row count after the failed save: **zero** — isolation held, nothing leaked. **The defect
was the failure shape, exactly as the review said.**

**And the brief named only half of it.** The update path assigns the ingredient identically to create and
**had the same hole**; both writers are fixed.

**Its refusal is deliberately indistinguishable between a foreign ingredient and one that exists nowhere** —
same code, status and sentence, **echoing only the caller's own id and never a name** — because
distinguishing them **would make the endpoint an oracle for other stores' ingredient masters.** It runs
*after* the frozen-week refusal, **and that precedence is pinned.** Existence is checked and **status
deliberately is not**: an ingredient thrown away is archived, not deleted.

**The cross-tenant pin actually crosses a tenant, and it proved that rather than claiming it:** dropping the
store predicate reds both cross-tenant pins **and nothing else** — while **a test using only a random
identifier stays green under the same mutation.** That is why the second store's ingredient is seeded for
real.

Base measured, and **the delta computed as a set-against-set diff of test names out of the two receipts**
rather than by subtracting totals.

**What it did not prove, stated plainly:** the SQL tier has not run on this tree, so **the same coded
refusal against the composite key SQL Server actually enforces** — a different error number from the cheap
tier's — **and that the freeze still wins over the new refusal on a chain-built database** are both owed.
Its diff touches **zero migration files and zero lines of the freeze's three layers**, which is the argument
that nothing moved.

One handover: **the sibling frontend lane now has a fifth waste code to render**, not four.
