Margin registers a resolver and its rows are the best-instrumented on the switchboard — the overruled
warning is truthful there. **Four modules register none**, so their effective value merely mirrors the
stored row.

The consequence differs by module and both halves are wrong. Events and Growth are ANDed under a
**deployment switch that is not on the screen at all**, so a flipped-on row prints as on while every
route answers 404, and the overruled warning cannot fire because nothing contradicts the row. Meals is
the opposite and worse — it reports off while the gate answers on.

Margin's resolver is the shape to copy; its own source comment states the case it exists to prevent.

**Built, and the brief held on all three modules** — each verified in source rather than trusted. The
Events deployment switch is **absent entirely** from the shipped settings, so that divergence is what every
deployment of this branch does today.

**The fourth resolver-less module is Training, and it correctly needs none:** its gate is literally the
same expression the endpoint already applies. That is why the exit named three.

**Both decisions were taken deliberately and reported.** Events and Growth report false whenever the
deployment switch is off, whatever the row says — and **the screen can already render that** with the
fields it has, because the row and the effective value disagreeing is exactly what raises the existing
overruled warning, whose copy already names a deployment switch. **No frontend change needed.** It cannot
name *which* switch; no endpoint exposes that.

**It fixed the reported value, not the reach**, and took a step to stop the two looking alike: rather than
count the new reporter as a fourth consumer of the Meals lever, it **subtracted** it from the enforcing
list — otherwise the pin would have said the lever grew when it did not.

named. A resolver that ignores the row reds exactly the three cases it had labelled as regression guards
rather than as resolver evidence.

flag must now be claimed or excused **by name with a reason**, and that immediately caught something nobody

would have been the third unfalsifiable assertion, in the lane written to fix two.

Four DOM tests close the other half: the note renders, renders above the first row, is stated **once** and

### Lane L-TIER-ARTIFACTS — a tier claim without a receipt stops being accepted
state: verified
class: node
pts: 1
exit: every lane branch carrying a tier claim has the corresponding trx committed at that commit, and the convention is written where a lane author will read it, recorded in lanes/L-TIER-ARTIFACTS/DETAIL.md
agent: tier-artifacts
needs: D-SPEC-L-TIER-ARTIFACTS
evidence: lanes/L-TIER-ARTIFACTS/DETAIL.md

Two reviews in a row found the same gap from opposite ends: one lane's frontend suite had **no receipt at
all** and its claimed count matched no reconstructable partition; another's fast and SQL tier numbers and
five mutation runs were **process claims with no artifact**, despite the estate having an in-repo
convention for recording exactly that as a trx at the commit.

The numbers are plausible in both cases. That is the problem — plausible is what a fabricated number also
looks like, and the estate has already been bitten by a model originating figures attributed to a machine.

**Landed 2026-08-06 under the `forward-only-plus-C8` ruling — and the lane's most valuable act was correcting
two of its own published figures.** Both were the exact shape this lane exists to catch.

**"~361 branches carry tier claims" was a branch-scale estimate that was never a census.** The measured count
is **92 commits**. The naive per-branch tally inflates roughly elevenfold **because lane branches share
ancestors** — 1,054 branch-hits collapse to 92 commits.

**"8 receipts estate-wide" was read off one working checkout**, and branches carry different receipt sets:
there are **28 receipt files naming 25 commits.** The convention had been adopted about three times more
widely than the lane itself had reported.

**The contradiction is how the bug was caught, and the tool now prints both columns because of it** — a first
run reported 61 backed in a repository holding 26 receipt files, which cannot both be true. A second mislabel
was caught the same way: it printed *"receipt files"* while counting commit hashes.

**The census imports its patterns from the checker rather than restating them**, so it counts what the
instrument enforces rather than what a second author thought it enforced.

**Its stated limit is the honest kind:** the census reads commit messages only, while **178 of 399 returns**
also state a tier figure — so **92 is a floor**, and the note says so at the point where the number is used.

**The constraint is drafted and `intent.md` is untouched — the clerk verified both.** One design note worth
keeping: the forward-only clause sits **inside the violation condition rather than beside it**, because only
the constraint block is copied into every brief, and an author who reads it and concludes *"then I must
receipt my older commits"* has to be stopped **where they read**, not in a document they will not open.

only *use your own address* would send that operator hunting for a typo that does not exist, so the copy
names both clauses and each is asserted per locale.

**It deleted two of its own assertions** because no honest mutation could kill them — a not-equal-generic
check sitting underneath an exact-key check, twice. That is the discipline this plan has been asking for,
applied unprompted to its own work.

**The derived-check question was answered in both halves.** Cheap and shipped: no error sentence may exist
in one locale and not another, derived from the union of the three files' own key sets and vacuity-guarded.
Deliberately **not** derived: which codes are mapped, because that expectation **shrinks in the same edit
that drops an entry** — the self-referential trap a sibling lane avoided yesterday. The remaining half is
not cheap, because the authority is in another repo on an unmerged branch, and the real fix is a
backend-published manifest.

**A trap worth carrying:** backing a test file up inside the repo made the runner discover it as an extra
suite and **run everything twice.**

### Lane L-GR-DEADLINE-ONWIRE — the article 12 deadline is the server's answer, not the page's arithmetic
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: the privacy request read carries the deadline the venue is held to, and the page renders it rather than deriving it, pinned by a wire test, captured at `artifacts/journeys/growth-privacy-queue.playwright.json`
agent: gr-deadline-onwire
evidence: artifacts/journeys/growth-privacy-queue.playwright.json

**The deadline the guest was promised exists nowhere on the wire.** The list carries only when a request
arrived. So the venue's queue derives it in the browser: one *calendar* month, clamped to the last day of
the target month per Regulation 1182/71 article 3(2)(c), so the last day of January plus one month is the
last day of February rather than spilling into March.

That derivation is correct and it is **in the wrong place.** The deadline is the thing the venue is
legally held to; it should be the server's answer, computed once, not recomputed by every client that
draws the list — and today only one client exists to disagree with.

The lane that built the queue also found the server sends the open list **newest first, which buries the
request about to run out of month**, and re-ordered it client-side. Same argument: that ordering is a
property of the obligation, not of the page.

**Built, and the trap in the brief fired exactly as warned.** Its first clamp assertion pinned *not thirty
days* on every row — **and two rows failed**, because the end of March plus a month and plus thirty days
are the same date. **The two rules only part at the end of January.** It split that pin into its own test
seeded there, and kept the thirty-day-month rows as clamp cases only.

**The port is exact rather than re-derived**: the platform's own month arithmetic *is* the Regulation
1182/71 end-of-month clamp, so the behaviour moved without being re-reasoned from the regulation — which
is what the brief asked for and the safer of the two ways to do it.

**No migration, and none needed** — the deadline is a function of the arrival time, derived on read.
Nothing stored, nothing to backfill, no fourth migration into the contested chain.

It deleted the browser derivation **with no local fallback**, which is what makes the server the single
answer; and it kept the two earlier bug fixes on the client deliberately, because those are the countdown
against the *viewer's* clock rather than the statutory date.

**Its sharpest mutation is the last one:** dropping the deadline from the e2e fixture reds **the journey
itself, at the on-screen date** — which proves the browser step reads the wire rather than the seed.

**No tier was run and none is claimed.** A doc note worth keeping: the Growth spec never stated the
article 12 deadline as a requirement at all, which is plausibly why it went unserved this long.

### Lane L-EV-REFUND-FAKE-ARG — three SQL-tier failures nobody has seen
state: verified
class: sql
pts: 2
exit: the refund-driving Events tests pass at the branch tip on a chain-built database, and the seeding helper cannot be called in a way that silently disarms the fake, recorded in lanes/L-EV-REFUND-FAKE-ARG/commit-events-sqlserver.trx
agent: ev-refund-fake-arg
evidence: lanes/L-EV-REFUND-FAKE-ARG/commit-events-sqlserver.trx

Found by a lane running an untargeted suite it had not meant to run. A commit added an **optional**
argument to an Events seeding helper that arms the refund fake. **Only two of twenty-five call sites pass
it**, so every refund-driving test fails deterministically.

It is not that lane's doing — all five files involved are byte-identical between its head and its base.

**It is invisible because the SQL tier has not run against these commits.** That is the whole lesson: an
optional argument with a default that disarms a fake is a defect that only a tier nobody runs can see, and
the fix is to make the helper impossible to call wrongly rather than to pass the argument twenty-three
more times.

**Built, and it corrected the count I gave it.** The call-site figures held exactly — twenty-five sites,
two passing the argument — **but "three failures observed" is not supported.** The real footprint is **one**
deterministic failure, and the reason is structural: **the two other sites that built a rail alongside a
seeded receipt were precisely the two that passed the argument.**

It measured rather than reasoned. The 121 failures in the earlier untargeted run were **a died container**
— eighty-one connection faults and thirty-nine socket faults — *the exact hazard that run was warned
about*, and **none of them was this defect.**

**It rejected both alternatives I offered, with reasons.** A required parameter is worse because the caller
still constructs the double *and* arms it with the same amount the receipt records — **two facts that can
drift apart, the defect one step removed.** A separately-named unarmed variant is worse because it leaves
the disarmed act in the vocabulary, **and the whole failure was that reaching for the disarmed thing looked
exactly like reaching for the right one.** It made the act return the rail it armed and deleted the
optional parameter.

**Its guard is stated over the whole surface, not the one method that broke** — no act may take a rail as
an optional parameter — so the next act written is in scope the day it is written.

**And it made the failure loud rather than silent:** an unarmed rail now gets past the ledger ceiling and is
refused by the provider call under a different code carrying the double's own signature, **so a test that
forgot to arm can satisfy neither a refusal assertion nor a success one.**

**Its source scan checks its own parser** — counting seeding calls reached inside test methods against
calls present in the files, **so a splitter that loses a method fails instead of narrowing the proof to
nothing.** That check caught a real offender on its first run: the lane's own counter-example.

### Lane L-EV-URI-RELATIVE — a relative origin becomes a file path instead of a refusal
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a relative configured origin is refused by the malformed-origin branch on every platform, pinned by a test that reds if the absolute-URI check is removed
agent: ev-uri-relative
evidence: lane/ev-uri-relative @ 6a7bf75b (wt-evuri) · artifacts/lanes/L-EV-URI-RELATIVE/RUN.md

Found by a lane's own falsifier, in code it had not written. Both guest-link paths compose the origin with
`new Uri(origin + path, UriKind.Absolute)`, **which on Unix does not reject a relative origin** — it
yields a `file://` URL. So the malformed-origin branch was **unreachable for the likeliest
misconfiguration**, and the guest would have been sent a link to a local file path.

**It throws on Windows, which is why no development machine ever saw it.** Pre-existing, and fixed by the
lane that tripped over it.

**Built, and measured rather than trusted** — on this host the shipped composition turns a scheme-less
origin into a `file://` URL and throws nothing, so the malformed-origin refusal really was unreachable.
**The fix is not on the integration branch**, so this is not a spec failure.

**It ported the sibling lane's version byte-identically, deliberately**, so the two add/add merges cleanly
— and judged that version *sufficient* rather than improving on it: **it checks the scheme, not mere
absoluteness**, which is the right call precisely because `file://` satisfies absoluteness. What it added
is a standalone pin: the sibling's assertions live inside a Vipps test entangled with an HTTP stub, on a
lane parked awaiting a ruling, **so the refusal now survives whichever lane lands first — or neither.**

**Its mutation record separated two assertions that would otherwise have hidden each other.** Quoting the
composed address in the refusal reds seven tests — but that mutation **short-circuits on the label
assertion**, leaving the log-scan assertion unproven. So it ran a second mutant where the label stays
clean and **only the log carries the link**, and confirmed the estate's own credential sweep reds there
too. Given sixteen unfalsifiable assertions in three days, that is the right instinct.

**And it corrected the brief:** *both guest-link paths* is not true on this branch — there is exactly one
composition site; the other belongs to the parked lane. It left the unused prefixes rather than rewiring,
because diverging there **would turn a clean merge into a conflict for a parked lane** — and said plainly
that a reviewer of its diff alone would fairly flag them.

**One hazard for everyone:** a suite run **dirties the tree**, because a test rewrites a committed journey
artifact with today's date. No full run leaves a clean status, so real edits can hide in it.

The one-clause fix the review named: require the confirmation flag alongside the email, matching the
precedent one file over.

**Two things must land with it or the fix has no evidence.** The shared test support seeds the email
**without** the confirmation flag, so **every positive control reds until it is seeded** — that is the
signal the fix is real, not a problem to work around. And the new pin is the one the suite does not have:
**an unconfirmed address is refused.**

Without that pin, the suite continues to encode *an unconfirmed profile address is an acceptable
test-send target* as the expected behaviour — which is what it encodes today.

left makes **four positive controls fail**, the same four that had been passing **with the hole fully

observed.

Which is the honest shape: the hole was invisible to everything that existed.

### Lane L-GR-TESTSEND-RATELIMIT — the arbitrary-address paths carry a limiter
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: the test-send route and the profile-email change are both rate-limited, pinned by a test that reds if either limiter is removed
agent: gr-testsend-ratelimit
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-gr-ratelimit @ c96cd21e (lane/gr-testsend-ratelimit, off 801d36a3, local, unpushed) · artifacts/tests/lane-fast-tier.trx 4403/4391/0/12 · artifacts/tests/base-801d36a3.trx 4376/4364/0/12, measured myself from a clean checkout of the base

Two halves of the same exposure, found by the review of the § 15 guard.

**The test-send route has no rate limit at all** — it is absent from the public limiter's type sets, while
the subscribe path it sits beside is covered per-address and per-IP.

And the profile-email change beneath it has none either, which the review flagged as out of its lane but
worth saying plainly: **it makes the core product an unrate-limited emailer of six-digit codes to
arbitrary addresses.**

Neither is the § 15 defect itself. Both are what make it cheap to exploit and cheap to repeat.

**Built — and it found a blocker in a file it was only passing through** (see the flag beside this lane).

**It corrected both the brief and the review it was built on.** Confirming an email is **not** on the
sign-up path — sign-in requires a confirmed *phone*. And lockout **is** configured, but **nothing anywhere
calls the failure counter**, so the review's conclusion held while its reason did not.

**It refused to ask for a ruling and argued why that is judgement rather than evasion:** the estate had
**already ruled every number** — five codes per recipient per quarter-hour, ten guesses then a cool-off for
a short numeric secret — so it applied those to the same acts on a different channel instead of inventing
thresholds.

**The detail that matters most: the guess budget lives in a separate key space**, so a throttled user can
still request the new code the refusal tells them to get. A limiter that locks you out of its own remedy is
worse than none. Its stated worst case is **the sixth send to one address in a quarter-hour, or an eleventh
mistyped code** — and **nobody loses account access.**

From the mid-flight correction it folded in two more: the code came from a **non-cryptographic** generator
that **could never issue the highest value**, and a spent budget now **retires the code**, so waiting out
the window resumes against nothing.

**Its return was refused for length and it re-emitted rather than being trimmed for it** — and its choice
of cuts is the interesting part: it kept the *derivation* of each threshold, because that is what a reader
cannot reconstruct from the diff, and dropped a claim **a test already makes**, on the reasoning that a
claim a test makes does not need making twice.

**And it named a defect in the dispatch itself:** the brief's workdir field pointed at **another lane's
live worktree**, while the same brief's constraints warned against shared paths. **The warning and the
instruction contradicted each other** — the generated slot should be validated against the live worktree
list before it ships.

### Lane L-GR-DEADLINE-COPY — three sentences and two comments stop asserting the old architecture
state: verified

Four stale claims left by the deletion, each small and each wrong in the same direction — they describe
the world before the deadline moved to the server.

The unknown-deadline sentence says **the receipt time cannot be read**. After the deletion the null case
means *the response carried no deadline*; the receipt time is typically perfectly readable and the page
no longer works anything out. **On the integration branch today that false sentence prints on every open
row.**

A template comment still says the deadline is derived on the page and that printing it as the server's
would be inventing authority — **exactly inverted** since the deletion, which updated the script-side
comment and missed this one. A test doc overclaims that every row discriminates the two rules when two of
six agree. And a locale guard greps only one language.

**Built, and the third finding was worse than briefed — including a mistake of mine.** It computed both
rules over all six clamp rows rather than eyeballing them, confirmed the two that agree, **and found the
summary was also backwards**: the second column is the calendar-month answer, not the thirty-day one. My
brief did not catch that.

**It found four more instances of the same stale claim than the brief listed** — a header comment above
the block in **each** of the three translation files saying the copy holds a deadline *derived from the
receipt time rather than told to us*, plus one more doc. **Five comments now agree with the wire**, which
is what the exit actually demanded.

**It proved each finding rather than assuming it**: that the null case genuinely means the response
carried no deadline, by tracing which parse sets it; that the deletion commit touched **only** the
script-side comment; and that the old locale guard really does miss an English phrasing, **by running the
pattern against one.**

**What it deliberately left alone is the better half of the judgement.** The three refusals and four
further candidates. Both viewer's-clock fixes. And one Norwegian sentence that reads *is computed* —
because it is **passive and still true**, the service computes it exactly that way, and **changing a
C6-scoped statutory sentence would be gain-free risk.**

Nine mutations, each killing exactly one test, each file restored byte-exact **from a copy held outside
the tree** — the trap a sibling hit yesterday when an in-repo backup made the runner discover an extra
suite and run everything twice. Three of the nine exist because the new guard is a **negative scan**, and
prove it cannot pass by reading nothing, by no longer matching its own language, or by firing on the one
legitimate sentence.

**It said plainly that the sequencing gap stands:** the sentence is now true, and it still prints on every
open row until the backend half merges. **Mitigation, not a fix.**

### Lane L-GR-DEADLINE-STATUTE — the two omitted counting rules are named
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: the working-day extension and the end-of-day expiry are either implemented or named in the obligation's own doc, and the timezone reading is recorded
agent: gr-deadline-statute
evidence: lane/gr-deadline-statute f7abfd8e (wt /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-gr-statute, off 3b42da1d) · lanes/L-GR-DEADLINE-STATUTE/growth-scoped.trx

Three limits the port does not cover, and the doc implies a completeness it does not have.

**The working-day extension** — a period ending on a weekend or public holiday runs to the next working
day — is not implemented and not mentioned. Conservative, so the venue is never shown false headroom; but
**the overdue sentence can be legally false for up to two days.**

**The end-of-day expiry**: the period ends at the expiry of the last hour of the due day, and the computed
instant carries the receipt's time of day, so the overdue flag trips up to a day early. Conservative; the
printed date is unaffected.

**And the timezone answer is yes, and it is the only break in the dangerous direction.** The clamp runs on
the UTC day-number while the page renders in the viewer's zone — so a request filed at half past one in
the morning on the 31st of March shows a deadline **a day later than the venue-local reading grants.** The
UTC reading is legally defensible and was deliberate; **the mismatch comes from computing on one calendar
and rendering on another.** A venue-local date-only value would dissolve it — but which reading is
operative is a legal question the code cannot answer.

**Built, and it checked the primary text rather than the brief's account of it.**

**It refused the working-day extension on evidence, not convenience.** The Regulation defines a public
holiday as a day designated as such **in the Member State where action is to be taken** — per-market data
**the product holds for no market**, confirmed by grep rather than assumed. Named with its direction, its
worst case, and what implementing it would need.

**And it judged the end-of-day rounding *not* cleanly implementable, which was the opposite of what I
expected.** Rounding to the last moment of the due day sounds like a pure improvement — it would **move the
printed date a day later for every row east of UTC**, applying the dangerous direction *universally*
instead of to a handful. Gated on the calendar ruling, correctly.

**Three new pins, each naming the rule it rules out**, and the mutation record is the proof: implementing
the weekend extension reds the Saturday pin and **exactly the three clamp rows the doc names**, while the
**Friday-holiday pin stays green** — which is precisely the claim that pin exists to make. And a
two-hour-offset clamp reds the calendar pin **and nothing else in the file**: it is the only assertion in
the suite that can see the calendar choice at all.

**It found two false claims in the existing suite.** The clamp table called a date *two days of headroom
that do not exist* — but that month-end **falls on a Saturday**, so the extension carries the period to the
same date. The rule being ruled out is still wrong; **the sentence was not.** And a test comment said *the
answer was given late* over a fixture resolved **twenty-six days early.**

### Lane L-GR-CONFIRM-STALE — a confirmation never expires and is never re-checked
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: an address confirmed long ago and since unreachable cannot authorise a send, pinned by a test that reds if the staleness check is removed
agent: gr-confirm-stale
evidence: OkamAPI-modules lane/gr-confirm-stale @ 771c0fc0 (own worktree /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-gr-confirm-stale, off 48950702) · artifacts/tests/771c0fc0a6504971fb1cfdab5eed4ab878582ab5/RUN.md + artifacts/tests/771c0fc0-fast-tier.trx (fast tier Database!=SqlServer, 4380 total / 4368 passed / 0 failed / 12 skipped) · WebApi.Tests/Growth/GrowthTestSendReachabilityTests.cs

**Nothing ever expires or re-checks the confirmation flag.** The only write of true is the confirm path,
and the only clears are on an address change. **So a confirmation made against a since-recycled mailbox
still authorises a test-send today.**

That matters more now than it did yesterday, because the flag has just become **the load-bearing proof**
that an address belongs to its sender. A proof that never expires is a proof about the past.

Related and cheap to fold in: **test-send consults no suppression list**, so a hard-bounced or
erasure-suppressed own address still receives a submission. Their own address, so § 15 is untouched — the
cost is deliverability and the provider's own terms.

**Built — and the judgement it made before writing code is the whole lane.** It did not invent a staleness
number. **It found a precedent pointing the other way:** Growth already rules that a permission proof does
not lapse on a timer — *consent does not expire in v1*, and the projection takes no age input. **What ends
a proof there is dated evidence.**

And the platform holds exactly such evidence about whether an address still accepts mail: **the append-only
suppression ledger**, which the provider webhook writes bounces and complaints into. **Test-send consulted
none of it** — which was also the brief's cheap-to-fold-in half, **so the two halves turned out to be one
fix.**

**Three placement decisions, each load-bearing.** The check runs **after** the ownership load, and on the
**account's** address rather than the requested one — asked earlier or on the request, **it would be a
channel-wide oracle over strangers' bounces.** It refuses only on reasons **a fresh mailbox-confirmed
opt-in can never lift**, reusing the estate's single classification, which is **fail-closed for an
unclassified reason.** And it added a read-only lookup so **a suppression on a crypto-shredded prior
version still binds.**

**No migration, no schema, no new threshold**, and the statutory clause and its four pins are untouched.

Its four pins each drive **both the served and the refused state through the same route, same actor,
byte-identical body** — and the first **advances the clock a year, so "confirmed long ago" is literal
rather than notional.** Four mutations, each red only its own pin.

**And it named what it could not close**, with a suggested flag id — see the flag beside this lane.

### Lane L-MEALS-QUOTE-RETRY — a transient failure inside the quote's own save loses the quote
state: verified
class: sql
pts: 2
exit: a quote survives a transient failure raised inside its own save, pinned by a test that reds if the retry-safety is removed, recorded in /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-mealsqretry/lanes/L-MEALS-QUOTE-RETRY/evidence.md
agent: meals-quote-retry
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-mealsqretry/lanes/L-MEALS-QUOTE-RETRY/evidence.md

Found by the lane proving the supersede release on a real database, in code **older than the change it
was testing.** The quote path is **not retry-safe against a transient failure raised inside its own
save**: the reservation and the receipt stay in the added state across the retry, **the receipt's unique
key collides**, and the caller gets an internal error saying no receipt was found — **instead of a
quote.**

It is the reason that lane injected its own failure at commit rather than inside the save. **Pre-existing,
and its own lane.**

**Built, verified by injection first** — the three new pins went 3 of 3 red against the unchanged service,
two of them carrying **the caller's own answer verbatim**: a quote race reporting a conflict where no
receipt was found.

**The cause, named exactly:** the retrying strategy **rewinds the transaction and never the change
tracker.** The failed attempt's rows stay staged, the retry stages its own alongside them, one save inserts
two receipts under one key, the unique index fires, **the existing duplicate-key handler rolls the retry
back too** — and the read that follows sees a database where nothing was ever committed.

**It rejected the two obvious fixes with reasons.** Clearing the tracker is wrong because the context is
**scoped — one per request, shared with every other service on it.** A catch-and-detach around the quote's
own save **stops the collision and nothing else.** Instead every attempt opens by detaching what the
previous attempt staged.

**And the same fix closed a second defect nobody had recorded**, in the same delegate: a transient failure
inside the *supersede release's* save leaves the reservation modified, the retry's re-read **identity-
resolves to it**, and the guard sees a released state **the rollback undid** — so it silently no-ops, and
**the re-quote is charged on top of the hold it was replacing.**

**Its three mutants prove the two halves are separately necessary:** the whole fix removed reds 3 of 3,
one half reds 1, the other reds 2.

It measured its base rather than inheriting it, and the eighth guard-zero pin **still holds** at its
commit.

**And the container attribution rule fired again, correctly.** A container appeared **inside its run
window** and is **not** its own — no testcontainers label, no sidecar, an operator name in the family of a
lane holding a live world. **A by-timing attribution would have blamed this lane.** Left untouched. That is
twice today.

### Lane L-FLAGS-EXCUSE-BYFLAG — the guard excuses by flag, not by module
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: deleting any effective-flag resolver registration reds the catalog guard, and every excuse names one flag with a reason that is true, recorded in /Users/svendaneel/okam/OkamAPI-flagsexcuse/lanes/L-FLAGS-EXCUSE-BYFLAG/mutation-receipt.md
agent: flags-excuse-byflag
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/OkamAPI-flagsexcuse/lanes/L-FLAGS-EXCUSE-BYFLAG/mutation-receipt.md

The derived guard was the lane's best idea and **it is a module-keyed denylist.** It excuses *any*
unclaimed flag of an excused module, so three things follow.

**Deleting a resolver registration does not red it** — the module entry absorbs the flag, and only a
separate HTTP pin catches that. **A future diverging flag inside an excused module passes unexamined**;
only a *new module* reds. And *every catalog flag must be claimed or excused by name* is **true in prose
and not in code.**

**One excuse is also factually wrong** — it opens by naming seven advertised flags where the module
advertises two. A wrong first sentence **inside the mechanism whose whole justification is named
reasons.**

**Built, and it proved all three findings by mutation rather than by reading.** Deleting the Workforce
registration left the guard **4 of 4 green** — only a separate HTTP pin caught it. Appending a new
advertised flag with no resolver and no excuse **also passed 4 of 4.** And the Training count was wrong as
described.

**Excuses are now keyed by flag** — eight entries, exactly the set no resolver claims — and **each reason
names that key's own seam, read out of the code rather than restated.**

**The self-correction is the part that makes it hold:** an excused key must be in the catalog **and claimed
by no resolver**, so **no claimed key can ever be excused** — which is what makes a deleted registration
surface instead of being absorbed.

**The exit was proved, not asserted: it deleted each of the five registrations in turn** — including one
that lives in a different file from the rest — **and every one reds the guard.** The new-flag mutant reds
and is **named in the message.** Every mutation restored and the tree verified clean before committing.

**And it kept the nuance rather than flattening it:** effective-off means writes are refused, while the
module gate keeps a store with existing data read-visible — the distinction a sibling review found and a
journey independently walked.

Its tier matches the measured base exactly, which is right for a change that adds no test method.

### Lane L-CONFIRM-SERVER-HALVES — the two silent failures the admin screen could only route around
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a failed confirmation send is reported rather than swallowed, and a malformed address is refused rather than throwing, each pinned
agent: CONFIRM-SERVER-HALVES
evidence: OkamAPI worktree /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-confirm-halves, branch lane/confirm-server-halves @ 8704ff63 (off c96cd21e, local, unpushed) - lanes/L-CONFIRM-SERVER-HALVES/evidence.md - artifacts/tests/base-c96cd21e-fast-tier.trx 4403/4391/0/12 from a clean checkout of the base - artifacts/tests/lane-confirm-halves-fast-tier.trx 4410/4398/0/12

**Refused deliberately by the lane that found them**, because both live in the backend and it was a
frontend lane — the right call, after two lanes this week over-reached across a repo boundary and had to be
unwound.

The send is **fire-and-forget, so mail failures are swallowed**: an admin who never receives a code cannot
tell whether one was sent. And a malformed address **throws unhandled at parse** rather than being refused.

The screen now closes the second for **its own** user by refusing before it calls, and says the code was
**ordered** rather than claiming it was delivered — which is honest and does nothing for any other caller.

**Built, and one finding was worse than briefed.** The send failure was not merely swallowed — **the mail
service does rethrow every failure and logs it redacted.** The failure was raised, **travelled one frame,
and died** on a thread the request never joins, and the route answered success regardless.

**It proved the 500 over the real pipeline rather than by reading**, getting the exception type and the
character offset back in the response.

**Its fix is not an invented shape:** the send is now awaited and a throw answers false — **which is what
the phone half of the same feature has always delivered.** And it adds **no log call**, because the mail
service already records the failure redacted and a second line here **could only add the address and the
code.**

**Nothing above the socket is stubbed.** Production identity configuration refuses the write, and the real
mail service with only its transport replaced **raises the failure through the production send loop.** All
seven pins were red first, each for its own reason, and every pin carries a positive control through the
same call — **including that an accepted send carries the stored code to the right mailbox.**

**One named cost, not hidden:** the route now blocks on the mail server where it used to return at once,
bounded by the send cap — **the same exposure the phone channel already carries.**

And a seam that proved load-bearing by accident: extracting a shared transport double dropped an override
on the first pass, **and the redaction suite caught it instantly.**

### Lane L-CLIENT-TRAILING-SLASH — one route is posted with a trailing slash and nothing notices
state: verified
class: node
pts: 1
exit: the confirm route is posted in the same shape as its siblings, and a check reds if a route path diverges from the convention, recorded in /Users/svendaneel/okam/Web-modules/lanes/L-CLIENT-TRAILING-SLASH/mutation-receipt.md
agent: CLIENT-TRAILING-SLASH
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/Web-modules/lanes/L-CLIENT-TRAILING-SLASH/mutation-receipt.md

**Found by a browser, and no mocked test could have found it.** The shipped client posts to the confirm
route **with a trailing slash**, unlike every other route in that file. The real framework matches either
form, **so production never notices** — but the fixture answered a not-found, and **the page reported
failure against a backend that was fine.**

That is the shape worth generalising: a divergence invisible to the product and fatal to the double that
stands in for it. Fix the path, and consider whether the convention is cheap to derive rather than
remembered.

**Built, and the brief was wrong on scale by a factor of thirteen.** It said one route was slashed *unlike
every other route in that file.* The lane parsed **all 418 call sites** in the repository: **thirteen paths
end in a slash, five of them in that same file**, and the rest spread across seven other services. **Every
one is declared bare on the backend.** It fixed all thirteen — **a guard with twelve exceptions is not a
guard.**

**Its check is derived rather than remembered.** It reads which methods take a path **from the request
service's own signatures**, walks the corpus with a comment-aware scanner, and asserts a normalisation
identity. **A new route is covered because the walk finds it.** Exactly one remembered fact remains, and it
is the one that makes a renamed parameter **red instead of silently shrinking the corpus** — the
self-referential trap a sibling lane avoided last week, handled the same way.

**Eight mutations, all red**, including a walk that stops reaching the shared submodule and a broken
argument scanner — **so the guard cannot pass by reading nothing.**

**And it proved the defect on the wire, because a tolerant fixture cannot discriminate:** it pinned the
fixture to the bare path and ran the journey three times on one warm server — **bare passes, slashed
fails at exactly the defect, bare passes again.**

**One judgement worth keeping:** a sibling repository carries its own copy and still posts a slashed path,
so it made that fixture **slash-insensitive rather than re-pinning it** — because **pinning either spelling
would fail a working client.**

It declined the wider cross-check — whether the fixture implements every route the client calls — noting
it is feasible from the same corpus, **because deciding what a missing route means is the other lane's
judgement.**

Three defects in one store, and the first is live right now.

**Last-writer-wins at a single join key**, so a fixture re-run overwrites a live pass — **which has already
happened to all three live journeys.** **Teardown-only writes**, so an interrupted run leaves the previous
artifact standing, live-labelled and passed. And **no backend identity**, so a live run against a stale
checkout is indistinguishable from one against the current one — the health probe answers one word and
**any API satisfies it.**

The fix shape the review named: **a per-backend filename or an append-only ledger**, plus a build recorded
at run time — the world script can export its own checkout into the environment the recorder copies.

Ruling the exact mechanism is this lane's; **what must be true is that a reader cannot mistake the weakest
run for the strongest.**

**Built, and it said plainly that one of the clerk's claims had gone stale** — other lanes had re-run all
three journeys, so the canonical paths already held live passes by the time it looked. **The mechanisms
were untouched by that**, which is why it built anyway rather than declaring the problem solved.

**The canonical path keeps its shape and stops being whoever ran last.** It now holds **the strongest run
on record** — live over fixture, passed over failed, **identified over unidentified** — backed by a
per-backend file and an append-only ledger, and **the slot is taken only by the same backend or by a
strictly higher rank.**

**It closed the third way the write could be skipped**, which nobody had named: the statistics fetch could
throw **past** the write. Now a provisional record is filed **before the browser opens**, and both
wrong-world guards still write before they re-throw.

**And it found backend identity a source that needs nobody's cooperation.** The health endpoint answers one
word on every world — **it confirmed the two standing on this machine were different checkouts satisfying
it identically**, and that every other version surface is absent or refuses. So the harness **asks whoever
holds the port what directory it runs from, and asks that checkout for its head.** That worked unaided on
another lane's live run, **which then correctly took the canonical slot from an unidentified record.**

**Proven by running the displacement twice:** a fixture re-run left a standing live pass byte-identical, and
**with the protection mutated away the identical command overwrote it.** And a live-labelled run against a
stub answering only the health word **passed the preflight exactly as predicted, was filed under its own
key with the stub's checkout named, and never touched the real artifact.**

**One deliberate non-change worth keeping:** it did not exclude live journeys from fixture mode, because
**that would drop three journeys other lanes count** — the per-backend key makes the re-run harmless
instead.

### Lane L-CONFIRM-CONAT-RETIRE — a co-located stranger cannot retire your code
state: built-unverified
class: suite

agent: confirm-conat-retire
evidence: OkamAPI 6771ba9a on lane/confirm-conat-retire (worktree /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-conatretire, local, not pushed) + lanes/L-CONFIRM-CONAT-RETIRE/evidence.md

The controller invalidates the outstanding code on **any** refusal — including one caused by **the shared
per-IP bucket that other accounts behind the same egress filled.** Its in-code rationale, that the code has
had every attempt it will get, is **only true for account-bucket refusals.**

Griefing rather than disclosure, and bounded — **the fix is nameable and small:** retire only when the
account's own bucket refused. A related cost to close in the same pass: request a new code and try it too
soon, and **the brand-new zero-guess code is retired** by the still-open window.

**Built — and it found a third defect that makes the briefed fix insufficient on its own.**

**The account guess bucket was charged before the shared one.** So even with the narrowing in place, a
stranger fills the shared bucket, **the victim's own ten attempts drain on refusals for which no guess was
ever evaluated**, and the eleventh refusal is an *account* refusal — **which retires the code anyway.**
Proved rather than argued: restoring the original ordering with the narrowing intact **reds both stranger
pins.**

So the refusal now reports **which** bucket refused, and **the shared bucket is consulted first — the
reverse of the send path**, and for a stated reason: there the per-address bucket belongs to **a victim who
is not the caller**, while here the account bucket belongs to the target and **must only be charged for
guesses actually evaluated.**

**It closed the second cost too**, with a single-claim retirement, so **the new code the refusal asks for is
no longer destroyed by the still-open window** — and the copy leads with the wait, since requesting a code
does not lift that window.

**And it corrected an assertion that was overstating.** A claim about the code space rested on retirement
firing the moment the budget runs out — **but retirement fires on a refusal, and an attacker who stops at
the cap never causes one**, so a code minted part way through a window could always meet twice the budget.
Now asserted at twice, with the reason.

**It also corrected a note in the wire suite that was simply wrong** about what else touches that route.

Its four mutations each red only their own pins, **and the claim mutation reds the wire fact too — so the
successor defect was reachable over the genuine pipeline.** Every pin fills a **named** bucket from a
**named** account and asserts **the code, not the status line.**

### Lane L-WF-ADJUSTMENT-ORDINAL — the adjustment window no index can close
state: open
class: sql
pts: 2
exit: two concurrent adjustments under different keys leave one succeeded batch, without refusing a delta the accountant is owed
agent: wf-adjustment-ordinal
needs: F-SQL-HEADROOM

**Named as an accepted residual by the lane that closed the full-export half, with its reasoning** — and
the reasoning is why this is a separate lane rather than an omission.

**No unique index can close it.** A delta may legitimately repeat an earlier one, so uniqueness on the
digest or on the superseded batch **would refuse a file the accountant is owed.** Its real invariant is
*differs from the last adjustment*, which needs an ordinal unique per store, period and provider — a
column, so a migration, into the chain this program has been stacking all day.

**Two landing conditions the money-path review added, 2026-08-02.** First, **claim MIG-26 in the
pending-migrations ledger before authoring** — four lanes claiming one migration number is a hazard this
estate has already hit, and the ledger as of this writing runs contiguously to MIG-25. Second, the chain this
column joins is **five migrations past the branch tip and not an ancestor of it**, so the ordinal's
migration must be authored on the stack, not on the tip.

The review also confirmed why no index closes the window and the ordinal does: uniqueness on the digest
or the superseded batch **refuses a delta the accountant is owed**, because a correction may legitimately
repeat an earlier one and several adjustments legitimately share one superseded full export. Computing
the next ordinal inside the transaction makes two concurrent adjustments compute the same value so the
database refuses one — and it serialises concurrent *distinct* adjustments too, which is desirable: it
forces a re-read against the newly committed last adjustment, which is the actual invariant.

not move; the pack reprinted them under a name that did not exist when they were written.

### Lane L-INVOICE-RETRY-RETIREMENT — a renderer outage stops retiring the invoices it could not mail
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: the bulk retry route is run twice against a failing renderer and the invoice it could not mail is still selected on the second run, shown by a test that reds when the pre-render stamp is restored
agent: invoice-retry-retirement
evidence: wt-invretire f18ffeda (fix+test) + receipt 1a0c0cbb, branch lane/invoice-retry-retirement off lane/pdf-nullderef (17198f14), local, not pushed - Services/InvoiceService.cs:89-102 - WebApi.Tests/Services/DocumentRendererFailureTests.cs - artifacts/tests/f18ffeda-fast-tier.trx + f18ffeda.../RUN.md

Found by the Fable review of the money-path pair, and it is **a regression the fix introduced**, not a
defect it inherited. `InvoiceService` selects unsent invoices by an empty send-address, stamps the
tracked entity with the store's address **before** attempting the render, skips on a render exception,
and then saves anyway. The skipped invoice leaves the filter **forever**, with a fire-and-forget chat
message as the only trace.

At base this could not happen: the null dereference killed the method before the save. Making the run
survive an outage is what let the stamp reach the database.

**The lane's own commit message states the principle it then violated**, about a different route:
*continuing would mail an empty report and then set the flag that stops a retry.* The send-address is
that flag for this route.

The named change, from the review: in the attach-failed branch, restore the send-address to its
pre-stamp value — or stamp only after a successful attach and feed the address to the model separately.
Then extend the outage test to run the retry **a second time** and assert the invoice is still selected.

The existing test passes today while the retirement happens, because it asserts the mail was skipped and
**never re-queries the row.** That narrow assertion set is what let this through.

Ruled `uninvolved-reservation-in-the-world`. **The exact defect shape this cluster exists to kill, reintroduced on the same day.** A reviewer walked a clamp mutant through **all nine tests and the browser journey — every one passes.**

The cause is structural, not careless: in every test where the release fires, the superseded reservation is the only other hold on the guard row. **The fix is to the fixture's world, not to the assertion** — which is why it recurs.

**Gated on `D-SPEC-L-MEALS-EIGHTH-READ`.** Returned `fail-spec` because the work it was sent at already existed; the
decision that settles how such a lane is closed is unruled. Without this `needs:` the scheduler
kept offering it at the head of the queue and the clerk held it by hand every cycle — **a hold that
lives in the clerk rather than in the plan is a hold the next clerk will not know about.**

**Ruled `re-scope-to-the-merge` on 2026-08-05.** **The exit below is superseded: the fixture gap it rests on is refuted and the pin already exists.** Re-scope onto the one hazard nothing else carries — **the re-quote release landing without the pin**, which leaves the fourth decrement site unaudited while the board reads as covered. The two residual flags this lane names cover actor parameters and SQL, not that.


**Re-scoped and measured 2026-08-05, and it refuted the clerk's own reopening condition.** That condition
said the hazard would be self-carrying if the pin were an ancestor of every branch bearing the re-quote
release. **It is not.** The clerk re-derived it independently: **seven branches carry the release and four
carry the pin**, and the three carrying release **without** pin are exactly the plan's landing and proof
candidates — including the one whose own name promises the merged state a full run.

**The one branch that carries release, pin and SQL twin together is no drop-in**, because it also adds its own
production retry change. **And the SQL twin does not cover the gap either**: it is trait-gated to SQL Server,
so it never runs in the container-free tier at all.

**The hazard was demonstrated rather than argued.** A trial merge — local only, zero conflicts — brings
release and pin together in one commit. The same clamp then behaves three ways: clean, **red on four**, and
**with the pre-pin fixture and the identical clamp, green on nine and invisible.** That third run *is* the
hazard.

**And a correction worth carrying to whoever merges Meals:** the release the tip already has is the
**explicit owner release**, not the re-quote's. The re-quote adds a **fourth entry point and a third SQL
statement** that bypasses the authority entirely — which is why the actor lane's required parameters cannot
reach it.

**The recommendation is a predicate rather than a paragraph:** gate the Meals merge on the pin being an
ancestor of the merge commit. Landing that one commit satisfies it in a single conflict-free, tier-green
merge — the first full container-free tier on a tree carrying both today's tip and the release.

**Stated as not measured rather than substituted for:** no SQL tier, no slot taken, no container started; and
no browser walk, so nothing here meets C5.

**One ops residue confirmed again:** a full tier run rewrites two tracked journey artifacts with the day's
date, so any `add -A` afterwards sweeps that churn. Restored by explicit pathspec.

**Both walks landed 2026-08-03, and the freeze walk does the thing this estate keeps failing to do: it

The honest difficulty was reaching a control the product intends to remove. It used **a second page in the
same browser context** to finalise the week, leaving the first tab holding a stale model with its editor
still drawn — because **a request forged from the spec would prove the fixture holds a rule, not that the
product enforces one.** Then the same page, the same button: refused, the server's own sentence quoted

withhold.

two names with nothing behind it, so the admin screen could be opened and nothing driven. Nine routes added,
verified route-for-route against the real controller.

thread and has no schema behind it. Needs the migration author slot.

### Lane L-EV-OUTBOX-GUID-SUBSTRING — a guest-data assertion matches inside a random identifier
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 1
exit: the outbox guest-data assertion cannot match a substring of a generated identifier, shown by a test that reds when the identifier-aware form is reverted and passes across repeated runs with seeded identifiers that contain the digits
agent: ev-outbox-guid
evidence: OkamAPI-modules lane/ev-outbox-guid-substring 79f9dd7d (worktree /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-evoutboxguid, off feature/restaurant-modules 3579bbbc, local, unpushed); after 4383/0/12 vs base 4369/0/12 measured myself, filter "Database!=SqlServer", no container started; .lane/base-3579bbbc.trx, .lane/after-lane.trx, .lane/repeat-runs.txt, .lane/L-EV-OUTBOX-GUID-SUBSTRING-detail.md

Found by the lane that merged the migration stack, which **proved it pre-existing rather than blaming its
own merge**: the file is byte-identical to the integration branch and the suite is green on re-run against
the same binary.

The assertion checks that a delivered message carries no other guest data by looking for a bare digit
string in the body. **It matched inside a randomly generated identifier in the proposal link** — not a
leaked amount. It fires roughly once in a hundred and thirty runs.

**It will keep failing merges**, and each time it will be attributed to whoever happened to be merging.
That is what makes it worth its own lane rather than a note: a red that is never about the change under
test teaches the next agent that one failure is normal, and a suite where one failure is normal has
stopped reporting.

**Closed 2026-08-03, and it measured the rate rather than repeating mine.** I briefed one in a hundred and
thirty. A probe over **two hundred thousand real bodies composed through the production delivery path**
gives **1,012 hits — one in 197.6**, and the arithmetic agrees: twenty-two three-character windows in a
formatted identifier at one in four thousand and ninety-six, plus seventeen four-character windows, is one
in a hundred and seventy-seven. **Still a merge-reddener, about one and a half times rarer than stated.**

**The fix does not weaken the assertion**, which was the risk. The expected token is masked **by exact
value** and the checks run over the remainder — so an amount elsewhere in the body **or elsewhere in the
same URL** still fails, because the whole link is deliberately not cut out. A stray-identifier guard makes
any *second* identifier-shaped run a failure, so a future second token cannot silently reopen the hole.

Three pins hold it: the amounts are now **derived from the seeded proposal's own values** instead of
spelled as literals — a changed fixture used to leave the check hunting for digits no leak could produce; a
negative control asserts the check still throws for each refused value planted outside the token; and the
mutation that deletes the amount checks proves that control fires.

**Proof deterministic rather than lucky:** tokens drawn to contain the digits in each identifier segment.
Reverting the mask reds all six seeded cases. The same two-hundred-thousand-body sweep against the fixed
assertion: **zero failures against 1,012.** The class run forty times consecutively, forty green.

**And it swept for the shape rather than only fixing the instance** — five other bare-digit absence checks
exist; all scan a list by equality or a fixed string, and **none can match inside an identifier.** This was
the only one.

### Lane L-BLOCKER-RESTATE — every open blocker is re-measured against the tip before another lane is sent at one
state: verified
class: analysis
pts: 1
exit: each open blocker flag is recorded as still-true, already-fixed, or partly-true-with-the-false-clause-named, each verdict citing the commit or the code that settles it, merged from a RETURN, recorded in lanes/L-BLOCKER-RESTATE/verdicts.md
agent: blocker-restate
evidence: lanes/L-BLOCKER-RESTATE/verdicts.md

**Four blockers today described defects that no longer existed**, and each cost a whole lane to discover.
One had been fixed **two days before the ruling that dispatched an agent at it.** One had the answer **in
its own body**, in a sentence read past every time the rest of it was quoted.

The lane that found the fourth named the mechanism, and it is exact: **the flags are being ruled on faster
than they are being re-measured.** Sixty-two items went to the owner in one sitting without a re-measure
first — that is the clerk's error, not the owner's.

**A stale blocker is not a harmless leftover.** It consumes a lane, it makes the queue look longer than it
is, and worst, it teaches whoever reads the board that some of these are not real — which is exactly the
habit that lets a live one sit.

This lane reads rather than builds. **Its verdict per flag must cite something** — a commit, a line, a
measured absence — because a re-measure that says *still true* on the clerk's word is the failure it
exists to remove.

Note the pattern the four share: **three of the four were partly true.** The defect was fixed and a
neighbouring clause of the same flag still held. So *cleared* and *open* are both wrong answers for that
shape; the third verdict is the useful one.

### Lane L-EXIT-INSTRUMENT-SWEEP — every unverifiable exit is either given an instrument or recorded as unverifiable
state: verified
class: analysis
pts: 1
exit: each built-unverified lane whose exit names no instrument is listed with the instrument it should name, or with the reason no instrument can exist, recorded at `lanes/L-EXIT-INSTRUMENT-SWEEP/map.md`
agent: exit-instrument-sweep
evidence: lanes/L-EXIT-INSTRUMENT-SWEEP/map.md

**Measured 2026-08-03: eighty-eight lanes sit at `built-unverified` with an exit that names no path and no
fact.** Under the standard, **nothing can ever verify them** — they are not waiting on evidence, they are
waiting on a sentence that could accept evidence.

This is the residue the evidence sweep found and could not fix: it produced the map for the ones whose
evidence exists, and this is the larger half where **the exit itself is the obstacle.**

**The instruction that makes this lane worth running rather than a rewrite exercise:** for each one, say
what instrument the exit *should* name — a fact key, an artifact path, a named journey — **or say plainly
that no instrument can exist for it**, which is itself a finding and probably means the lane was never
scoped to be provable.

**It must not invent an instrument that does not exist.** An exit naming an artifact nobody will produce is
worse than an exit naming none, because it reads as satisfiable. A sibling lane found that seven of eleven
prescribed paths **live in worktrees and die with them** — verifying against those buys a green that
evaporates.

And it must not touch the plan: it produces the map, the orchestrator makes the edits, and the edits are
made by rebuilding the file rather than splicing it — a batch edit spliced by offset deleted twenty-two
lane blocks this evening.

### Lane L-ROLLBACK-TRACKED-SWEEP — no guard throws after mutating a tracked entity
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a sweep names every site where a guard throws after mutating a tracked entity, each site either stages the write after the decision or is pinned as safe, shown by a test that reds when a throw is moved back after a mutation, recorded in /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-rbtracked/lanes/L-ROLLBACK-TRACKED-SWEEP/evidence.md
agent: l-rollback-tracked-sweep
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-rbtracked/lanes/L-ROLLBACK-TRACKED-SWEEP/evidence.md

**A defect class, not a site.** Found when a coherence guard threw **after** setting a reservation
released: the database rolled back correctly, **the scoped context kept tracking the mutation**, and the
next operation on that scope answered *already released* for a row the database still held as bound.

**A refusal that works and a rollback that works together produce a lie, and neither half is wrong on its
own.** One site was fixed by staging the write before the mutation. **Nothing sweeps for the shape**, and
every module has guards that throw.

**Built 2026-08-03, and the shape was present at three sites nobody had looked at — one of them a VAT
hazard.** A goods-group guard checking whether a tax profile is retired **ran after the entity was
written**: if it refuses, a taxable sale journals at zero VAT. A table-settings guard ran after the row was
mutated **and after a range removal had already marked child rows deleted.** A giftcard guard wrote the
payment type before checking capture and validity, **inside a payment callback whose scope goes on to
complete other giftcards.** All three now stage the guard first.

**The idea that made the sweep work is the ordering test:** a mutation precedes a throw **only when its
chain of enclosing blocks is a prefix of the throw's.** Same block or enclosing block is ordered; siblings
are not. That cut seventy-seven naive hits to fourteen — and, more importantly, **it is what stops the sweep
flagging the estate's own correct idiom**, where the guard is a sibling callback that runs ahead of the work.
**A sweep that flagged that would be refusing the fix it exists to ask for.**

**It named its own largest blind spot, and it is the shape that caused the flag:** a guard throwing from
inside a helper is interprocedural and invisible to this sweep — and the original coherence guard is exactly
that. One of the three defects was found **by hand, not by the sweep.** Its own words: this raises a floor,
never a ceiling.

**Nine remaining findings are pinned with the argument *and* what would invalidate it, so a stale entry
fails** — the list cannot rot into a silencer.

**Two smaller things worth keeping.** It found a detector bug in an existing control: a filtered catch clause
has nested parentheses, so a naive matcher **mis-classifies save-failure rethrows as ordinary guards.** And
it noted the staleness trap does not apply here, because the sweep reads source at runtime — **a stale test
binary cannot manufacture a false green** — yet it checked the assemblies anyway rather than reasoning that
it did not need to.

**The Meals funding interface is untouched**, so the collision is unaffected and no side is picked; when that
lane lands, its site is **already staged guard-first** and will not appear in this sweep.

### Lane L-EF-INDEX-SHADOW-SWEEP — no index configuration silently replaces its neighbour
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 1
exit: a check names every entity configuration that adds an index by columns alone where another index on those columns exists, and reds when one is reintroduced
agent: l-ef-index-shadow-sweep
evidence: OkamAPI lane/ef-index-shadow-sweep @ 08309e39, off integration/mig-stack-land 4b37f81b; WebApi.Tests/Modules/IndexConfigurationSweep.cs + ModelIndexShadowSweepTests.cs + ModelIndexShadowGuardSelfTests.cs; lanes/L-EF-INDEX-SHADOW-SWEEP/evidence.md; fast tier 4450/0/10

**Found only by running, and the failure it would have shipped has no red anywhere.** The mapper keys an
unnamed index **by its columns**, so adding a second index on a column that already carries one
**reconfigures the existing index rather than adding one.**

The consequence measured: **every roster read quietly loses its index, while the new constraint still works
and every test still passes.** A performance defect produced by a one-word omission, invisible to the
suite. One migration lane found it by accident; nothing looks for it.

**Built 2026-08-03, and it closed the census rather than sampling it.** It runs the real model configuration
through subclassed builders and counts configuration **calls**, grouping them by the mapper's own identity
rule. **199 calls, 198 non-convention indexes, zero unaccounted — and the one-index deficit *is* the one
live replacement.** A sweep whose arithmetic closes cannot be quietly incomplete.

**Its blind spots announce themselves** rather than being listed: three configuration routes are not
intercepted, so the model's own index set is re-derived and **every entry must match a recorded call** — an
un-intercepted route shows up as an unaccounted index, not as silence.

**And it asserted its own premise instead of assuming it:** a self-test pins that two unnamed calls collapse
to one index, so **if the mapper ever changes that behaviour the rule fails loudly rather than
over-reporting forever.**

**The parked finding is self-invalidating** — keyed by slot *and* claim count, so it fails the day it is
fixed and fails again if a third configuration joins the slot. A rule sitting red for a known reason cannot
mask a new arrival.

**One trap it found and closed:** the framework caches a model per context type, so **every synthetic probe
after the first would have silently examined the first probe's model and reported no collisions** — a
sweep that passes because it is looking at the wrong object.

**Base chosen by measurement:** the merged stack strictly contains the integration tip and carries **eighteen
more index configurations**; sweeping the older tip would have been blind to all of them.

### Lane L-CENSUS-FLOORS-DERIVED — the actor census computes its floors instead of carrying them
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 1
exit: the module actor census derives its coverage counts from the assembly rather than storing them, so a merge cannot leave a floor asserting a number the tree no longer has
agent: l-census-floors-derived
evidence: OkamAPI worktree /Users/svendaneel/okam/OkamAPI-censusfloors, branch lane/census-floors-derived @ 75dcc2ff, base feature/restaurant-modules @ 3579bbbc

**Three lanes edit that file, not the two first recorded** — one adds a pin, one a known-file entry and an
integer, one raises a module floor. The files **merge cleanly by region**, so git never objects.

**What a clean merge silently invalidates is the floors** — the stored counts that make the census assert

### Decision D-WF-CORRECTION-FLAG — whether the personalliste correction answers to a stage flag
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-WF-STATUTORY-LAND
options:
| ungated — pro: bokforingsforskriften § 8-5-6 makes recording a rettelse part of keeping the register, so a lever that switches it off is a lever that switches off compliance ; con: it becomes the only Workforce write answering to no stage flag, so "every write has a lever" stops being true and the census carries a permanent exemption
| own-flag — pro: restores the invariant that every write has a lever, and a venue not yet keeping the register digitally can keep the surface dark ; con: a dark flag on a statutory correction path puts a venue out of compliance silently, and it needs a catalog change plus an extension to WorkforceFlagCensus.Mutations
| reuse-clock — pro: no catalog change, no census extension, ships as it stands ; con: the lane measured this as wrong, because pausing the till clock is exactly when yesterday's window most needs correcting, so the lever would darken the path precisely when it is needed
default_if_unruled: none
reopen_when: a legal reading holds that a venue may lawfully keep the register on paper while clocking digitally in this product
ruled: ungated 2026-08-05 by @sven

**Raised by `L-WF-CORRECTION-PATH`, which built the write and then declined to choose its lever.**
The correction is behind **no** stage flag today. `WorkforceFeatureFlags.Withheld` records why, which keeps
`WorkforceFlagConsumptionTests`' "the two withheld keys gate nothing" true with no catalog change.

This is a Sven call because the two failure modes are not symmetric and neither is a code question. An
ungated write means one Workforce surface permanently outside the flag model. A gated one means a
configuration exists in which a venue silently stops keeping a register the law says it must keep.

If the ruling is `own-flag`, the honest execution is **both** halves — un-withhold the flag *and* extend
`WorkforceFlagCensus.Mutations`. This estate has counted eleven advertised-but-ungating flags; adding a
twelfth while ruling against them would be worse than leaving it ungated.


**Fable recommends `ungated`, and the built state already encodes the ruling with its legal argument at the
site.** The flag file withholds the personnel-list flag **precisely because § 8-5-6 makes recording a
rettelse part of keeping the register** — a flag that paused corrections *"would leave a venue holding a
register it knows is wrong and may not fix."*

**`own-flag` manufactures a configuration in which a venue silently stops keeping a statutory register.** The
census law survives because withheld-with-a-reason is the estate's established mechanism, with a Training
precedent and a probe already showing the route refuses on the module master only. **And the honest scope of
"every write has a lever" is preserved:** the module flag still fences it.

### Lane L-JOURNEY-PROXY-BLINDSPOT — a subject fetched through the same-origin proxy stops reading as zero

agent: opus

**Found by the Fable review of `L-LIVE-ASSERTION-FLOORS`, which approved the new guards and then named
the one shape they cannot see.**

`nuxt.config.js:138` mounts `server-middleware/okam-api-proxy.js`. A client built with
`API_BASE_URL=/okam-api` fetches its subject **same-origin** — and the recorder excludes same-origin
traffic (`origin !== this._appOrigin`). So a run that signs in at the named backend and then fetches its
whole subject through the proxy files `backendSubjectServed: 0, foreignSubjectServed: 0`: the judge stays
silent, every floor is green, and the artifact names a backend that answered **only the door**.

That is the same defect class the lane was built to kill, one layer down — a guard that cannot fail
because the world it measures never reaches it.

The reviewer named the change: count subject-shaped `xhr`/`fetch` whose origin is `_appOrigin` and whose
path begins `/okam-api/` into their own counter, file it in the artifact, red when
`subjectFromBackend == 0` while that counter is positive, and add a guard-proof arm for it. **Scope to
the `/okam-api/` prefix** so Nuxt dev-server fetches do not false-red.

### Lane L-WF-IDEMPOTENCY-REFUSAL — a refused write stops poisoning its own key
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a refused correction replays its refusal on a same-key retry rather than answering idempotency-in-progress, pinned by a test that reds if the refusal stops being recorded as a completion
agent: opus
evidence: backend OkamAPI lane/wf-idempotency-refusal @ a1d57208, worktree ~/okam/OkamAPI-wfidemref, based on feature/restaurant-modules @ 9888178f, NOT pushed - container-free tier (dotnet test --filter "Database!=SqlServer") 4402/0/12 vs a 4394/0/12 baseline measured in the same worktree at a clean 9888178f, delta +8 = WebApi.Tests/Workforce/WorkforceIdempotencyTests.cs (6) and WebApi.Tests/Workforce/WorkforceShiftExchangeTests.cs (2)

**Found by the Fable review of `L-WF-BLIND-BIND-NAME`, which ruled the ordering itself correct and then
named its permanent cost.**

`ReserveAsync` commits its own row before the domain refusals run. So a **refused** correction — opaque
404, or 409 moved — leaves a `Reserved` row with no completion, and **a later retry with that key
answers `workforce.idempotency-in-progress` forever**: `ExpiresAtUtc` is advisory only, with no purge
and no reuse-after-expiry.

**The wire is dishonest in exactly that case.** The problem claims the write is still running, with
`retryable: true` and no fresh-key hint — but for a stuck key, same-key retry is futile permanently.
And `retryWithFreshKey` cannot simply be added, because for a genuinely in-flight duplicate a fresh key
would execute the write twice.

The only honest fix is structural: extend the idempotency outcome payload with an outcome-kind
discriminator so a refusal is recorded as a completion and **replays its refusal**. That fixes the
sibling endpoint's race backstop by the same change.

Today's mitigation is that the shipped client mints a fresh key per call, so no user is stuck. That is
a property of one caller, not of the endpoint.

### Lane L-WF-OPERATOR-UNIQUE — one operator cannot hold two live links
state: verified
class: sql
pts: 3
exit: two concurrent imports of one operator leave exactly one live link, refused at the database rather than by a pre-commit read, shown on the SQL tier with an assertion from the system catalogs that the chain built the index, recorded in /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-wfopuniq/lanes/L-WF-OPERATOR-UNIQUE/evidence.md
needs: D-INTEGRATION-FASTFORWARD
agent: wf-operator-unique
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-wfopuniq/lanes/L-WF-OPERATOR-UNIQUE/evidence.md

**Found by the Fable review of `L-WF-BLIND-BIND-NAME`. Pre-existing, and it is a money path: the link
decides whose pay a punch becomes.**

There is **no unique index on `(StoreId, OperatorId)` in either the model or the chain**, and the
resolver picks with `FirstOrDefaultAsync`. Two concurrent imports of the same operator under different
idempotency keys can commit **two live links** — two *new* persons defeat the D1 active-engagement
backstop, because that index is on `(WorkforcePersonId, LegalEmployerId)`, not on the operator. The
till then pays an arbitrary one of them, and the candidates read's `GroupBy(...).First()` would mask it.

**This is a migration, so it holds the single migration-author slot** — a filtered unique index
`(StoreId, OperatorId) WHERE OperatorId IS NOT NULL AND IsActive = 1`, or the dedicated link table the
blind-bind lane's own detail already specifies.

The exit demands the catalog assertion because this estate has shipped the mirror defect twice: an
index in `OnModelCreating` and in no migration is a constraint production does not have.



**Built 2026-08-06, and the base the clerk flagged as wrong was deliberate — the lane held it and was
right.** The integration tip's migrations are a **strict prefix** of the stack's; the clerk verified it
independently, with **zero tip files absent from the stack**. So the stack tip **is** the post-merge chain
tip, and parenting on the integration tip would have forked this migration **plus the stack's own nine onto
one parent** — the exact collision the constraint exists to prevent. **No re-parenting is owed** unless the
merge lane drops or renames one specific migration.

**And it avoided snapshot contention with the sibling by hand-authoring rather than generating**, so the
model snapshot is untouched and the new designer's target model is **byte-identical to its parent's**,
verified programmatically. Two lanes held SQL slots at once and neither wrote the other's file.

**The defect it closed decides whose pay a till punch becomes**, and had no unique index in the model **or**
the chain.

**Two findings beyond the brief, and the second is the honest kind.** A service change turned out to be
**required rather than optional**: without it the losing racer got a raw database exception — **a 500 on a
routine double-tap** — so the refusal is now a typed conflict.

**Its own first mutant was equivalent by accident and it said so rather than crediting it.** Renaming the
index to a longer name that **contains** the original meant every substring check still matched, so only the
catalogue reddened. Re-run with a genuinely different name it reds three arms. **A second mutant is
behaviourally equivalent and is labelled as such rather than counted.**

**The catalogue assertion is built from the chain replayed from empty**, with the mirror on the same
container showing a **model-built database does not have the index** — which is the third time this estate
has needed exactly that comparison. And **the refusal is asserted to come from the database rather than the
pre-check**, because those two outcomes are distinguishable and **a row count alone would pass either way.**

**Found by `L-EV-FAMILY-LAND` while checking the double-landed-CORS hazard — and what it found was the

The estate has been carrying "did the named CORS policy land twice?" as a merge hazard. It did not land
**at all**. For Events this is harmless — the guest client sends no credentials — which is exactly why
