**The Growth preference centre is credentialed, and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` cannot serve a
credentialed request.** A browser refuses the response; the surface does not fail loudly at the server,
it fails in the client of a person trying to change their own consent.

This is also where the correction already recorded in this plan bites: **the same *site* is not the same
*origin*.** A false "or" was written here once and withdrawn — the named policy is required under
**either** reading of the host ruling, not only one of them.

Verify before building: the integration tip moved to `9888178f` and one CORS-bearing branch is unmerged.
If the policy has landed by the time this runs, return `fail-spec` naming the commit.


### Flag F-SHARED-REF-CLOBBER — two landers moved the integration ref and one merge was discarded
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: every lane that moves feature/restaurant-modules does so with update-ref and an old-value guard, and no reflog entry on that ref reads `Reset to`
cleared_by: L-MEALS-POSREL-LAND

**This fired for real, between two of this plan's own merge lanes.** `L-MEALS-POSREL-LAND` moved the
integration ref to `d776f9e7` with a guarded `git update-ref <new> <old>`. Seconds later a sibling
lander overwrote it with `9888178f` — the reflog records `branch: Reset to 9888178f` — **discarding a
merge without merging it.**

Nothing was lost, because the lander held its work on a local branch, re-merged onto the new base,
re-measured from scratch and moved the ref guarded again. Verified independently: `d776f9e7`'s successor
`b9c95082`, `21f79514`, `5c3a9be1` and `9888178f` are all ancestors of the tip, and the six exit files
of three merge lanes are present on it.

**The rule, and it belongs in every merge brief: move the shared ref with `git update-ref <ref> <new>
<old>`. Never `git branch -f`, never a reset.** The guard is what turns a silent clobber into a
refusal. A lander that cannot move the ref should say so and stop, not force it.

Parallel merge lanes are the right shape — this is not an argument for serialising them. It is an
argument for the one primitive that makes them safe.

### Flag F-MERGE-BREAKS-BUILD — a clean merge of two green lanes did not compile
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: every merge lane's receipt records that it built the merge commit before running any tier, so a non-compiling merge is reported rather than measured
cleared_by: L-MEALS-POSREL-LAND

**The seventh merge hazard, and the first one found by a lane rather than predicted.** Git merged
`lane/meals-pos-tender-wire` and `lane/meals-release` with **zero conflicts**, and the result did not
compile: `CS0535` at `WebApi.Tests/Meals/MealsPoisonedModuleGraph.cs`.

The release lane introduced a **new test double** against a four-member interface. The pos-tender lane
added a **fifth member** to that interface, against a graph that had no such double. **Textually
disjoint. Both green alone. Neither lane could see it, and no conflict count would have caught it.**

The six hazards this plan already carries are all *semantic* collisions in code that merges and builds.
This one is different in kind: **the merge does not compile at all**, so a lane that runs its tier with
`--no-build`, or that inherits a per-lane green instead of re-running at the merge commit, reports a
green that was never produced.

Both existing merge-brief rules are what caught it — re-run the tier **at the merge commit**, and never
`--no-build`. This flag exists so the rule is carried as a finding rather than as a habit.

The fix belonged in the test double only, with the same body as its four siblings; no production file
was touched. That is the right shape for this hazard: an interface gained a member, so every double of
it owes one.


### Lane L-PHONE-IN-PATH — a phone number stops travelling in the URL
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: neither the giftcard transfer nor the store phone-number route carries a phone number in its path, pinned by a route-shape test that reds if a personal identifier is reintroduced into a path template, and the stale finding in ../OkamAPI-modules/artifacts/security/L-VIPPS-LOG-mutation.md is closed against the commit that closed it
agent: opus
evidence: ../OkamAPI-modules/artifacts/security/L-VIPPS-LOG-mutation.md

**Unclaimed until now. This plan had no record of it** — found by re-reading a security artifact a merge
lane flagged as stale, and verified live at the integration tip before authoring:

```
Controllers/GiftcardController.cs:232   [HttpPost("transfer/{giftcardId}/{newReceiverPhoneNumber}")]
Controllers/StoresController.cs:918     [HttpPut("{storeId}/phonenumber/{phoneNumber}")]
```

**A URL is not a sink you can redact.** The security lane's own wording is the argument: the telemetry
initializer keeps these out of Application Insights, but a URL is seen by every intermediary, every
reverse proxy and every access log on the way — **redaction at one sink is not a fix for a personal
identifier in a path.** C7's `holds_because` is the same reasoning one layer up: the estate has twice
paid for a credential reaching a log sink, and both times the rotation cost more than the code fix.

Move the identifier into the request body. Both routes are writes, so neither needs it in the path.

**Second item, same artifact, and it is the reason this was found.** That file still lists
`Helpers/ApplicationInsightsLoggingMiddleware` as an **OPEN** finding. It is not open —
`L-AI-MIDDLEWARE-DELETE` landed with the composition-root family and **no file by that name exists
anywhere at the tip**, which I verified rather than inferred. Close it against the commit that closed it.

**A security artifact that reports a shut hazard as open is not harmless.** It is the RF-1313 shape
inverted: the estate has already shipped a document asserting a control that does not exist, and a
document asserting a danger that no longer exists spends the next audit's attention on nothing and
teaches its readers to discount it.


### Decision D-WF-LINEAGE-PRODUCIBLE — whether a corrected personalliste entry shows what was corrected
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-WF-STATUTORY-LAND
options:
| screen-only — pro: an inspector who asks can be shown the superseded row on screen without changing what the paper register is ; con: the paper sheet remains half a document, and an inspection that starts from paper never learns a correction had a before
| screen-and-paper — pro: the printed register carries its own lineage, so the document is complete in the medium an inspector actually asks for ; con: a sheet with struck-through history is longer and harder to read, and no one has asked for it
| leave-as-is — pro: the letter of § 8-5-6 is already met, who and when are both recorded and rendered ; con: C6 asks whether the document can be produced, not whether the field exists, and the before-value is producible only from the database
default_if_unruled: none
reopen_when: Skatteetaten guidance or an actual kontroll requires the superseded values on the printed register itself
ruled: screen-only 2026-08-05 by @sven

**Raised by the Fable review of `L-WF-CORRECTION-PATH`, which ruled the statutory claim backed and then
named what is still missing from the document.**

The correction records **who** and **when**, and both render on screen and on the printed sheet as
*"Rettet av {actor} {date} {time}"*. The original row is retained and cannot be altered — verified in
two real layers, an EF guard and an AFTER UPDATE, DELETE trigger that throws 50017, both present in the
migration chain rather than merely claimed.

**But `BuildAsync` filters superseded rows out and no endpoint resolves `SupersedesEntryId`.** So the
sheet says a correction happened and by whom, and cannot say **what it changed**. The letter of § 8-5-6
is met. C6's standard is producibility, and by that standard this is half a document.

A second, smaller question rides along and is worth ruling in the same breath: **"hvem" prints as an
opaque Guid.** It is resolvable through the roster read, so it is producible in-product — but an
inspector reading paper sees a reference, not a person. Resolving it to a display name at render is a
join, not a register change.


**Fable recommends `screen-only`, and rules a rider in the same breath: resolve the actor to a display name at
render.** The register build filters superseded rows, and rows carry the supersession and actor references
**with nothing resolving either** — so the before-value is producible only from the database, **which fails
C6's standard even though § 8-5-6's letter is met.**

**Producibility is C6's test, not default printing.** An inspector reading *"Rettet av …"* on paper can ask,
and the product must then be able to produce the superseded row; printing it by default lengthens a statutory
sheet in a form **no inspector has asked for.** The name resolution is a join at render, not a register
change, and should not wait for a second decision cycle.

### Lane L-WF-CORRECTION-PINS — the correction's own refusal cannot be defeated, and its audit stops lying
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: the rowversion allowlist entries name whole methods rather than fragments, the stale-revision frontend test reds if the client resolves, the flag census probes the correction route, and a correction that moved neither time stops auditing a field it did not change, recorded in lanes/L-WF-CORRECTION-PINS/mutation-log.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-WF-CORRECTION-PINS/mutation-log.md

**Four conditions from the Fable review of `L-WF-CORRECTION-PATH`. None is large; two are the kind that
quietly turn a guard into a formality.**

1. **The allowlist is not narrow enough.** The two `Allowed` entries match by `Contains` on the
   fragments `already_superseded` / `already_replaced` across whole files, and the module's one wire
   suite is still growing. A future test named `An_award_already_replaced_...` asserting a **genuine**
   rowversion refusal would shelter under them silently. Widen both to the full method names — still
   within the file's own convention, strictly narrower.
2. **A frontend test that can assert nothing.** The stale-revision test asserts only inside a bare
   `.catch()`. If the client ever resolves on 409, **zero assertions run and it stays green.** The same
   file's 403 test already guards with `rejects.toMatchObject` first; do the same here.
3. **The census does not probe the route the withheld text names.** `WorkforceFlagCensus.Mutations`
   never exercises the correction, so "the two withheld keys gate nothing" is **unmeasured** for
   precisely the write that decision is about. Expected refusals: the module master only.
4. **An audit record that states something false.** `ChangedFields` reports `adjustedField: "onSiteEnd"`
   for a correction that moved neither time. The allowlist constrains keys, not values, so nothing
   catches it. Return `none` or `reaffirmed` in that branch.

Also fold in the backend zone coercion the review named as should-fix: the `Z`/offset refusal lives only
in the frontend client, so **a third-party caller sending `07:00:00Z` is silently reinterpreted as venue
wall clock**. That matches estate convention elsewhere, but this is a statutory register write. Refuse a
non-Unspecified `Kind` at the controller.

### Lane L-WF-CORRECTION-UNIQUE — two concurrent corrections cannot both append
state: open
class: sql
pts: 3
exit: two concurrent corrections of one entry leave exactly one superseding row, refused at the database rather than by a pre-commit read, shown on the SQL tier with an assertion from the system catalogs that the chain built the index
needs: L-WF-OPERATOR-UNIQUE, D-INTEGRATION-FASTFORWARD

**The one place the correction's own refusal can still be defeated — named by the Fable review that
otherwise approved it.**

The supersession check is **check-then-insert with no rowversion and no unique constraint**:
`SupersedesEntryId` carries **no index of any kind** in the migration. Two concurrent corrections of the
same entry under different Idempotency-Keys both pass the check and both append. The result is **two
live rows for one window** — exactly the self-contradicting register the `StaleRevision` refusal claims
cannot exist.

The same window exists between a manager correction and a concurrent clock-out closing the same open
entry, which is not an exotic race on a till.

Unique filtered index on `(StoreId, SupersedesEntryId) WHERE SupersedesEntryId IS NOT NULL`, in
`OnModelCreating` **and** the migration, and translate the unique violation into the same
`WorkforceErrorCodes.StaleRevision` the pre-commit read returns.

**This holds the single migration-author slot**, so it queues behind `L-WF-OPERATOR-UNIQUE`. The lane's
own claim that no migration was needed was true for what it built; the concurrency fix is where schema
becomes owed.

**One test must be retired by this lane, not worked around.** `L-WF-LINK-DEADEND` seeds a second live
link for its tie-break test. That state is reachable **today** precisely because this index does not
exist — two concurrent imports both pass the pre-check. Once the index lands the state becomes
impossible, and the test will start failing at its own seed. **Retire it with the index.** A test kept
alive by working around the constraint it was written to survive is worse than no test: it teaches the
next author that the constraint is optional. The lane recorded this in the test's own doc comment.

The exit demands the catalog assertion because this estate has shipped the mirror defect: an index in
`OnModelCreating` and in no migration is a constraint production does not have.


### Flag F-CORS-ORIGINS-BY-INDEX — the allowed-origin list is overridden by position, not by value
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: the deployed configuration is shown to carry the production origins with no localhost entry, measured on the resolved options object rather than on a settings file
cleared_by: L-CORS-CREDENTIALED-ORIGIN

**Named by `L-CORS-CREDENTIALED-ORIGIN` as residue, and it is the kind of configuration defect that reads
as correct in every file you would open.**

**.NET configuration overrides arrays by index.** So in Development the base entry `https://www.okam.no`
is not extended by the environment file — it is **shadowed** by `http://localhost:3000` at position 0.

The consequence to hold on to: **"www is listed in appsettings.json" does not mean "www is allowed in
dev".** Anyone reading the base file to answer "which origins are permitted" gets the wrong answer, and
the file they read is not wrong — the merge rule is.

The other direction is the one that matters at go-live: **production must never inherit the localhost
origins.** A credentialed surface whose allow-list contains `http://localhost:3000` in production is a
credentialed surface trusting anything on the operator's machine.

Harmless today because the surface is not deployed. The clear condition is deliberately written against
the **resolved options object**, not against a settings file, because reading the file is exactly the
mistake this flag records.


### Lane L-GROWTH-AUDIT-INDEX — the growth audit indexes exist in production, not only in the model
state: open
class: sql
pts: 3
exit: the two GrowthAuditEvents indexes are created by the migration chain, shown on the SQL tier with an assertion from the system catalogs that the chain built them, and the append-only guard's second layer is present on SQL Server
needs: L-WF-OPERATOR-UNIQUE, D-INTEGRATION-FASTFORWARD

**Carried in by the growth family merge, which flagged it rather than closing it — correctly, since it
held no migration slot. This is the dangerous direction of model/chain divergence.**

`ApplicationDbContext` now gains two `HasIndex` calls for `GrowthAuditEvents` with **no migration
creating them**. Recorded upstream as MIG-22.

**This is the `AccountingSummaries` shape exactly**, and that one is a live production defect: an index
declared in `OnModelCreating` exists in every model-built test database and **in no deployed schema**, so
the tier is green against a constraint production does not have. A reviewer this week contrasted the two
directions deliberately — chain-only means production is *stricter* than the fast tier and fails loudly;
model-only means **production is missing a constraint the tests believe in**, and fails silently.

`GuardAppendOnly` also records that its **second layer is absent on SQL Server** for this table. So
today the growth dispatch attribution is enforced on SQLite and **nowhere on SQL Server** — which is to
say, enforced in the tier that runs and not in the one that ships.

**Holds the single migration-author slot**, so it queues behind `L-WF-OPERATOR-UNIQUE`.

The exit demands the catalog assertion rather than a passing test, because a model-built test database
cannot distinguish "the chain built this" from "the model did".

### Flag F-CORS-EXPOSURE-REVERT — landing the CORS lane silently narrows the download headers
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: the merged AddOkamCors default policy exposes BrowserReadableHeaders.All, asserted by the download header wire tests at the integration tip
cleared_by: L-CORS-CREDENTIALED-ORIGIN

**A collision that did not exist when the CORS lane was cut. Found by the integration-branch audit
reading both sides at the tip.**

`2a052800` moves the inline `AddCors` block into an `AddOkamCors` extension — and that extension
**hardcodes `WithExposedHeaders("ETag")`**. Since that commit was written, the pdf family changed the
same line at the tip to `BrowserReadableHeaders.All`.

So landing `lane/cors-credentialed-origin` produces a modify/delete conflict on `Program.cs`, and
**resolving it to the extension as written silently reverts the download exposure** — the browser stops
seeing the headers the download work exists to expose.

**The tier would catch it** — `DownloadHeaderWireTests` asserts response headers — which is exactly why
it is worth naming now rather than discovering it as a red nobody expected. A conflict resolved toward
the incoming side is the ordinary, reasonable move here, and it is the wrong one.

The change for whoever lands it: use `BrowserReadableHeaders.All` on the default policy inside the
extension, and decide separately whether the named guest policy needs the same exposure.

### Lane L-EV-OUTBOX-FLAKE — the outbox test stops failing on a coin flip
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 1
exit: the guest-data assertion in EventsOutboxDeliveryTests cannot alias onto a random token, pinned by a seeded token that reproduces the historical failure when the guard is removed
agent: opus
evidence: OkamAPI lane/ev-outbox-flake 59a1d607 (base 5df07afa, worktree /Users/svendaneel/okam/OkamAPI-evoutboxflake)

**The flake this estate has been unable to name, finally named.** A lane hit an unreproducible red and
could not capture it; the integration audit identified it:
`EventsOutboxDeliveryTests.The_message_carries_the_link_and_no_other_guest_data`.

The mechanism is worth recording because it is a shape, not an accident: the test asserts
`DoesNotContain("250", ...)` to prove a guest's data is absent — and the message carries a **random**
`PublicToken`. When those three characters happen to occur in the token, the assertion fires on its own
fixture rather than on a leak.

**An assertion that can be satisfied by its own test data is the mirror of the twenty-two shapes this
plan already catalogues.** Those cannot fail; this one fails at random. Both mean the same thing — the
test is not measuring what it claims.

Seed the token deterministically so the substring cannot alias, and keep a case that **reproduces the
historical failure when the guard is removed**, so the fix is shown to address the real path rather than
to silence the symptom.

An unnamed flake is unfixable and, worse, teaches everyone to re-run until green. This one is now named.

state: built-unverified
class: suite

exit: an import conflict, an invitation issue conflict and an invitation claim conflict each record a Refused outcome so a same-key retry replays the refusal, pinned by a test per site that reds if the recording is removed, and the SQL-tier race test asserts the Refused row rather than no row
agent: opus
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/OkamAPI-wfrefusalrest @ 02684ecc (branch lane/wf-idempotency-refusal-rest, base a1d57208 = the sibling lane; 0 Workforce files drifted between 9888178f and the tip, so it merges clean)

**The Fable review of `L-WF-IDEMPOTENCY-REFUSAL` ruled that lane correct at every site it touched — and
found the follow-up claim short by three.** These predate that lane, so they are not regressions; but

Each takes a post-reserve refusal and records nothing, so the key strands permanently:

The change at each: `await _idempotency.RefuseAsync(scope, idempotencyKey, refusal, ct)` before the

### Flag F-C5-NOT-WALKABLE — some work has no journey a person can walk, and owing one is dishonest
state: open
severity: info
owner: @sven
clears_when: the plan records, per item, either a walk a person can complete or a stated reason no walk can exist
cleared_by: L-WF-IDEMPOTENCY-REFUSAL-REST

**C5 says acceptance is a person completing the journey, never a suite reporting green. A reviewer has
now named the first item where that cannot be satisfied, and said so rather than inventing a walk.**

`L-WF-IDEMPOTENCY-REFUSAL` changed a primitive. Reaching its defect requires a refused first attempt
followed by a **same-key retry** — and every shipped client mints a fresh key per call, so no UI journey
can reach the stuck state. From a browser a replayed refusal is **pixel-identical** to a recomputed one.

So the honest evidence is the test pair plus the `Refused` row discriminator, and **owing a walk here
would be owing a ceremony that can prove nothing.** A walk performed on a state the product cannot reach
is worse than no walk: it produces an acceptance signature over a thing nobody saw.

This is not a softening of C5. C5 exists because this estate repeatedly shipped green suites over
unreachable features, and the remedy is that **a capability is accepted by a person**. The narrow
carve-out is for changes that are *not capabilities* — primitives whose behaviour no surface exposes.
The test is whether a person could in principle reach the state, not whether walking it is inconvenient.

Sven rules whether that carve-out exists. Until he does, the item stays C5-unmet rather than quietly
exempt.

**Second instance, from the Fable review of `L-WF-CORRECTION-PINS` — and this one is sharper, because a
walk here would not merely prove nothing, it would prove the wrong thing.**

Items 1-3 of that lane are test-tier guards. Item 4 surfaces only in an audit table no UI renders. And
item 5's refusal is **unreachable from the shipped UI**, because the client refuses the bad shape
*before the network* — so **a UI walk would demonstrate the client guard while the new server guard sat
untouched**, and produce an acceptance signature naming the wrong control.

The reviewer offered the honest alternative rather than a ceremony: a curl sequence against a live
backend, which needs the SQL stack. And it named the fallback plainly — if that stack cannot come up,
the wire tier's observed `Expected: BadRequest / Actual: OK` **is** the demonstration.

Two instances now, found independently, both by reviewers who looked for a walk first and said so when
there was none. That is the evidence for the carve-out, and it is still Sven's to rule.


### Flag F-CAPABILITY-URL-BLINDSPOT — the route-shape guard is a rule about names, and a bearer token has no name
state: open
severity: info
owner: @sven
clears_when: the deposit token's path placement is either ruled deliberate in this plan with its logging treatment named, or the token moves out of the path
cleared_by: L-PHONE-IN-PATH

**`L-PHONE-IN-PATH` built a guard that reads route templates off the compiled controllers and reds on
personal-identifier names in **English and Norwegian** — `{mobil}`, `{tlf}`, `{telefonnummer}`,
`{epost}` fail exactly like `{phoneNumber}`. A check keyed to the literal `phoneNumber` would have
passed its own rename mutation. That guard is real.**

**It stated its own limit, and the limit is the interesting part: it is a rule about *names*, so a
credential bound as `{value}` or `{token}` is invisible to it.**

Verified live at the tip: `Controllers/EventsDepositsController.cs:77` is
`[AllowAnonymous] [HttpGet("deposits/{token:guid}")]`. **That GUID is not an identifier of a row the
caller already has access to — it is the only thing authorizing the request.** A bearer credential in a
URL path is seen by every intermediary, reverse proxy and access log on the way, which is precisely the
argument the phone lane made, applied to something that is literally an auth token.

The route is **deliberate** — the controller comment cites spec §5, public, no login. This is the
ordinary capability-URL tradeoff that magic links make everywhere, and naming it is not a claim that it
is wrong.

**What is worth ruling is the treatment, not the design:** whether that token is redacted at the log
sinks the way the phone numbers were, and whether the plan says so anywhere. Today it does not.

The second half of this flag is the durable part: **do not read the new guard as proof that no
credential travels in a path.** It proves no *named* personal identifier does. That distinction is the
same one that let a deposit token travel as `{vippsOrderId}` past earlier review.


### Lane L-WF-PUSH-LAND — the push delivery lane and its honesty fix land together
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: WorkforcePushNotificationDelivery is on feature/restaurant-modules with the registration probe and the withheld state, recorded in lanes/L-WF-PUSH-LAND/merge-receipt.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-WF-PUSH-LAND/merge-receipt.md

**`L-WF-PUSH-SILENT` built on an unmerged parent and said so.** `Services/Workforce/WorkforcePushNotificationDelivery.cs` exists on **exactly one branch** — `lane/wf-push-notify` — and that branch is not on the integration branch. The honesty fix sits above it on `lane/wf-push-silent`.

**They land together or not at all.** Landing the delivery lane alone puts back the defect the second lane exists to remove: Azure Notification Hubs **accepts a send whose tag matches nothing**, so "no exception" was never evidence a device was reached, and a publication that reached no phone was recorded as sent.

This lane is deliberately **not** gated on `D-WF-CORRECTION-FLAG`, unlike `L-WF-STATUTORY-LAND`. The push family shares no file with the correction work and no ruling changes what it merges — putting it behind a decision it does not depend on would stall it for nothing.

**A collision you must resolve, named by the lane that found it rather than left for you to hit.**
`L-WF-PUSH-STILL-LIES` and `L-WF-WITHHELD-BOUND` both edit `WorkforceNotificationDispatcher.cs` **and**
`WorkforceSchedulePublishService.cs`. The hunks are **adjacent, not identical** — a superseded-cancellation
block just above `FlipRecipientAsync`, and the `LogicalDedupeKey` line just below the changed `foreach` —
so a three-way merge should hold textually.

**It is the semantics that need checking, not the conflict count.** Both lanes move recipient and outbox
state. **Re-run the workforce slice after combining**, and read the merged bodies rather than trusting a
clean merge — a zero-conflict merge failed to compile twice in this program, and a third auto-merged a
method that was only correct because someone read it.

Seven merge lanes have run. Their findings apply here in full: build the merge before any tier, read auto-merged bodies rather than trusting a zero conflict count, diff the discovered-test sets rather than reporting a net delta, resolve `artifacts/tests/README.md` as a union, and move the ref only with a compare-and-swap.

### Lane L-ALIASING-NEEDLE-SWEEP — no absence assertion can be satisfied by its own random fixture
state: verified
class: analysis
pts: 2
exit: every DoesNotContain-style absence assertion whose needle can occur by chance in a random fixture value is named with its probability, and each is either excised-haystack, pinned-fixture or ruled safe with the reason, recorded in lanes/L-ALIASING-NEEDLE-SWEEP/census.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-ALIASING-NEEDLE-SWEEP/census.md

**Carried forward by `L-EV-OUTBOX-FLAKE`, which fixed the one instance and said the shape deserves a
sweep beyond its own module. It grepped `WebApi.Tests/Events/` and found no second case there. Nobody
has looked anywhere else.**

**The shape, stated so it can be recognised:** an assertion proves a value is *absent* by searching for a
short needle in a haystack that also contains a **random** fixture value. When the needle occurs inside
the random part, the assertion fires on its own fixture rather than on a leak.

This estate catalogues 22+ assertion shapes that **cannot fail**. This one is their mirror: it **fails at
random**. Both mean the test is not measuring what it claims, and the random one is worse in one
specific way — it teaches everyone to re-run until green, which is how a real red gets discarded.

The instance was quantified rather than hand-waved: `"250"` fit inside the Guid at 22 positions, `"2000"`
at 17 — roughly **one run in 180 failing on its own fixture**. That is exactly the frequency at which a
lane hits it once, cannot reproduce it, and moves on. **One did, and it cost an hour and went unnamed
until an audit found it.**

Three remedies, in order of strength, all demonstrated by that lane:
1. **Excise the random part from the haystack** before asserting absence — structural, not lucky.
2. **Pin the fixture to the worst case** — a token that *contains* the needles, so the historical failure
   stays reproducible on demand rather than living in a lane's memory.
3. **Replace a bare needle with an inventory** of what the message may contain. The lane's point is worth
   keeping: the bare needle was weak *even when it did not alias* — `"2000"` does not match `2 000,00`,
   which is how a Norwegian money leak actually renders, so the assertion would have missed a real leak
   while failing on a fake one.

Report probabilities, not impressions. A needle that cannot alias is a finding worth recording too.


### Lane L-CORS-FOLLOWUPS — production cannot inherit a loopback origin, and the false "or" comes out of the copy
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: AddOkamCors drops loopback origins outside Development with a unit test that reds if the filter is removed, and neither the guest client nor the preference page states that same-site serving or the named policy would suffice alone, recorded in /Users/svendaneel/okam/Web-modules/lanes/L-CORS-FOLLOWUPS/evidence.md
agent: opus
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/Web-modules/lanes/L-CORS-FOLLOWUPS/evidence.md

**Two follow-ups from the Fable review of `L-CORS-CREDENTIALED-ORIGIN`, which approved the lane and
verified the configuration mechanism independently.**

**1. Nothing in code stops production inheriting the dev origins.** `appsettings.Development.json` ships
in the publish output — the csproj excludes nothing — so **the only gate is `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` not
reading `Development`**, and the origin resolver is environment-blind: it accepts `http://` and loopback
everywhere. A prod host mis-set to Development would grant `http://localhost:3000` a **credentialed**
CORS trust, which is trust in anything running on an operator's machine.

The reviewer was careful about the degree: that same misconfiguration already degrades OpenIddict to dev
certificates and drops the `__Host-` cookie prefix, so it is not a new hole in *degree* — but it is new
**in kind**, because the others do not hand out ambient credentials. This codebase already has the
fail-fast guard pattern twice in the same file. Pass the environment in and drop loopback origins when it
is not Development, skipping quietly to match the resolver's existing posture.

**2. The false "or" is alive again, in the frontend.** `growth-guest-client.js:44-47` and the header of
`pages/preferences/communications.vue` both say the surface starts working when the API is served
same-site **or** the policy names the web origin. **For the credentialed endpoints that "or" is false**:
the named policy fixes CORS, but a `SameSite=Strict` cookie still never rides a cross-site request, so
**both are required.** The backend's own comment in `AddOkamCors` already says it correctly — *neither
substitutes for the other*.

This plan withdrew that same false "or" once before, in the reverse direction: the same **site** is not
the same **origin**. It has now been written twice from two different directions, which is a good reason
to state it in the copy rather than in a comment nobody reads.

Both comments' premise also goes stale the moment the CORS lane lands, since they assert the code builds
CORS with `AllowAnyOrigin`.

other modules and found it live and reachable in each. This is the Meals half.**

`Services/Meals/MealsCommandReceiptService.cs` is Reserve/Complete only. The reservation commits at
`:158` **ahead of the checks**, so a retry gets `meals.idempotency-in-progress` — and there is **no
expiry column at all** and no purge, so the key strands permanently rather than eventually.

**~18 stranding sites**, including 8 `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` backstops.

**The defect is documented as accepted at `MealsCommandReceiptService.cs:32-37`.** That comment was
honest when written. It stops being honest the moment the sibling primitive exists in the estate and is
merely not applied here — an accepted-defect note is a decision record, and a decision made against a
world that has since changed is a claim, not a decision. Replace it with what the code does.

Meals is a **money path**. C4 applies: a refusal row copies the actor **by value** off the reservation,
never rebuilt from a prefix plus an id.

The Workforce lane's shape is the model, and two of its lessons transfer directly: key the refusal by
`(scope, key)` rather than by a reservation object, or the backstops decided in the calling service are
stranded; and **clear the change tracker before the refusal's own save**, or it commits the very mutation
the refusal rejected.

### Flag F-ZSH-WORD-SPLIT — a shell loop over a variable silently checks nothing
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: no brief instructs an agent to iterate a list in zsh, and every ancestry or existence check in a receipt shows its per-item output rather than a summary
cleared_by: L-WF-PUSH-LAND

**Three times in one session, twice by the clerk and once by a lane. It is worth a flag because the
failure mode is silence, not error.**

**zsh does not word-split an unquoted variable.** A `for` loop over `$list` iterates **once**, with the
whole string as a single item. Every command in the loop then runs against a nonsense argument.

What makes it dangerous here is what those commands do when handed nonsense:
- `git merge-base --is-ancestor "a b c"` prints **usage** and exits non-zero — which a `&&` chain reads
  as "not an ancestor". A lane hit exactly this and its first ancestry pass answered `NONE(tip)` for
  every branch in every family. **It caught it because it read the output instead of the exit code**, and
  re-ran every check.
- `read -r a b` with `-a` fails outright — that one is loud.
- A verify sweep looped this way attempted **zero** verifications and reported 97 refusals. The refusals
  were fabricated by the loop, not by the tool.

**The remedy is not "quote it".** It is: do list work in Python, and in any receipt **show the per-item
result rather than a count** — the clerk's fabricated 97 and the lane's fabricated `NONE(tip)` were both
summaries that looked plausible. A per-item line would have shown `usage:` in the first row.

This belongs beside the assertion-shape catalogue rather than in it: those are tests that cannot fail;
this is a **check that never ran** and reported an answer anyway.


### Flag F-IDENTICAL-EXPRESSION-DIVERGENT-MEANING — two call sites read the same and mean different things
state: open
severity: info
owner: @sven
clears_when: a reviewer checking a duplicated expression records, per call site, which row each identifier resolves to rather than that the expressions match
cleared_by: L-CREDIT-NOTE-NUMBER

**Named by `L-CREDIT-NOTE-NUMBER` when asked why nobody had caught a defect two lanes had already
reported. The answer is the useful part.**

`GetPdf` and `CreateCreditNote` built their download filename with the **identical expression** from the
route parameter. In `GetPdf` that is correct — the route parameter and the document's own number are the
**same row**. In `CreateCreditNote` it is wrong, because the service returns a model for a **newly
inserted** row whose number the database has just assigned.

**So the two call sites look the same in source, and one of them is a defect.** Reading the diff, the
grep, or the two lines side by side all agree; only asking *which row does this identifier resolve to
here* separates them.

This is a reviewing failure mode rather than a coding one, and it belongs beside the assertion-shape
catalogue for the same reason: it describes something that **looks like evidence and is not**. A grep
proving two sites are consistent proves they are consistent — not that either is right.

The lane also did the right thing with the test that covered it: an existing wire test **pinned the
defect** as intended behaviour. It flipped that pin rather than adding a second test beside it. A pin
asserting the wrong behaviour is not neutral — it is a standing instruction to keep the defect.

**Found by `L-LIVE-WORLD-DISCOVER` outside its own subject, and it is a dated fault rather than a
present one — which is why nobody has noticed.**

`events-enquiry-to-settlement` already discovers, and is still **not live-re-runnable**:

1. It finds its row by the **constant** `"Nina Nordmann"`. A second live run against the same world
   creates a second row with that name, and the journey then picks one of two arbitrarily. The first run

Per-run subject names are the remedy the sibling used for its own journey; the expiry should be derived
from the run's own clock, not written down.

This is small and unglamorous. It is also the difference between a journey that proves something in
November and one that has to be deleted in a hurry.


### Lane L-WF-PUSH-STILL-LIES — the delivery record stops claiming more than it knows
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: no code comment or return claims the uninstalled-device case is closed, the recipient is not flipped to Delivered on a push that was never confirmed, and the publish audit actor is asserted by value
agent: opus
evidence: OkamAPI lane/wf-push-still-lies 100ae000 (base feature/restaurant-modules 569887a5, unmoved); WebApi.Tests/Workforce/WorkforceNotificationTransportTests.cs, WebApi.Tests/Workforce/ScheduleAuditLedgerTests.cs, WebApi.Tests/Wire/WorkforceWireTests.cs

**A Fable review of the landed push work found that the defect those lanes existed to remove is still
reachable on two paths, both live on the integration branch. Neither is a regression — the lanes made
things strictly more honest — but "the manager believed the shift was announced" is still true.**

**1. The probe proves a record, not a device.** Azure Notification Hubs does not remove a registration at
uninstall; it prunes lazily, on PNS feedback after a send or at expiry. So a worker who uninstalled
yesterday, a reinstall that left a dead handle, and a phone with notifications OS-disabled **all answer
the probe present** — the hub accepts the send and the row goes `Sent`.

The fix removed the *never-registered* arm of the lie and kept the *registered-but-unreachable* arm. That
is real progress. **The defect is that the code claims otherwise:** the adapter's own comments say the
uninstalled-worker case is closed. `NotificationService.cs:133` already names the counterexample — *"a
stale one per reinstall"* — without drawing the conclusion.

**By this plan's own standard a narrowed lie recorded is fine and a narrowed lie claimed as solved is
not.** Change the comments and the return; the next rung (per-send PNS outcome telemetry) is a different
lane.

**2. The recipient is flipped to `Delivered` regardless of the push outcome**, on the first pass, in the
in-app inbox write. The tests say this out loud and designate the outbox row as the only honest record —
and the only surface carrying that record, `GET .../schedules/notification-failures`, **has no frontend
caller at all.** The honest record exists; no operator's screen renders it. C3: a capability exists only
when it is reachable.

**3. C4 is named but not asserted.** The publish stamps `PublishedByActorReference` and an audit row, and
**no test asserts the `schedule.publish` audit actor by value** — the ledger test asserts action names and
counts only. The module already has the pattern for `clock.ingest`; copy it.

Also fold in: the operator endpoint is only ever reached by **direct controller-action invocation**, so an
attribute-routing failure would not red; and two comments now misdescribe `Withheld` as a *failure* with a
retryable code, which it is not.

### Lane L-WF-WITHHELD-BOUND — a store that never gets a credential stops accreting forever
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a superseded publication's outbox rows reach a terminal state and a withheld row whose week has ended stops being re-polled, pinned by a test that reds if either transition is removed
agent: opus
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/wt-wfwithheld @ 74405b34 (lane/wf-withheld-bound off feature/restaurant-modules 569887a5); pin WebApi.Tests/Workforce/WorkforceNotificationBacklogBoundTests.cs; four-state record lanes/L-WF-WITHHELD-BOUND/mutation_check.py + trx/

**The same review asked what bounds `Withheld`. There is no bound, and nothing ages it out.**

For a store that never gets a hub credential, measured rather than supposed:
- every publish adds one push row per claimed worker, forever, and **superseding a publication does not
  cancel its outbox rows** — nothing outside the dispatcher ever moves an outbox status — so republished
  weeks accrete;
- each withheld row costs two `SaveChanges` writes every five minutes, forever;
- the due-query is a **shared batch of 100 across all stores**, so once the overdue withheld backlog
  exceeds dispatcher throughput it **starves fresh `Pending` rows for every other store**;
- and when a credential finally lands, the drain sends that worker a push for **every historical
  publication in the backlog** — months of stale "week published" notices at once.

**The last one is the one to hold on to.** The withheld state was built so a waiting store is not
mistaken for a broken one. Left unbounded, the day it starts working is the day it spams every worker
with news about weeks that are already over.

The reviewer named the change: transition a superseded publication's non-terminal rows to a new terminal
`Superseded` status inside the publish transaction, and expire a withheld row whose notice's range end
has passed to `DeadLettered` with a named reason so it lands on the operator surface rather than
vanishing. That gives the bound a sentence: **at most one live push row per worker per store, and none
for weeks already over.**

**If this is not built, the return must say "unbounded, no age-out" in those words** rather than leaving
the reader to infer it.

defect, not a fix.

**Third instance, 2026-08-04, and it was caught by two lanes independently in the same hour.** I put
*"the tree now stays clean after a full run — a sibling fixed the dated-output writer and pinned it"* into
two briefs. **False at the integration tip.** The fix and its pin are `b10eb11c`, reachable only from
`lane/dated-test-output`; `git merge-base --is-ancestor b10eb11c feature/restaurant-modules` is **NO**.
Both lanes restored the files and reported the discrepancy rather than assuming their own run was odd.

**Note what makes this instance worse than the first two.** Those quoted a fix as landed. This one told
agents that a **dirty tree is now a finding** — so a lane that saw the expected dirt would have been
pushed toward treating normal behaviour as a defect, and the honest ones spent effort proving it was not.
A wrong fact about the tip does not just mislead; it inverts what an agent is supposed to be alarmed by.

**Fourth and fifth instances, both 2026-08-04, and the fifth is the sharpest because it was not in a
brief — it was in a mid-flight correction I sent to a running lane.**

Fourth: I told two more lanes the tree stays clean after a full run. `L-XZ-CREDIT-FIELDS` disproved it
**against an untouched baseline checkout of the same commit**, establishing it as the base's behaviour
rather than any lane's.

Fifth: I messaged `L-MEALS-AGREEMENT-PIN-INVERTS` that a defect-asserting test needed inverting, and
authored a whole lane for it. **`54714dd6` had already inverted those assertions and replaced the comment
in the same commit.** `L-MEALS-DOCSYNC` caught it and said so plainly.

**The escalation is what matters.** The first three were briefs written from stale returns. The fifth was
a *correction* — the very act of fixing a stale fact carried another one, into a lane that was already
running, where it had a live chance of producing duplicate work against an unmerged branch. I sent that
lane a stop-and-re-measure the moment I learned.

**The remedy is the same and I still had not applied it**: name the commit a claim was read at. A
correction needs it more than a brief does, not less.

**The remedy already recorded is the right one and I did not apply it**: a brief quoting a file, line or
state names the commit it was read at. The two briefs that carried this named a tip for the *code* and
not for the *claim*.

**The mechanism is worth naming, because it will keep happening.** Reviews and returns describe branches;
briefs describe work. When the clerk carries a sentence from a return into a brief, the branch it was
true on travels silently and the tip does not. The remedy is not more care — it is that **a brief
quoting a file, line or symbol names the commit it was read at**, so a lane can check the quote instead
of inheriting it.

This estate already pays for the same confusion in the other direction: a lane reporting `built` against
code no caller on the integration branch can reach.



**Third and fourth instances, 2026-08-04, both caught by the lane and not by me.**

`L-REPLAY-PINS-CLOSE` was briefed against four named tests and found **three of the four absent** at the
integration tip `8e2b57de`, because the lanes that wrote them are unmerged and
`MealsIdempotencyRefusalTests.cs` is absent from that commit entirely.

**Correction, entered the same day, because I repeated the lane's own overstatement.** Both the lane and
this flag first said *all four* were missing. A Fable review checked and the fourth **does exist** at
`8e2b57de:WebApi.Tests/Meals/MealsAgreementWriterTests.cs:173`, receipt assertion included at `:193` — so
the census line number that was called "from the wrong tree" was in fact from the right one. The finding
this supported is unharmed and slightly strengthened: that test already reds under the mandated mutant **at
the true base, under every landing order**, rather than only after one lane lands. **A flag that
overstates its own evidence is the defect it exists to catch**, so the wrong sentence is corrected here
rather than removed. It did not stop — it constructed a
base of `8e2b57de` plus both lanes and worked there — but its green now stands against **a tree nobody
else has**, which is a cost the brief imposed rather than a choice the lane made.

`L-HOSTED-SERVICE-FLOOR` was told `8e2b57de` was an `integration/*` tip. The commit was right and the
branch name was loose: `8e2b57de` is the tip of `feature/restaurant-modules`, while the integration refs
are `be-cutover` `18660066`, `confirm-family` `eeb1b8c4` and `mig-stack-land` `4b37f81b`.

**The remedy has not changed and has still not been applied**: a brief quoting a file, line, symbol or
branch **names the commit it was read at**. Twice today a lane spent its opening moves establishing that
its own brief was describing somewhere else. Both times the lane was right to check, and both times the
check was work the brief should have made unnecessary.

### Lane L-DI-COLLECTION-SILENT — a missing registration behind an IEnumerable stops passing for present
state: verified
class: analysis
pts: 2
exit: every IEnumerable-shaped injection point is named with what an empty sequence does at runtime, and each is either guarded by a floor the composition-root check enforces or recorded as deliberately optional, in lanes/L-DI-COLLECTION-SILENT/census.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-DI-COLLECTION-SILENT/census.md

**A fourth reachability failure mode, found by `L-WF-TIMESHEET-WIRE` while proving the first three.**

C3 has been enforced against three shapes: routing, binding, DI. The DI shape has always been assumed
**loud** — remove a registration and the controller cannot be constructed, which surfaces as a 500.

**Not when the injection point is a collection.** `ITimesheetExportProvider` is `IEnumerable`-shaped, so
removing its registration yields an **empty sequence**: no exception, no 500, the controller constructs
fine and **ten of twelve wire facts stayed green**. The capability was gone and the suite did not notice.

It was caught only because the refusal reads `availableProviderKeys` **back out of the response body** —
had that test asserted a status code, the mutation would have been invisible.

**This is the C3 hazard in its most dangerous form**, because the estate's whole defence is "a missing
wire shows up as a failure to construct". For a collection it shows up as **a feature that quietly does
nothing**, which is precisely the state four of five module journeys were found in on 2026-07-29.

Sweep every `IEnumerable<T>` / `IReadOnlyList<T>` constructor parameter resolved from DI and say, per
site, what an empty sequence does at runtime — refuse, no-op, or silently succeed. A site that is
deliberately optional is a finding worth recording; a site that silently succeeds needs a floor the
composition-root check enforces.

### Flag F-JOURNEY-LEAVES-LEVERS-ON — a journey run changes the world it ran against
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: a journey that pulls a feature lever restores it, shown by two consecutive runs against one world where the second starts from the state the first did
cleared_by: L-EV-JOURNEY-TIMEBOMB

**Observed, not theorised.** `L-EV-JOURNEY-TIMEBOMB` was proving re-runnability when its run was killed
by a session limit. Its last recorded line is the finding: *"Arm A run 2 failed — the pipeline is not
dark, because run 1 left the levers on."*

This is a **third** re-runnability fault, beyond the two that lane was authored for (a constant subject
name, and a future date literal). Those two make a second run *unreliable*. This one makes it **run
against a different world**: the journey enables a feature lever and does not put it back, so run 2
starts from a state run 1 created.

**Why it matters more than it looks:** the estate has been treating a green journey as evidence about the
product. A journey that mutates its own world is evidence about **the product plus whatever the last run
left behind** — and the failure surfaces as an unrelated assertion failing on run 2, which reads as
flakiness rather than as contamination.

It also explains a constraint several lanes have been honouring by instinct: three declined to borrow a
standing world for exactly this reason, and one noted that a pending acceptance walk asserts *zero flag
overrides*, so borrowing would have reddened another lane's evidence. **They were right, and this is why.**

### Flag F-OVERBROAD-TEST-FILTER — one filter spelling starts a container the other does not
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: no brief, script or receipt in the estate uses FullyQualifiedName!~SqlServer, and every container-free run names the Database!=SqlServer form
cleared_by: L-WF-TIMESHEET-RACE

**A lane started a SQL container today. It said so itself, unprompted, and cleaned up:** *"I started a
SQL container by using an over-broad filter. Recording that; it was mine and Testcontainers already
removed it. Switching to the mandated filter."*

Every brief in this program says **`dotnet test --filter "Database!=SqlServer"`, never
`FullyQualifiedName!~SqlServer`**. The two look interchangeable and are not: the name-based form misses
any SQL-tier test whose class name does not contain the string, so those tests run — and a
Testcontainers fixture starts a container.

**The reason this is a flag rather than a note is the host.** The container budget here is roughly two to
three concurrent SQL containers before the VM OOM-kills; five foreign containers have been up for most of
this session, three holding worlds for an acceptance walk. An accidental start is not a tidy-up problem,
it is a lane killing somebody else's pending evidence.

**The behaviour to keep is the lane's, not the mistake's.** It attributed the container to itself,
verified it was gone, and switched — rather than discovering it later in a receipt or leaving a sibling
to find an orphan. That is what the never-touch-a-container-you-did-not-create rule is for: attribution
by name, never by count.


### Lane L-WORLD-STAMP-WINDOWS — the build stamp cannot name a commit the binary was not built from
state: verified
class: node
pts: 2
exit: the stamp records the process holding the socket and refuses when the repository head has moved since the build, pinned by a test per window that reds if either guard is removed, recorded in lanes/L-WORLD-STAMP-WINDOWS/evidence.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-WORLD-STAMP-WINDOWS/evidence.md

**A Fable review attacked the claim `L-LIVE-BUILD-EXPORT` rests on — *"it can lose its answer; it cannot
invent a wrong one"* — and found it holds everywhere it walked **except two windows, both in the
`live-world.sh` wiring that was never executed end to end.** Neither is acknowledged by the lane.

**W1 — the head moves between build and stamp.** The script builds, and `writeStamp` reads `rev-parse
HEAD` **at stamp time**. A rebase or checkout in the API worktree between those two moments — a recorded
hazard in this estate, where shared worktrees are routine — makes the stamp name a commit **the running
binary was not built from**. It is verified-alive, origin-matched and confidently wrong.

**And the guard then dresses it up:** the override branch would print *"this overrode E2E_API_BUILD"*,
presenting a wrong answer as the guard working correctly. That is worse than no stamp.

**W2 — the stamped launcher is alive and a stranger holds the socket.** The stamp records `$!`, which is
the `dotnet run` **launcher**, not the process holding the port. Liveness then proves *"launcher alive"*,
not *"this origin is served by this build"*. If the WebApi child dies and another process takes the port,
the stamp still validates and answers the old build.

The lane's own residual note names only the **safe** direction of this — dead launcher, live child, falls
back — and not its twin. **A residual recorded in one direction reads as a bound; it is not one.**

Fixes named by the reviewer: stamp the socket holder rather than the launcher (safe at that moment, since
the port was proven free, the bind-failure check proved our process took it, and `/health` had answered),
and refuse to stamp when the head no longer matches the one built.

Two smaller items from the same review, both real: `host === '::1'` is **dead code** in two files —
Node's WHATWG URL returns `'[::1]'`, so IPv6 loopback is treated as remote. Conservative, so not a
defect, but it is a comparison that can never be true. And `writeFileSync` is not atomic; write-tmp-then-
rename is optional hardening rather than a condition.

**One thing the review established that must travel with the probe.** `json:$.backendBuild.source` cannot
read a forged value — only a verified stamp produces `stamp:` — but it **can keep reading
`process:127.0.0.1:5961` after a correctly stamped world has run**, because the standing canonical
artifact is *equal rank* and equal rank from a different key does not displace. **The probe instruction
must carry that handover step or it will go red against correct code.**



**Both windows closed at `997936ad`, and the lane opened each one rather than reasoning about it.** W1
lands a real second commit in a real checkout; W2 stands a real child process on a real socket under a
real launcher — **then builds the launcher-shaped stamp by hand after killing the server and shows it still
verifies**, demonstrating the defect beside the guard.

**W2 is the finding that reaches further than this lane.** `$!` is the **`dotnet run` launcher**, not the
`WebApi` child holding the socket — so every liveness check proved only *"the launcher is alive."* The
writer now resolves the socket holder and refuses unless it is the launched pid or a descendant. **Every
`backend: live` artifact taken before this was making a weaker claim than it appeared to.**

**W1's fix is required, not optional, and that is deliberate:** the caller must pass `builtFrom` — the token
printed when the binary is built — and the writer recomputes it and refuses on any difference. **A guard
that can be lost by a caller dropping an argument is not a guard.** `live-world.sh` additionally dies if
the commit moved *while* `dotnet build` ran, which is the half no stamp-time check can see.

**Both fixes live in `world-stamp.js`, not in the shell — and the lane said why: "a guard in a script
nobody runs is exactly how these two survived the original review."**

**One line worth keeping as a general rule.** The residual is now recorded **in both directions** in the
header, because **recording only the safe direction is what made it read as a bound.**

**The stamp was not weakened to make it safe**: it refuses more and invents nothing, which was the property
under protection.

### Lane L-ROUTE-GUARD-GAPS — the route guard learns the words it is missing, and rule 2 stops being half-vacuous
state: built-unverified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: mottaker, kontonummer and navn red as route parameters, and a wire test per phone-bearing action reds when the bound body value is ignored rather than merely deleted
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-ROUTE-GUARD-GAPS/mutation-log.md

**Two real gaps in the guard `L-PHONE-IN-PATH` built, found by a Fable review that otherwise approved it.
The headline is worth stating precisely: a personal identifier can still travel in a path — but only
under a name that does not admit it, and no such route exists today.**

**1. Missing words, and one of them is this estate's own idiom.** The vocabulary already carries
`fodselsnummer`, `personnummer`, `email`, `mail`, `msisdn`, `ssn`, `birthdate`, `fnr`, and deliberately
stays quiet on `orgnr` (a public registry identifier — firing on it cries wolf). It misses:

- **`mottaker`** — Norwegian for *recipient*, and **the giftcard transfer's receiver is exactly a
  phone-identified party.** The estate's own parameter was `newReceiverPhoneNumber`.
- **`kontonummer`** — the ordinary Norwegian word for a bank account number. The stems carry `iban` and
  `kortnummer` and not this one.
- **`navn`** — English `Name` got a documented exact-match ruling elsewhere; the Norwegian generic got
  nothing.

**2. Rule 2 proves *bound*, not *used*.** The pin proves the action is verb-bound, has exactly one
`[FromBody]`, and the model carries a phone-named property. **It does not prove the value flows
anywhere:** a mutant that keeps the parameter and passes `null` to the service **passes all 39 tests**,
and no other test in the suite references either service method. The lane's M3 killed only the *deletion*
shape.

Close it with a wire test per action driving the request through the pipeline and asserting the body
value **arrives as the service argument** — then run the ignore-shape mutant against it once.

**3. The claim to correct while in there, because it is the load-bearing one.** The guard's own comment
says the opaque-name gap is covered by the telemetry initializer's second trigger. **That trigger covers
opaque *guid* capabilities only.** A phone number is not guid-shaped, so **an opaque-named personal value
in a path has no defence at any layer.** The comment says the opposite.

**Worth ruling while there:** `{handle}` on the two notification controllers is credential-shaped — likely
a push-registration device handle — and is invisible to **both** vocabularies. A cheap rule 3 could
enumerate credential-shaped path names against a deliberate-capability allowlist with a reason, which is
what the seven `{token}` routes already are. **Extend for names only; do not claim it covers values** —
a credential under an opaque name is a genuinely different check no name rule can perform.


### Lane L-WF-FAILURES-SURFACE — the honest delivery record reaches an operator's screen
state: verified
class: node
pts: 2
exit: a manager can see which publications reached nobody without curl, with waiting distinguishable from broken on screen, shown by a browser journey that reds if the surface stops naming the withheld state, recorded in lanes/L-WF-FAILURES-SURFACE/evidence.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-WF-FAILURES-SURFACE/evidence.md

**Two lanes have now built the honest record and neither could reach a person with it. C3: a capability
exists only when it is reachable.**

`GET /workforce/stores/{storeId}/schedules/notification-failures` returns the only truthful account of
what a publication actually reached. `L-WF-PUSH-STILL-LIES` measured its reachability rather than assuming
it: **0 hits for the path, for `notificationFailures`, and for any delivery-failure identifier across 929
frontend files.**

So the state of things is: the push adapter now refuses to record `Sent` for a worker with no
registration; the recipient's state names the tier it is about; a store awaiting its first hub credential
reads as **waiting** rather than **failed** — and **none of it is visible to anyone without a bearer token
and a command line.**

**That is the exact shape this constraint exists for.** On 2026-07-29 four of five module journeys stopped
at a missing wire while the suite was green: a service with no controller, a flag with no lever, a seed
with no caller, a page nothing linked to. This is the fifth of that family, built by lanes that each
correctly said it was out of their scope.

The surface must keep the distinction the backend paid to create. **A list that renders withheld and
failed identically throws away the whole point of the withheld state** — a store that has not started is
not a store that is broken, and a manager reading one screen must be able to tell which they are.

Client method, page, and a navigation entry that leads to it — all three, in the same change, or the
capability still does not exist.



**Built, and it did not flatten the distinction — which was the whole risk.** Three separately-headed,
separately-counted groups and **no combined total anywhere**: *"Kom aldri fram"* in red, *"Forsøkes på
nytt"* in amber, and *"Venter på butikkens push-nøkkel"* in **neutral grey**, reading *"Ingenting har
feilet her … Dette er ikke en feil"*. Client method, page and nav entry landed in one change.

**A domain fact it established rather than assumed:** only the **push** adapter can withhold, so on a
single store at a single moment `Withheld` and `NoPushRegistration` are **mutually exclusive** — the first
needs the credential absent, the second needs it present. The fixture therefore seeds one historical dead
letter, documented in place, so the worker-tier reason is reachable from a browser at all.

**A defect in its own journey, found and fixed rather than shipped.** The first *passing* version staffed
roster rows **by index**, published **2 recipients instead of 3**, and so **silently never exercised the SMS
tier**. It now walks every row and asserts the count. A green walk that quietly covers less than it claims
is the same family as the assertions this program has been removing all day — and this one was caught by its
author.

**The stale fixture caught it too, and it discarded rather than reconciled.** Its first run took the default
ports, `reuseExistingServer` adopted PID 73160, and the panel honestly rendered *"we do not know"* off a
404. Everything reported comes from private ports `4021/3021`, and PID 73160 was left running.

**A second unreachable route found in passing, and not fixed:** `getPublicationHistory` exists in the client
with **zero callers**. Same shape as the one this lane closed, waiting for someone to decide whether it is a
missing surface or dead code.

**What it does not prove, stated plainly.** The artifact stamps itself `backend: fixture`. **No live backend
ran** — the SQL cap was 2/2 with both containers foreign and the brief granted no slot. This proves the wire
with the tiers intact; an `@live` re-point is the remaining step and is not claimed as accomplished.

### Flag F-PROOF-HARNESS-NOT-THE-GUARD — a failing proof is not evidence the guard is wrong
state: open
severity: info
owner: @sven
clears_when: no lane changes a guard in response to a proof-harness failure without first showing the guard is the cause
cleared_by: L-LIVE-WORLD-BANNER

**`L-LIVE-WORLD-BANNER` hit a failure that did not reproduce, captured it as instructed, and then did the
part that is easy to get wrong: it diagnosed the harness rather than the guard.**

Its mutation proof reported six unexpected arms. The cause was **the proof**, not the check — the harness
handed mutants named `arm-N.sh` while the check identifies both files by their own basenames. It fixed
the harness with per-arm directories keeping canonical filenames, recorded the diagnosis in the proof's
docstring, and **the check was never changed in response.**

**That order is the whole point.** The tempting move when a proof reds unexpectedly is to loosen the
thing being proved until the proof goes quiet — and the result looks identical to a guard that was
correct all along. This estate has already paid for the same instinct twice: a flake re-run until green
because nobody could name it, and a tree always dirty so nobody noticed real dirt.

Two other properties of that lane's proof are worth naming as the standard, because they are rarer than
they should be:
- **Arm 0 reds on the real text that was on the branch**, not on a mutant invented to make it red. A
  guard that has never been shown to fail on the actual defect is a guard nobody has tested.
- **Two arms deliberately green**: a rename applied to both files, and a world where the text and a
  missing reset honestly agree. That is what makes it a **contradiction** check rather than a rule that a
  filename must appear — and it is the difference the exit asked for.

### Flag F-CLERK-EXITS-NAME-NO-INSTRUMENT — the clerk is still authoring unverifiable lanes
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: every lane authored after this flag carries an exit naming a fact key or a repo path, and a verify sweep refuses none of them for the instrument rule
cleared_by: L-EXIT-INSTRUMENT-SWEEP

**This is a live defect in my own authoring, not a historical one, and it is measured.**

A sweep this session offered every `built-unverified` lane its own recorded evidence. **114 had a
resolvable candidate; 7 verified and 107 were refused.** A targeted re-run over the twelve lanes merged
since refused **all twelve**. The refusal is always the same sentence:

> exit: "…" does not name lanes/<ID>/<file>

The seven that verified are exactly the lanes whose exit says **"recorded in `lanes/<ID>/…`"**. Every
merge lane I authored says that. **Almost none of the build lanes do** — they say *"pinned by a test that
reds if X"*, which is a good exit in every respect except the one the tool checks.

`plan verify` requires the evidence to **be the instrument the exit named**. So a lane can be built, its
mutation watched red and green, its receipt written — and still be unverifiable **forever**, because the
sentence it was dispatched against never named where the proof would live.

**I am not rewriting those exits.** The exit is the contract a lane was dispatched against, and editing it
afterwards so the evidence fits is the same move as editing a test until it passes. Those lanes stay
`built-unverified` and honest.

**The correction is forward-only: every lane I author from here names its instrument** — a `fact:` key or
a repo path — *in addition to* the observable and the mutation. The plan-hub standard has required this
since v1.0 (*"observable + instrument… if you cannot name the instrument, the lane is not designed yet"*);
I have been meeting half of it and calling the other half a detail.

**The cost is not theoretical.** It is the difference between 49 verified and a 127-lane backlog that no
amount of good work can drain.


### Lane L-MEALS-VIOLATION-EXACT — a meals NOT NULL failure stops answering as a uniqueness clash
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a non-uniqueness constraint failure on a meals write is not mapped to a uniqueness refusal, pinned by a test per direction that reds if the loose result code returns, recorded in lanes/L-MEALS-VIOLATION-EXACT/mutation-log.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-MEALS-VIOLATION-EXACT/mutation-log.md

**`L-WF-VIOLATION-EXACT` fixed this in Workforce, found the identical line in Meals, and left it — right
call, different module, and it needs its own lane.**

`Services/Meals/MealsDbViolations.cs:94` carries the same loose disjunct: `IsUniqueViolation` accepts
SQLite's **primary** result code `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT` (19).

**19 is the whole constraint family, not uniqueness.** NOT NULL (1299), CHECK (275) and FOREIGN KEY (787)
all reduce to it — and a NOT NULL failure **names its table in the message exactly as a UNIQUE one does**,
so every by-table discriminator built on this predicate cannot tell them apart. The caller is told
"someone beat you" and retries forever against something a retry cannot fix.

The sibling's fix: accept only the extended codes (2067/1555) and the `"UNIQUE constraint failed"`
message. The SQL Server arm (2627/2601) was already exact and needed no change — **check whether that
holds in Meals too rather than assuming it.**

**Meals is a money path.** The wrong refusal here lands on funding, tender and release writes, so a
misread constraint is a caller retrying a payment decision.

`EventsUniqueViolation` and `Helpers/DbExceptionHelper` were checked by that lane and are **exact** —
this is the last known instance, not one of many.

**Provoke it honestly, as the sibling did.** No production path can null a non-nullable column, so the
failing statement will be the test's — but the **exception must come from the database enforcing the
real schema**, not be hand-built. Say what a SQL Server run would still have to show, since the
container-free tier cannot see 515 or 547.


### Lane L-JOURNEY-TEARDOWN — a journey that dies halfway stops poisoning the next run
state: verified
class: node
pts: 2
exit: every journey that pulls a module flag restores it from a teardown rather than a final step, and a run killed mid-walk leaves no flag lit, pinned by a test that reds if a restore moves back into the body, recorded in lanes/L-JOURNEY-TEARDOWN/mutation-log.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-JOURNEY-TEARDOWN/mutation-log.md

**`L-EV-JOURNEY-TIMEBOMB` closed the lever leak for its own journey, then stated plainly what it did not
close. Both items are real and neither is its scope.**

**1. The restore is a step, not a teardown.** A run that dies halfway still leaves the levers up and
poisons the next run. The fix that lane shipped works when the walk completes — which is exactly the case
that was never the problem. **A cleanup that only runs on the happy path is not cleanup**; it is a second
assertion that the happy path happened.

**2. Ten unregistered journeys also end with a module flag on.** Each is fine alone. **None survives a
live world where another journey needs that flag down** — and that is not hypothetical here: a lane
declined to borrow a standing world this session precisely because a pending acceptance walk asserts
*zero* flag overrides.

The lane proved the shape rather than arguing it. With the per-test reset suppressed so run 2 inherits
run 1's world: **arm A passed twice; arm B — the constant-name control — failed at run 2 with
`toHaveCount expected 1, received 2`.** The coin flip, reproduced in a browser.

Two details from that proof worth carrying: it labelled its result a **proxy** for a live re-run
everywhere, claimed no live run, and started no container. And its mutation K **falsified the lane's own
written prediction** — the rule fired for a different reason than predicted, and it corrected the
prediction in place rather than deleting it.

**Recorded, not a task:** that lane's work is **split across two refs**. Its earlier commit `4b5c5c2` is
the tip of the frontend integration branch, made before the do-not-move instruction was in force; its
remaining commit `b7a9f389` is one fast-forward ahead with nothing between. **Whoever lands it must take
`b7a9f389`, not stop at the tip** — the branch already looks like it has this lane's work and has half of
it. It also left a fixture on `:4971` and a dev server on `:3971` in `wt-evtb` for re-verification; those
are processes, not containers, and are the lane's own.



**Built at `b3e60a0`, and three of this block's own statements were wrong — corrected here by the lane
that had to work around them.**

- **`b7a9f389` is no longer a fast-forward ahead of the tip.** The sentence above saying it is one commit
  ahead with nothing between was true when written and is not now.
- **The step this lane was sent to convert did not exist at its baseline at all** — it lives only on that
  unlanded ref. The lane merged the ref in and built on the union rather than reporting the brief
  impossible, and said so.
- **The leak is 14 journeys, not 10.**

**The design decision worth carrying beyond this lane:** it records levers from **the wire**
(`PUT /stores/{id}/feature-flags`), not from the `flags.js` helper, because **two journeys move levers
without calling that helper at all.** A helper-keyed ledger would have covered twelve while reporting
fourteen — and all fourteen are covered without editing fourteen files.

**The negative was proven by killing a run, not by reasoning about one.** SIGKILL to the process group
mid-walk with a real browser: as shipped, `Events.Core` came down with the seeded override intact; with
the lease suppressed it stayed up. Isolating the teardown separately, the control left **`Events.Core`
and `Events.Settlement` up on a walk that passed** — a green run leaking two levers, which is the thesis
in one line.

**Three bugs the lane's own proof caught that its 25 static tests could not**, the worst being a `lease()`
POST with no `end()` against a fixture that awaits `readBody` before routing: it **hung every journey at
its first line until the 120s timeout**. Trusting the green suite there would have broken the entire e2e
tree. That is the sharpest argument on this page for proving a teardown by killing something.

**Stated as a smaller claim rather than closed:** a SIGKILLed *live* run still leaves levers up — there is
no lease on a SQL row, and the ledger carries no credential by design under C7.

### Lane L-DATED-TEST-OUTPUT — a test suite stops dirtying the tree it runs in
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 1
exit: a full container-free tier run leaves the checkout clean, pinned by a test that reds if dated output is written into a tracked path, recorded in lanes/L-DATED-TEST-OUTPUT/evidence.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-DATED-TEST-OUTPUT/evidence.md

**Root-caused by `L-WF-WITHHELD-BOUND` after most lanes this session worked around it without naming it.**

Every brief in this program has carried the same instruction: *"the wire tier dirties two tracked
`artifacts/journeys/ev-dietary/` files — restore, do not commit."* A dozen lanes have restored them. **None
had asked why.**

The answer: **an Events test writes dated output into a tracked path**, rewriting
`run-sheet.{md,json}` with the current date. So **any full run dirties the tree**, every time, for
everyone.

Three costs, and the third is the one that matters:
1. Every lane spends attention on a restore step that should not exist.
2. Every brief carries a line teaching agents that a dirty tree after a test run is normal.
3. **A tree that is always dirty cannot be used to detect a tree that is dirty for a real reason.** This
   estate already had one lane find five tracked `test/e2e/` files modified by somebody else and have to
   reason about whether that mattered. A checkout that is reliably clean makes that a one-second check;
   one that is reliably dirty makes it a judgement call every time.

The fix is small — write the dated artifact to a gitignored path, or freeze the date through the
injectable clock the estate already has. **Then delete the restore line from the brief template**, which
is the actual deliverable: the instruction has been teaching the wrong lesson to every agent that reads
it.

### Lane L-MARGIN-VIOLATION-ANCHOR — a constraint named UNIQUE stops being mistaken for a uniqueness failure
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a CHECK or FK failure whose constraint name contains the word UNIQUE is not classified as a uniqueness clash, pinned per site by a test that reds if the match goes back to an unanchored substring, recorded in lanes/L-MARGIN-VIOLATION-ANCHOR/mutation-log.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-MARGIN-VIOLATION-ANCHOR/mutation-log.md

**A third instance of the misclassification family, and it fails by a different mechanism than the first
two — which is why the sweep that found them did not find this one.**

Workforce and Meals both accepted SQLite's **primary** result code 19, which is the whole constraint
family. `L-MEALS-VIOLATION-EXACT` fixed the second and then found two Margin sites that are loose in a
**different** way:

- `Services/Margin/MarginRecipeSupport.cs:64`
- `Services/Margin/MarginPriceImportService.cs:694` — which also accepts `"duplicate"`

Both classify by an **unanchored `Contains("UNIQUE")` on the base message.** So **a CHECK or FK failure
whose constraint name happens to contain the word is read as a uniqueness clash.** Constraint names are
authored by us; nothing stops one being called `CK_..._UNIQUE_...`.

**The lesson to carry, not just the fix:** the first two were wrong about a *code*, these two are wrong
about a *string*. A guard matched by a substring of something a human names is a guard whose correctness
depends on nobody choosing an awkward name — which is the same shape as the assertion matched by a
literal that can never match, inverted.

`Helpers/DbExceptionHelper` and `EventsUniqueViolation` have now been independently verified exact
**twice**, by two different lanes. This is the last known family member.

### Lane L-VIOLATION-EXACT-LAND — both misclassification fixes reach the branch together

agent: opus

other live** — the Meals lane measured this and said so: `WorkforceDbViolations` still carries the bare 19
