### Lane L-WF-INVITE-LIST-REVOKE — a manager can see live invitations and withdraw one
state: verified
class: suite
pts: 2
exit: a manager lists pending invitations for a store and revokes one, and the revoked code is refused thereafter, pinned by a wire test recorded in lanes/L-WF-INVITE-LIST-REVOKE/evidence.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-WF-INVITE-LIST-REVOKE/evidence.md

**The only genuinely unbuilt part of the Workforce invitation story**, established by `L-WF-INVITE-SURFACE`
after it found its own brief stale: the UI, routes, nav and a green browser walk are **already landed** at
the integration tip, and so is the refusal handling.

**What does not exist is backend.** `WorkforceStaffController` binds **issue and nothing else**. There is no
list route and no revoke route, and **`WorkforceInvitationState.Revoked` is declared and written by no code
path at all** — a state the schema knows and the product cannot reach.

**The consequence for a manager is concrete.** They cannot see whether a code they sent is still live, and
they cannot withdraw one sent to the wrong person. **The only available remedy is to reissue**, which
supersedes in place through a filtered unique index on `(StoreId, StaffMemberId) WHERE State='Pending'` —
so the wrong recipient's code stops working, but only as a side effect, and only if the manager thinks to do
it. **The UI already says exactly this on screen**, which is why this is a missing capability rather than a
lie.

**Do not make the refusal informative.** Invalid, expired, revoked, already-claimed, wrong-recipient and
archived-person **all answer an identical `404 workforce.invitation-invalid`** with no discriminating field
— a deliberate anti-oracle pinned at `WorkforceInvitationTests.cs:493`. A revoke route must leave that
property intact: **a revoked code must become indistinguishable from an invalid one, not distinguishable as
revoked.** Breaking that would be a security regression wearing the costume of a better error message.

**C1 applies**: an invitation record is append-only. Revocation is a state transition through the documented
path, never a delete and never an in-place repair of history.

**C7 applies**: the token is a credential. A list route must not return token values — a manager needs to
know *that* a code is live and to whom it went, never what it is.

**C4**: the revoke is an act somebody will later have to explain, so it names the actor that caused it.

### Lane L-FE-WF-INVITE-LIST-REVOKE — ~~the roster panel stops saying the routes do not exist~~

class: node

retracted: Built at e8d69fc on lane/fe-wf-invite-list-revoke; its return was refused for a needs placeholder and its agent's transcript is gone and unresumable, so the return can never be merged as written. Retracted to stop it holding budget. The work is safe at that commit and is recorded on F-NEEDS-PLACEHOLDER-REFUSES-A-GOOD-RETURN.

**Filed by `L-WF-INVITE-LIST-REVOKE`, which built the backend and then found the frontend half carries a
statement its own commit makes false.** The panel binds **issue only**, and its on-screen copy — in **three
locales** — says literally *"the API has no such routes"*. **Two frontend tests actively pin that
sentence.** So the moment the backend lands, the product asserts on screen something that is no longer true,
and a test guards the falsehood.

**That is why this is urgent rather than cosmetic**: it is the same shape this program has removed four
times today — a screen naming a control's absence, or a comment asserting a control, that the code
contradicts. Here the direction is reversed and the effect is the same.

**The lane did not wire it, and stopping was correct.** `translations/{en,no,de}.ts` and
`test/e2e/fixture/api-server.js` were held dirty by another lane in a shared checkout carrying **204
uncommitted files**; editing them would have corrupted that lane's work or guaranteed a four-file conflict.
**Never bulk-edit those three translation files** — a conflict resolved that way once shipped the app with
no client bundle. Add keys surgically as pure additions, built against the committed blob.

**Invert the two pinning tests rather than deleting them.** A test asserting a defect is worth keeping in
inverted form — four such were found this session — so they should end up asserting the routes *do* exist.

**Two backend behaviours the surface must not flatten**, both established by the lane that built them:

- **A stored `Pending` does not mean live.** `Expired` is written by no code path; expiry is a **read-time
  `ExpiresAtUtc` comparison**, so a code that lapsed a month ago still reads `Pending` in the row. **A list
  that reports the stored state would tell a manager a dead code is live** — the question answered
  backwards while looking correct. Use the derived `isLive`, computed by the same comparison the claim path
  makes.
- **Revoking an already-claimed code is a 409, not a success.** A manager revokes because the code went to
  the wrong person; a 200 there would say *safe* at the exact moment they are not.

**Do not make the refusal informative.** A revoked code must stay indistinguishable from an invalid one —
the backend keeps that **structurally**, by never adding a revoked branch to the claim path, and the pin
compares status, title, detail, type **and the full extension member list** so a later "better error
message" cannot slip a discriminating field in beside a matching code.

**C7: never render or log a token.** A manager needs to know *that* a code is live and to whom it went,
never what it is.



**Built at `e8d69fc` — and its RETURN cannot be merged, because the placeholder defect cost this one an
author.** The return was refused for a single line, `needs: -`. When the clerk went to ask the lane to
delete it, **the agent's transcript was gone and it could not be resumed.**

**The work itself is safe and verified**: `lane/fe-wf-invite-list-revoke` resolves to `e8d69fc`,
*"Workforce: the roster panel stops saying the routes do not exist"*. Nothing is lost. What is missing is
the plan's record of it.

**The clerk did not hand-edit the return, and will not.** A RETURN is the audit chain; editing one to make
it merge is the failure the rule exists to prevent, and the rule does not stop applying because the author
became unreachable. **So the lane stays `running` and this note is the honest record until Sven rules
whether the clerk should accept it.**

**This is the concrete cost of `F-NEEDS-PLACEHOLDER-REFUSES-A-GOOD-RETURN`**, and the fourth instance was
already the one that defeated the prose fix — this lane's brief carried an **explicit warning** about that
exact trap and it was filled anyway. Now it has also produced an unrecordable lane.

**What was actually built, so the record is not only about the refusal.** The panel lists outstanding
invitation codes and withdraws one. **Both pinning tests were inverted rather than deleted**, and the unit

**Sven has directed composition: bring all the work onto our own branch in both repositories, prove it
there, and merge it nowhere else.** This lane is the measurement that makes that safe. **It merges
nothing.**

**Two things are already settled and must not be re-litigated.** `feature/POS` is **fully contained in
both repositories** — frontend 0 ahead with ours 105 ahead; backend `origin/feature/POS` 0 ahead, ours 411
ahead, merge-base **is** the POS tip, **0 files differing.** There is nothing to bring across, and a merge
attempt there would be motion without change.

**The raw counts are misleading and that is the first thing to fix.** 74 frontend and 187 backend branches
are *ahead* of the integration tips, but that set includes old parallel stacks — `feature/restaurant-control-stage0`
at 387 ahead, and nine `a1`–`b3` lanes at 380 each. **249 plan lanes are `built-unverified` or `verified`
and name ~117 distinct branch strings between them**, some of which are false positives from evidence prose
(`.md` and `.trx` paths). **Resolve the strings to real refs; do not trust the extraction.**

**Classify every candidate into exactly one bucket, with the command that proves it:** **contained**
(already an ancestor of the tip — merge is a no-op), **superseded** (its content lands via another branch;
name which), **outstanding** (real work not yet on the tip), or **not-a-branch**.

**Then the part that decides the order: the collision matrix.** For every pair of outstanding branches,
which files both touch. **Tonight proved three separate ways this goes wrong silently, and all three must
shape the order you propose:**
- **A lane commit can carry hunks its author never wrote** — the shared checkout went 204 → 246 dirty
  files in one evening.
- **The conflict is a decoy.** A rebase's damage landed in the file that **auto-merged**, not the one that
  conflicted, and would have broken every download filename.
- **A branch's recorded green may come from a tree nobody ran** — the private-index recipe can build one.

**So the deliverable is an order plus a re-run point, not just an order.** For each proposed step, say what
must be re-run **after** it and why — because a branch's own green does not transfer.

**Name the branches that must land together.** At least three pairs exist: `lane/wf-w5-timesheet` with
`lane/wf-digest-tautology` (`4b911917`), `lane/wf-invite-list-revoke` with `lane/fe-wf-invite-list-revoke`,
and `lane/pdf-creditnote-name` which **supersedes** `lane/credit-note-number`. **Merging either half of a
pair alone is the failure mode.**

**Flag anything that cannot be composed at all**, and say why. `F-CORE-PIN-ON-NO-REMOTE` means a fresh
clone cannot build this branch today — **note it in your order, do not try to fix it**; it needs a push and
that is the owner's.

**Merge nothing. Push nothing. Check out nothing in a shared checkout.** Your output is a document and a
script.



**Measured. 139 mergeable heads, not 260** — FE 95 refs → **61**, BE 315 → **78**. The raw *ahead* count
**overstates by 46 percent** through containment, aliases and a superseded epoch.

**Five of the brief's claims failed measurement, and they were mine.**

1. FE is **73** ahead, not 74. 2. Lanes are **250**, not 249. 3. The "nine `a1`–`b3` lanes" are **eight
refs at one commit** `e88af796` — there is no `a4`. 4. **POS containment holds, but the proof I cited does
not**: **1636 backend and 516 frontend files differ**; the actual evidence is `ahead=0`, and *"0 files
differing"* was wrong. 5. **Two of the three "must land together" pairs are not pairs** —
`lane/wf-w5-timesheet` is a **strict ancestor** of `lane/wf-digest-tautology`, so merging the digest branch
alone lands both; and `pdf-creditnote-name` / `credit-note-number` are **production-identical**
(`InvoicesController.cs` byte-identical), differing only in a test.

**The ~117 figure was wrong in the opposite direction to the one I assumed.** Plan prose **under-names the
population six-fold** — 39 branch-shaped strings against 260 refs ahead — and **all 39 resolve; none was a
false positive.** The population had to come from `refs/heads`, not from evidence prose.

**The C2 finding is the load-bearing one, and it turns seven steps into one.** Fifteen branches add
migrations, but **fourteen carry strict prefixes of a single ten-deep stack** — a chain at twelve depths,
not a fork. **The genuine fork is `lane/margin-finalize-lag` alone**: it duplicates the stack's
`Margin_PeriodStatementFinalizedImmutable` under id `20260731203011`, which **sorts before the tip's chain
tip** — a mid-chain insert *and* a double table change. **Rebuild, not merge.** Landing the deepest head
first makes the serialised set **one step rather than seven**.

**Its matrix keys on `(path, blob)`, and that choice paid for itself**: name-keying would have scored
**three phantom collisions while missing the real one** — exactly the add/add hazard the guest-link sweep
found.

**And it extended that sweep's worst finding.** The `-2` branch **rewrote the sweep test's own allowlist
justification**, deleting the *"this is the single place that changes"* claim — so **the test stays green by
construction** rather than by accident. The ruling to land `9e3a607b` is supported.

is empty and only the local unpushed `lane/core-ore-label` holds it. Plus **76 stale-epoch branches**, cut
where the behind-histogram is **cleanly empty between 150 and 300**, so the boundary is measured rather

**Merged nothing, pushed nothing, checked out nothing.** The order and its re-run points are §6 of

overstates by 46 percent through containment, aliases and a superseded epoch.

**Three things that will go wrong silently if you merge on autopilot, all measured today:**

- **The conflict is a decoy.** A rebase's damage landed in the file that **auto-merged**, not the one that

what it contains.

named** — the meals-admin-setup fix onto the candidate. The integration tip was re-read and is **unmoved**;
the clerk confirmed both refs directly. Nothing pushed, no container started.

makes the comparison mean anything. 126 suites and 2,959 tests green with the submodule populated; journeys
**27 passed, 2 failed**, up from 26 and 3, with the repaired walk recording a completed outcome over thirteen
steps.

defect that poisoned an earlier run's numbers. And the merge's decoy surface was one file changed on both

evidence: lanes/L-EVIDENCE-CITATIONS-RESOLVE/citations.md

**Two flags describe the same doubt from opposite ends, and neither has ever been measured.**
`F-EVIDENCE-GITIGNORED` asks whether a lane's evidence pointer names a path git ignores;
`F-COMMIT-TREE-LEAVES-NO-REF` asks whether a commit a lane reported is dangling. Both are answerable by
reading this file and this repository, and until they are answered the plan's record of what was built
rests on citations nobody has dereferenced.

**The scale is the reason it matters.** There are over two hundred and fifty lanes. If the unresolvable
share is small the doubt is closed cheaply; if it is large, then a document that reads as a complete
account of the work is partly pointing at nothing, and that is worth knowing **before** a pull request
is opened rather than during review of one.

**Three distinct failures, and they must not be reported as one number.** A path that never existed, a
path that exists but is ignored by git and so would not survive a clone, and a commit id that resolves in
this repository but sits on no ref. The middle case is the quiet one: the file is on the author's disk,
the evidence reads as present, and a fresh checkout has nothing.

**Check both repositories.** A lane whose evidence lives under the backend names it relative to its own
root, and a checker run only from here will score every one of those as absent — which is the shape
`F-CROSS-REPO-EVIDENCE-UNVERIFIABLE` already records. Distinguish *not found here* from *not found
anywhere* or the census will manufacture a crisis out of a path convention.

**Validate the instrument before trusting its zero.** Prove the detector fires by feeding it a citation
known to be absent and one known to be present. An absence sweep whose pattern was never shown to match a
present instance is the exact defect `F-EMPTY-GREP-READS-AS-ABSENCE` names, and it would be an unusually
poor result to commit it inside the lane measuring citations.

Read only. Do not repair a single citation — name them. Repair is a later lane's work and some of the
repairs are not the clerk's to make.

### Lane L-CHECK-DISCOUNT-SUM-COUPLED — a sum that manufactures a zero and a guard that then hides the row
state: verified
class: node
pts: 2
owner: agent
exit: a check whose line discount is absent renders the discount row rather than dropping it, and the rendered group total agrees with the backend finalAmount, shown by a mounted test over present, zero and absent worlds in lanes/L-CHECK-DISCOUNT-SUM-COUPLED/mutation-log.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-CHECK-DISCOUNT-SUM-COUPLED/mutation-log.md

**Handed over by `L-XZ-RESIDUAL-SITES` as its `spec_gap`, after it ruled the site it was sent to look at
**keep**.** `CheckPanel.vue:293` is safe — `g` is not a wire object; `groups` seeds `discountAmount: 0` and only
ever adds a number, so the coercion there cannot be reached by an absence.

**Line 266 is the real one.** `g.discountAmount += line.discountAmount || 0` takes `line` straight off the
wire, so an absent line discount becomes a manufactured zero in the group total.

**And the two defects are coupled, which is why one lane owns both.** A null group discount then fails the
`> 0` guards and **deletes the discount row entirely**, while the backend's `finalAmount` still carries the
discount. The check shows a total that does not match its own lines, with nothing on screen to explain the
difference. **Fixing the sum without the guard moves the error rather than removing it.**

**Three worlds at every site, and the middle one is what a truthiness guard swallows.** Present, genuinely zero,
absent — `!0` is `true`, and a genuine zero discount on a check is a real reading. The distinction that survives
is `isAmountStated`, already in `utils/price.js`.

**Prove it against the backend number, not against itself.** The assertion that matters is that the rendered
group total agrees with `finalAmount` in the absent world — a test that only checks the row is present will
pass on a sum that is still wrong.

**The largest single reduction available to the blocker count, and it needs no ruling from anyone.**
The recheck re-derived all 41 sustained verdicts at the refs their document names and found **26 holds, 13
stale, 2 false.** The thirteen stale ones were true when written and have been overtaken by work that landed
since — the backend branch has moved **59 commits** past `3579bbbc`, and *"has not moved since 2026-08-02"* is
the document's largest stated fact and the one thing about it that expired.

**Stale is not the same as false and the distinction is the whole point of this lane.** A stale verdict's
premise was answered by a landing; a false one was never true. **Re-deriving at the tip tells you which
blockers a merge already closed** — and this program has spent two corrections today on people who conflated
the two, the clerk among them.

**Re-derive at `8e2b57de` and say what changed it.** For each, name the commit or the merge that overtook the
premise. A verdict that reads *overtaken* without naming what overtook it is an assertion, not a finding.

**Some will still be true at the tip, and that is a result.** A premise can go stale in its details while its
condition still holds. **Do not treat the thirteen as a list to clear** — treat it as a list to read.

**You may not clear a flag.** That is the clerk's act on a met condition, and several of these conditions name
no `fact:` key, so the tool will refuse them regardless. Say which are met; the clearing is somebody else's
step.

**Two instrument traps this shell has already produced, both worth avoiding by construction.** In zsh a bare
`$REF:path` applies a **history modifier** — `$T:WebApi.Tests/Wire/Foo.cs` becomes `8e2b57deryPinTests.cs`, and
git then reports the file absent. The recheck hit it, caught it, and re-ran every negative with a literal ref.
Use `"${REF}:path"` or a literal. And **a UTC stamp compared against a local mtime inverts an ordering by two

agent: opus

**Named by the lane that fixed the locator, as something it deliberately did not fix.** The e2e fixture serves
**no `GET /v1/meals/programs/{id}/members`**, so the membership read never answers, and the walk **always** takes
the unknown branch. **The pretick the enrolment panel was built for is never exercised by the journey that
covers it.**

**This is the reachability failure one layer out from where it is usually caught.** The panel is reachable, the
route is wired, the walk completes — and the capability under it has never been walked by anybody. A green
journey over a branch nobody takes is the same shape as a green suite over code nobody calls, which is why C3
exists.

**Closing it changes what the journey walks, which is why it is a separate lane and not a fix in passing.** The
existing walk is correct for the withheld-read world and that world is real — the panel renders a what/why
split precisely because the read can fail. **Keep an arm for it.** Both branches must be walked, or fixing this
merely swaps which one is dark.

**The locator lane's method is the standard here and it is worth copying exactly.** It refused to reason about
which of four matched elements the assertion meant: it dumped all four from real mounted DOM at the assertion's
own point in the walk, found exactly one that satisfied both conditions, and then ran the counterfactual —
showing that **had the read answered, two would still have matched**. That counterfactual is what proved the
spec wrong rather than the panel.

**Use the hook convention the panel already established** — `data-test` names, with `toHaveCount(1)` so a
duplicate hook cannot pass silently. `.first()` was explicitly refused on the sibling lane because under
mutation it would go on reading a different element and stay green with the subject deleted.

**Harness settings are load-bearing and already proved.** `CI=1` so Playwright never reuses a server — a
**foreign `api-server.js` holds port 4010** and a default-port run would silently walk another lane's fixture
and report a result about it. **Never kill that server.** Use your own ports with a free-port precheck; the
sibling used 3778/4778 and the bisect used 3777/4777.

sufficient: `meals-statement-month` defeated one in a **single hardcoded expression**, and every receipt from

newly-arrived journeys would 404** — and that is exactly the split that was observed. **A mechanism that
predicts which cases fail is a diagnosis; one that merely explains them afterwards is a story.**

nothing on its own. **Construct the world where a spec bypasses the granted port** — the hardcoded expression

and a divergence comparison in no suite. It is worth fixing at the cheapest layer first: **make it runnable,
and say what would have to run it.**

**Do not add a CI workflow.** Nothing in this repository runs any suite in CI today, and changing that is a
decision about cost and gating that belongs to Sven. **Name what a gate would need and stop there** — a lane
that quietly introduces the first CI gate has made a decision nobody asked for.

**Prove it reds.** A `lint` script that exits 0 on a clean tree proves only that eslint started. **Introduce a
violation of a rule already set to `error`, show the command reds, remove it, show it greens** — and assert the
violation actually landed before reading the result. A sibling's falsification run reported a *stronger* red
than reality because `head` closed a pipe and the workers took SIGPIPE.

**Expect the clean run not to be clean, and report the number rather than fixing it.** A repository whose
linter has never run will have accumulated violations. **How many, of which rules, is the finding** — and
fixing them is not this lane.

**Say whether the husky hooks should be repaired or removed.** Hooks that read a key the manifest does not have
are worse than no hooks: they look like enforcement to anyone reading the tree.

and this estate has already been bitten by a script that silently measured another tree.

### Lane L-LINT-TWO-REAL-DEFECTS — a dropped watcher and a property Vue silently ignores
state: verified
class: node
pts: 1
owner: agent
exit: pages/admin/overview.vue declares storeOverview once in its watch literal and components/admin/pos/ClockScreen.vue no longer declares a data key Vue cannot proxy, each shown by a test that reds when the defect is restored, in lanes/L-LINT-TWO-REAL-DEFECTS/mutation-log.md
agent: opus
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/Web-modules/lanes/L-LINT-TWO-REAL-DEFECTS/mutation-log.md

**Two of the 678 lint errors are defects rather than style, and the linter found them the first time it ran.**

**`pages/admin/overview.vue` declares `storeOverview` twice in one `watch` literal — at :533 and :541, the
clerk confirmed both — and the first is silently dropped.** It reads as dead code rather than a live money
defect, because another watcher performs the same reductions, **but that is a judgement about today's siblings
rather than about the code.** Establish which of the two bodies actually runs and whether they differ before
deleting either.

**`components/admin/pos/ClockScreen.vue:149` declares `_tick` in `data()`.** Vue 2 does not proxy
underscore-prefixed keys, **so the declaration is dead** and anything reading `this._tick` is reading something
else. Latent, and on the shared checkout only.

**This is the duplicate-key shape outside the guard that now catches it.** The dictionary guard is scoped to
translations; `no-dupe-keys` catches this one and nothing invokes eslint. **So the two findings together are the
argument for the wiring, not just two fixes.**

**Prove each by restoring the defect, not by asserting the fix.** A test that passes on the corrected file
passes equally on a file where the whole watcher was deleted. **Put the duplicate back and show the test reds**,
and do the same for the underscore key.

**Do not fix the other 676.** Three rules account for three quarters of them and are mostly auto-fixable; that
is a separate act with a separate review.



**Both defects were real and the interesting part was that "de-duplicate it" had a wrong answer.**
**The two watcher bodies differ.** The dropped one recomputed the order count and amount sum; **the surviving
one is the only thing normalising a store with no KAM id**, so keeping the earlier body would have silently
removed that. The lane built it as a mutation and the result is the finding: **lint-clean, zero `no-dupe-keys`
errors, and behaviourally broken.** That is why the guard is two behavioural tests as well as a rule.

**The dead property was measured rather than assumed, and against the wrong Vue than declared.** Installed is
**2.7.14 where `package.json` declares `^2.6.14`**. Against it, the underscore key is a plain instance property,
`$data` holds `null` forever, proxying is false, and there are **zero warnings at any level** — so the timer was
never broken and removal is behaviour-preserving.

**Each defect was restored one at a time rather than together**, so the two guards are shown independent: the
duplicate reds one test with the other component green, the property reds three with the first green, and the
lint delta is exactly one error per file with the other 676 untouched.

**Two instrument traps caught mid-flight, and the second is the nastiest of the set.** zsh applied `:c` as a
parameter modifier inside a quoted `"$ref:components/…"`, so git resolved a mangled ref; `2>/dev/null` hid the
fatal, **and the empty output hashed to the empty-string md5 — making four branches look as though they held an
empty file.** And a `grep -c` on the corrected file returned 1 by matching **its own new comment** rather than
code.

agent: opus

**Three German strings substitute a German institution for a Norwegian one, and one of them is on a fiscal

**organisasjonsnummer** prints on a receipt as a German **VAT identification number**, which is a different

commercial-register number. And **fødselsnummer** becomes **Sozialversicherungsnummer**, a social-security
number.

**English is faithful in all three**, so this is not a translation gap — it is a substitution, and it is
German-only.

**The receipt one is the reason this is a lane rather than a note.** A receipt is a kassasystemforskrifta
artifact. **Naming the number wrongly on it makes a claim about which authority issued it**, and it is the sort
of thing an inspection asks about precisely because it looks deliberate.

**Keep the Norwegian term and gloss it rather than reaching for a German near-equivalent.** That is the standard
the VAT lane set and the reason it flagged three of nineteen for a person instead of deciding them. **There is
no German identifier that means "Norwegian organisasjonsnummer"** — so the honest rendering names the Norwegian
one.

**Prove it on the rendered surface, not on the key.** Mount the receipt modal and the supplier surface in
German and read the labels back — a test asserting the dictionary changed passes on a screen that never shows
it.

**Check the fødselsnummer case for a second problem before touching it.** A social-security label on a personal
identity number is a data-protection wording question as well as a naming one, and if the surface should not be
showing that number at all, **say so and leave the string** — that is a different lane and a different owner.

### Lane L-IDENTITY-STUB-TESTS — fifteen suites that cannot see a wrong sentence
state: verified
class: analysis
pts: 1
owner: agent

agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-IDENTITY-STUB-TESTS/stubs.md

**A lane found one by accident and the clerk counted the rest: fifteen test files stub `$i` with a function
that returns the key.** Those suites mount a real component, drive a real path, and **assert on key names rather
than on sentences** — so a surface can render the wrong words in every locale and the suite stays green.

**It has already mattered twice tonight.** A supplier page test mounts the same page with that stub and **would
have passed either way** while a German string named the wrong issuing authority on a fiscal document. And a
receipt component turned out to have **no unit test of any kind**, which is how the same defect survived one
line above.

**This is not an argument for deleting the stub.** A test about layout or behaviour has no business resolving
copy, and the stub makes those tests readable. **The finding is the gap between what they cover and what a
reader would assume they cover.**

**So classify rather than condemn.** For each of the fifteen: what does it assert, and **is there any other test
that would catch a wrong sentence on that surface?** Where the answer is no, that surface is uncovered for copy
and saying so is the deliverable.

**The pattern that does work is already in the tree.** Two lanes tonight drove the **real** resolver at a real
locale and read the string back off rendered DOM — and each proved it by reverting the dictionary and watching
the assertions red. **Name that as the alternative where it is worth the cost, and say where it is not.**

Read only. Do not rewrite a test; the point is the map.



**My count was wrong in both directions, and the correction is more interesting than the number.** The
population is **23, not 15**. Over 128 non-e2e suites, 60 exercise the translator: **26 resolve the real
dictionary** — the multi-line shape **reads as a stub and mostly is not**, so counting by shape would have
inflated it — 4 use the real resolver outright, 7 are mixed, and **23 mount copy-blind with no copy assertion
anywhere.**

**Fourteen are the identity shape my regex found; nine stub `key + params` instead.** That echo shape is
exactly as blind and **matches no identity pattern** — which is where the missing eight lived. **There is no
global blinding**: every blind translator is a per-mount mock, which is why a setup-file sweep would have found
nothing.

**The worst row mounts four surfaces over 179 keys with zero sentence assertions in jest and zero in e2e** —
and a live defect is visible from it today: the X report prints **`MVA-samenstilling`**, a typo for
*sammenstilling*. The clerk confirmed the string. **Both suites mounting that view are green over it, and would
be green over any replacement.**

**Both worked cases held, and one classification was corrected in the useful direction.** The receipt component
is **uncovered rather than stubbed** — 23 keys, no jest test at all — which is a different remedy from
converting a stub.

**And the recommendation is not twenty-three conversions.** Convert the seven fiscal and money rows plus a first
receipt test; leave two that already resolve real dictionaries; and **one locale-parameterised journey re-run at
`de` would put a floor under every top-tier surface at once** — and would have caught both of tonight's
findings.

### Lane L-BUILT-BUT-ON-NO-REF — which reported work exists nowhere a clone could reach
state: verified
class: analysis
pts: 1
owner: agent
exit: every lane whose return reports built work is checked against whether that work is on a ref, and each case where it is not is named with the branch, what it holds, and where the work actually lives, in lanes/L-BUILT-BUT-ON-NO-REF/onref.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-BUILT-BUT-ON-NO-REF/onref.md

**Three instances found by accident in one night, so the question is worth asking on purpose.**
`lane/vat-keys-monolingual` **resolves to the modules tip and carries nothing** — nineteen VAT keys and a test
exist only in that lane's worktree. A till component and its **twenty-five translation keys are both untracked**
with four branches poised to overwrite them without conflicting. And the journey-guard repair sat on **0 of 115
refs** until a later lane committed it.

**None of the three was found by looking.** Each surfaced while somebody was measuring something else, which is
the definition of a gap nobody is covering.

**The check is cheap: a branch that resolves to the tip carries nothing.** Start there, then widen — a branch
can also carry a commit that touches only evidence, which the manifest review has already shown is easy to
count as a fix.

**Distinguish four states and do not collapse them.** On a shared branch; on a lane ref only; **in a worktree
only**; and **untracked in the shared checkout**. The last two are the ones that vanish, and they vanish
differently — a worktree can be removed, and an untracked file can be overwritten by a merge **without
conflicting**.

**Read the returns, not the plan's summary of them.** A lane's own words say what it built and where it put it;
this plan's prose is a second-hand account and has been wrong about containment twice tonight, both times in the
same direction.

**Do not commit anybody's work.** Where a lane's output is at risk, **name the lane and the path** — the lane
owns its commit, and a clerk or a sibling committing on its behalf is how a synthetic tree nobody ran gets
built.

**Enumerate all four ref namespaces** — `refs/heads`, `refs/lanes`, `refs/salvage`, `refs/remotes`. A
heads-only sweep has produced two published wrong answers in this program already.

**Two instances found by accident in one night, both in components nobody was auditing.** A focus trap declares

And a till screen declared `_tick` in `data()`, which **Vue 2 does not proxy**, so the declaration was dead and
anything reading it through the instance was reading something else.

**Neither was caught by a suite and neither could have been.** They do not throw, they do not warn — **they are
declarations the framework silently ignores.** Both were found by somebody reading the file for an unrelated
reason, which is not a strategy.

**The version question is part of the sweep, not background.** The installed Vue is **2.7.14** while
`package.json` declares `^2.6.14` — measured by a sibling. **2.7 accepts some Vue 3 shapes and not others**, so
"is this called?" has a version-specific answer and **the declared range is not the one running.**

**Enumerate the shapes rather than grepping for two.** Vue 3-only lifecycle hooks; underscore- and
dollar-prefixed `data()` keys; `emits` and `expose` options; composition-API imports in an options component;
setup-only constructs. **Say which shapes you looked for and which you could not check** — a sweep that finds two
because it searched for two is worth nothing.

**Prove one, at least.** For the strongest candidate, **show the declaration is not called** — a counter, a
throw, a log in the body that never appears. A sibling proved the dead property by measurement against the
installed Vue rather than by reading the docs, and that is the standard.

**Say what depends on each.** A dead teardown leaks; a dead data key is read as `undefined` somewhere. **The
consequence, not the count, is the deliverable** — and where nothing depends on it, that is a deletion somebody
can make safely.

Read only. Fix nothing; two of these live in components other lanes are editing right now.



**Reviewed 2026-08-05: APPROVE-WITH-CONDITIONS, and the one refuted claim was the one a lane was already
being dispatched on.** The clerk had copied it into that lane's brief, so the error was propagated before it
was caught; the correction was relayed mid-flight.

**Refuted, by reading the installed rule source rather than the documentation:**
`vue/no-unsupported-features` **does not read the version from `package.json`.** It takes its version **only
from its own rule option** — default `null`, and with none configured it returns an empty visitor and
**silently does nothing.** So *"fix the `^2.6.14` declaration and the rule gates correctly"* is wrong twice:
enabling it without an explicit `version` checks **nothing**, and in 6.2.2 its feature table gates four Vue
2.5/2.6 **template** syntaxes only — **it could never express the Vue 3 option-name class under any
configuration.** A guard built on that premise would have been inert, which is the failure this whole sweep
was about.

**Verified by independent re-derivation, not re-reading.** The denominator 317 was rebuilt from both
populations — 301 tracked plus 16 untracked, split 197/117/3 — and then checked with a **separate AST
instrument** over all 317 files, immune to the masker class that desynced one file. **All 22 aggregate key
counts reconcile exactly.** So the regex desync had exactly one casualty, it failed **loudly**, and nothing
among the 313 was silently mis-parsed. `_tick` verified non-live including all four branches; the
two-accepted/two-rejected hook split verified against the runtime source.

**The escalation was narrowed, and the narrowing matters.** *"Focus goes to a detached node in the next
modal"* is **refuted by the code and by measurement** — a later trap always outranks a stale entry, so the
sequential case is unaffected. The stale entry decides only when nothing live was pushed after it. **And even
then the symptom is enforcement lost, not focus landing in the detached subtree: a detached node cannot
receive focus.** The escalation is real; its mechanism and its observable symptom are not the ones a reader
of the lane alone would take away. **The clerk's own relay carried the wrong version of this too.**

**One arm marked non-probative and left standing:** an *activeElement was INPUT before and INPUT after*
reading is identical whether or not the restore works, because **the restore target is that input.** The
conclusion holds on the zero-call arm plus the code.

**Two conditions are edits to the lane's own evidence and to its return.** The return is not the clerk's to
edit — that is what made six earlier second returns unmergeable — so the correction is recorded here beside
it rather than written over it.

**A nuance the guard must carry:** `renderTracked` and `renderTriggered` are valid option names
unconditionally, but their wiring sits in a **dev-only block**, so their *invocation* is development-only.

### Lane L-VUE3-SHAPE-GUARD — a Vue 3 declaration in this Vue 2 app fails the build rather than doing nothing
state: verified
class: node
owner: agent
exit: a check reds on a planted `unmounted()` hook and on a planted `emits:` block, and passes on the tree once the two known instances are repaired, recorded in lanes/L-VUE3-SHAPE-GUARD/vue3-shape-guard.md
agent: vue3-guard
evidence: lanes/L-VUE3-SHAPE-GUARD/vue3-shape-guard.md

**The gap was measured, not assumed.** `vue/no-reserved-keys` **is** enabled and does catch the data-key
class — it errors on a planted `_tick`. But the same config reports **zero errors** on a real `unmounted()`
hook, because `eslint-plugin-vue` is **6.2.2**, which predates Vue 3: **no rule in it knows `unmounted` or
`emits`.** One class of this defect is guarded and the other has no guard installed at all.

**That asymmetry is why "somebody read the file" has been the only mechanism.** Two live instances were found
that way rather than by any tool — a teardown that never runs, and an inert `emits` declaration.

**The version declaration is load-bearing and must be fixed first.** `vue/no-unsupported-features` reads the
version from `package.json` (`^2.6.14`), **not from `node_modules` (2.7.14)** — so enabling it today gates
against a Vue this application does not run. Fix the declaration, then the rule.

**Do not over-reject: two Vue 3 names are valid in 2.7.** `renderTracked` and `renderTriggered` are real
hooks here; only `unmounted` and `beforeUnmount` are rejected. `LIFECYCLE_HOOKS` is exactly 14 names, and
`emits` has zero occurrences in the runtime. **A guard that reds on all four teaches people to disable it.**

**Prove it by planting, both ways.** A check that has never been shown to red is indistinguishable from a
check that matches nothing — which is the failure this whole class is made of.



**Built on 2026-08-05, and the lane made the guard a jest test rather than a lint rule — measured, not
preferred.** `@nuxtjs/eslint-module` is a devDependency but is **not** in `nuxt.config.js`'s `buildModules`,
there is **no `lint` script**, and the CI workflow runs only `npm run generate`. **`npm test` is the only
check runner this repository executes**, so a lint rule would have been precisely the failure class this guard
exists to catch: a control that is advertised and gates nothing. Reachability was confirmed from the
full-suite output rather than assumed — **C3 applied to the guard itself.**

**The version fix needed something the brief could not have known, and getting it wrong would have broken
CI.** `package-lock.json` carries its own root record of `vue`, and **`npm ci` refuses when that disagrees
with `package.json`** — so bumping the declaration alone would have traded a dead declaration for a broken
build. Both were moved and no resolved version changed.

**And it declined to run `npm ci` to verify, for a reason worth keeping.** `node_modules` here is a **symlink
shared with the main checkout and roughly a hundred worktrees**; `npm ci` would have deleted it. The sync
check was replicated across 48 dependencies instead. **That is the difference between proving a thing and
breaking the estate to prove it.**

**The deny list is subtracted from the live runtime rather than written down.** It asserts
`VUE3_OPTIONS_API_HOOKS − Vue.config._lifecycleHooks` equals exactly `[beforeUnmount, unmounted]`, and asserts
`renderTracked`/`renderTriggered` actually **run**. `emits` is denied on its zero occurrences in the runtime
bundle; `expose` and `compatConfig` are **deliberately not denied**, as unjustifiable from this runtime. **A
guard that cannot be wrong about which names are valid cannot teach anyone to disable it.**

**Planted both ways, in temp dirs and on the real tree.** Restoring `emits` reds at `Modal.vue:97`; restoring
the old version declaration reds; renaming the repaired hook back reds at the code site and **not** at a
comment that literally contains `unmounted ()` — the comment-matching trap this program has recorded before.

**Two things for whoever composes.** The guard's branch **stacks on the focus-trap lane's commit**, so if that
lane is not accepted this lane's exit needs rebasing. And `test/focus-trap-teardown.test.js` already carries a
**narrower duplicate** — a comment-stripping regex sweep for the two hook names with no `emits`, no planted
control for the sweep itself, and **files it cannot parse indistinguishable from clean**. It was left
untouched as instructed; **two answers to one question should become one.**

### Lane L-DUPLICATE-KEY-IN-THE-BUILD — the tier that ships is measured, not the tier that tests
state: verified
class: node
owner: agent
exit: lanes/L-DUPLICATE-KEY-IN-THE-BUILD/finding.md states what a duplicated translation key does to the production Nuxt build, shown by planting one and building
agent: dupkey-build
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/Web-modules/lanes/L-DUPLICATE-KEY-IN-THE-BUILD/finding.md

**A gap a lane named rather than papered over, and it is the half that ships.** The standing belief here was
that a merge can add a duplicate translation key cleanly, JS keeps the later entry, and nothing complains.
**At the test tier that is now known to be false**: the dictionaries are `.ts`, ts-jest type-checks them, a
duplicate raises **TS1117**, and the suite fails to *run* — loud, not silent.

**Nobody has measured the production build.** The lane that found TS1117 said so explicitly instead of
generalising from the tier it had. Nuxt may strip types with a transpiler that never type-checks, in which
case the duplicate **is** silent exactly where it matters and the guard lives only in a tier a release can
skip.

**Plant one and build.** Anything short of a real build answers a different question — a `tsc --noEmit` run
proves what ts-jest already proved. **Restore the plant byte-for-byte afterwards and show the tree is
clean**, because the dictionaries are shared with six other lanes' working copies.

**Report the answer either way as the deliverable.** *Silent in the build* and *loud in the build* are both
useful; what is not useful is a third document asserting the test-tier result again.



**Answered on 2026-08-05, and the answer is the one that mattered: a duplicated translation key is
completely silent in the production build.** The TS1117 result does **not** generalise to the tier that
ships.

**The command that ships is `npm run generate`, not `nuxt build`** — both deploy paths use it. Planted in
both editions, because the deployment config sets the Swiss edition: **exit 0 both times, 212 and 106 routes,
no TS1117 in either log, and the entire warning set byte-identical to each build's own pristine baseline.**

**The cause is one line.** `nuxt.config.js:37` sets `typeCheck: false`, so ts-loader runs transpile-only and
the type checker is never constructed. Measured on the planted file rather than assumed: transpile returns no
diagnostics, semantic analysis returns `1117`. **TS1117 is semantic, and a transpile-only loader cannot see
it.** The build then actively **preserves** the duplicate — Babel rewrites the literal so the later entry
wins. **The plan's original belief is exactly and deterministically true at the shipping tier.**

**The locale scoping in the brief was wrong, and getting it right is what makes the answer general.** The
edition locale list does **not** gate which dictionaries compile: the translations index statically imports
all three, so the Swiss build renders **zero Norwegian routes and still ships `no.ts` whole.** A duplicate
planted into a locale that edition never renders is compiled and shipped anyway.

**A one-line lever was measured in both directions and deliberately not pulled.** With type-checking on, the
pristine tree is still exit 0 at effectively the same build time, and the planted tree exits 1 with **exactly
one** diagnostic naming the file and line. **Changing the integration branch's gate affects roughly 130
in-flight worktrees, so it is a decision and not a lane's to take.**

**And the counts in the brief named a commit while describing a tree.** 4817/4782/4782 is HEAD; the shared
**working tree** is 5164/5129/5129, and the composition candidate is 5090/5055/5055 — verified independently
by the clerk. **That is the clerk's own instance of the error it has briefed five lanes to avoid.**

acknowledged**, and no such item can exist. **Fixing the render without fixing that condition changes
nothing.**

**No component test could have caught it, and this is why the exit names a journey.** Every part works in
isolation: the receipt is stored, the inbox reloads, the unread filter is correct. **The defect lives only in
the sequence a person performs.**

**The finding lane asserted the defect in its own journey, so your fix will red that walk. That is
deliberate.** Invert the assertion rather than deleting it — four tests asserting a defect have been found in
this program, and inverting is what keeps the record of what was once wrong.

**C5 binds the shape of the proof**: a green component suite is not evidence a worker can see their receipt.



**Built on 2026-08-05, fixed at the condition rather than the template — and the receipt line was left
untouched because it was always correct.** The act that fills the receipt is the act that marks the row read,
so the notice was removed and took the receipt with it. The repair keeps the row the worker pressed,
preferring the server's copy and falling back to the row as it was pressed, **so a failed inbox re-read cannot
take the receipt with it either.**

**Four arms, and the third is the one that earns the lane.** Green as committed; **red** with the receipt
render cut from the *final* file; **red with the render fully intact and only the feed reverted** — that arm
**measures** the claim that fixing the render alone changes nothing, instead of repeating it from the brief;
then green on the restored tree, and that run is the committed artifact.

**The journey's two assertions were inverted, not deleted, each keeping in a comment the mechanism it used to
pin.** And the old tracked capture that asserted the notice was *simply gone* was removed rather than left
sitting beside its own contradiction.

**A second gap closed as a consequence rather than as scope.** Because the acknowledge button now survives,
the idempotent replay and its already-acknowledged string finally have a **browser-reachable caller** — a
reachability gap the finding lane had recorded and nobody had claimed.

**C5 is explicitly not claimed.** Four fixture browser runs are a record that code behaves; the screenshot
showing the worker's actual screen is at
`lanes/L-WF-ACKNOWLEDGE-RECEIPT-VISIBLE/04-after-confirming-the-receipt-is-on-screen.png`, and the gate is Sven

### Lane L-ACK-RECEIPT-SURVIVES-A-RELOAD — a worker's receipt is still there after the page reloads
state: verified
class: analysis
owner: agent
dir: ../OkamAPI-modules
exit: lanes/L-ACK-RECEIPT-SURVIVES-A-RELOAD/finding.md states what the worker-side inbox read would have to return for an acknowledgement to survive a reload, and whether any existing endpoint already carries it
agent: ack-reload
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/Web-modules/lanes/L-ACK-RECEIPT-SURVIVES-A-RELOAD/finding.md

**The receipt a worker sees after confirming is session-scoped, and a reload loses it.** The inbox read
carries a read flag and **no acknowledgement field**, and the acknowledge endpoint has **no read sibling** —
so the confirmation exists only in the browser tab that produced it.

**It is the same defect one layer back from the one just fixed.** That repair made the receipt appear at all;
this is whether it is still there tomorrow. **A worker who confirms a published week and returns to check has
no way to see that they did** — and a personalliste surface where the worker cannot re-read their own
confirmation is worth little as evidence.

**Answer what the read must carry before proposing where it lives.** An acknowledgement timestamp on the
existing inbox row, a read sibling to the acknowledge endpoint, and a separate receipts collection are three
different contracts with different costs; **the finding should make the choice answerable, not take it.**

**Check whether something already carries it.** This estate has spent a lane re-deriving a fact that was
already correct on disk. **Read at the integration tip with `git show` and name the ref** — the backend
checkout sits on a lane branch, and reading the working directory has produced six wrong answers here.



**Answered 2026-08-05 at the backend tip, and looking before concluding paid: the write already exists —
twice.** Every confirm persists the acknowledgement to **two stores of different natures** — a **new row** in
an append-only receipts table, and an **in-place update** of a recipient column. **Nothing needs re-deriving.**

**The gap is one column.** The inbox read already loads the exact row that holds the answer and **stops one
column short of it**; the model it fills has nowhere to put it.

**No existing endpoint carries it, and the three failures are distinct.** The acknowledge endpoint returns
the original instant when one exists — but for a worker who has not confirmed, **the same call creates the
acknowledgement**. A reload calling it would **manufacture the evidence it claims to read**, on a table the
guard forbids deleting: **a write wearing a read's answer.** The manager endpoint does carry the column but
requires a manager role and returns coworkers' names, which the worker shell may not show. And the
**receipts table has no reader at all** — written by one path, read by no endpoint on any surface.

**C1 rules none of the contracts out, because all three are reads and the write already happens. What C1
decides is which store counts as evidence** — and there the cost inverts against intuition: **the cheap
contract reads the mutable store that *is* uniquely indexed, while the evidence-grade contracts read the
append-only store that is *not*.** Its race test is expected-red pending the duplicate-migration ruling.

**A scoping correction to the brief, and it matters for C6.** The acknowledgement is **not** a § 8-5-6
record — that artifact comes from three other tables. The worker surface carries no statutory reference
today, and **C6 would bite the moment a UI string called this row personalliste evidence.**

**The lane made the choice answerable and did not take it**, which is what it was asked for.

pre-existing red. **Not one suite and not one test differs**, compared key-by-key from the two JSON reports
rather than by totals — which was the exact failure mode the brief warned about. **All four templates stay
red in both arms.**

**No version of this upgrade can work on the Vue 2 line.** Every candidate routes templates through a
compiler utility that calls the buble fork **unconditionally**; the option surface has no opt-out, and the
transpile options only tune buble — they cannot make it parse. The latest such compiler was measured
directly: it throws on the modern form and accepts the older one. **Only the Vue 3 transpiler drops the
dependency, and it requires Vue 3.**

**So the two-line rewrite is not a workaround awaiting a real fix — on this line it is the only fix**, and
the real fix is a Vue 3 migration. **This closes the reopening condition attached to that ruling.**

**A useful boundary the lane drew:** the modern form is fine in a `<script>` body, because Babel handles it —
**only templates break.** A rewrite never has to touch script bodies, and one site in the same file needed
nothing.

**It caught a false pass while building its own probe, and the shape is worth keeping.** A failed transform
leaves an **empty module** in the registry, and Vue mounts it with only a console warning — so the first
probe reported **four green mounts for four templates producing no DOM.** It now asserts a compiled render

**And it measured pre-repair, deliberately noted:** the commit carrying the two-line fix is **not an ancestor
of the commit measured**, so the receipt modal was a genuine fourth case there. Its lines were not touched.

number and nothing else. **A German social-security number is twelve characters and contains a letter**, so it
fails that test, **passes the guard, and lands on statement lines the service's own comment says are frozen.**

should exist before rewording it, found the surface *forbids* a personal number rather than displaying one —
so no privacy leak in the label — and then found this underneath.

**Decide and state which exit you are meeting.** Refusing the broader shape is one answer; recording the
acceptance as deliberate, with what makes it safe on a frozen line, is the other. **Do not widen the guard by
guessing at a pattern** — a rule that refuses "things that look like identifiers" will refuse legitimate
references and be switched off.

**C1 is why the frozen line matters**: a value that should never have been recorded has no later repair, and
the comment saying the line is frozen is the point rather than colour.

**The SQL trap is live — three lanes hit it today.** Put `Database!=SqlServer` in the filter explicitly; a
SQL-tier red is one you have no grant to interpret. **Read at the tip with `git show 8e2b57de:<path>` and name
the ref** — the checkout sits on a lane branch and the world doctor reports it as a mismatch.



**Built 2026-08-05 on the refuse exit — and the ground it chose rules the other exit out rather than merely
losing to it.** The controller states its own read scope: a statement's company admin **or its store billing**
may read and export it. So a foreign identity number in this field is **disclosed to the restaurant, a third
party to the employment relationship**, through the export. C1 then forbids the repair, because the line is
frozen by a trigger. **A disclosure with no undo has no "what makes it safe" to record**, so the
record-it-as-deliberate exit had nothing honest to say.

**What is refused is stated precisely rather than by shape.** Three independent conditions must all hold —
the twelve-character form, a real calendar birth date, and the official check digit — verified against the
published example. **Roughly one in 274 false positives, better than the existing arm's one in 121.**

**And what is deliberately *not* constrained is the sharper judgement.** The regional prefix is left open,
because its issued list has gaps and moves — **a stale allowlist would make the guard accept a real number**,
which is the failure direction C1 punishes. Every unnamed format stays accepted, **each pinned by its own arm
with checksum-valid vectors, so adding one remains a decision rather than becoming a discovered gap.**

**The mutation pass found a real defect in the lane's own tests, which is the third time today a lane has
refused to stop at fourteen reds.** One mutant killed only one of six arms — checked for equivalence rather
than credited, and the cause is that a weight position multiplies a digit that is **zero for every month
before October**, so the single December vector is load-bearing and now says so. **Another mutant originally
survived**: both impossible-date vectors broke the day *and* the month, so neither could isolate either rule,

**One string claimed this control and was false; it is now true.** Two others now **understate** the guard,
naming only the Norwegian number — left to the translation lane deliberately, given the live collision flag.

### Lane L-CANNOT-BE-REBUILT-CENSUS — what a fresh clone of this estate cannot do, listed once

**Three separate things in this estate cannot be reconstructed from their own source of truth, and nobody has
listed them together.** A submodule pinned at a commit **reachable from no remote ref** — a fresh clone cannot
check out its own dependency, cannot build and cannot test, and today's work survives only because the object
already sits on this disk. A **dependency install that fails repository-wide** on an unresolvable
edge-channel package. And a **migration chain that cannot replay from empty**, recorded twice before.

**The census is the deliverable because the three are one question**: what does a person with a clean machine
and a clone actually get? **Nobody has answered it, and each finding was made separately by a lane looking at
something else.**

**Walk it, do not reason about it.** A clone into a scratch path, then each step in order, recording the exact
command and the exact failure. **A list assembled from three existing flags would repeat their assumptions**;
the point is to find the fourth thing nobody has hit yet.

**Do not repair anything.** Two of the three are owner-only — one needs a push to a remote, one a dependency
ruling — and a lane that fixes the third in passing makes the census unreproducible.

**Clone into a scratch path and never near the shared checkout.** Never run `npm ci` or `npm install` **in any
existing tree**: it deletes a `node_modules` shared by roughly 124 worktrees. In your own fresh clone it is
exactly the step under test, and its failure is a finding rather than an accident.

**Brace your refs** — `"${ref}:path"` — and never trust a `|| echo 0` fallback as a measurement; both have
produced false answers here today.



**Walked 2026-08-05, and the one-line answer is: a clone gets `main`.** It clones, initialises its submodule,
installs and builds. **None of the module program is reachable** — 135 frontend commits, 507 backend commits,
the pinned submodule object and the entire plan hub exist on this laptop and nowhere else.

**The gate nobody had named comes before the submodule, and the clerk verified it independently.**
`feature/restaurant-modules` **does not exist on either remote** — the checkout fails at `pathspec did not
match`, so the submodule pin and the dependency install were never the first failure. The check was proved
working before its empty answer was trusted.

**Two of the three inherited flags did not survive the walk, which is why walking beat assembling.** The
dependency install **succeeds** on a fresh clone — that hazard traced to an inference the same passage had
correctly declined to test, and *unsafe in this estate* and *fine in a clone* are **both true**, because 98 of
133 worktrees share one module tree. The real break is narrower and still owner-only: **any lock-free
resolution dies**, so the lock can never be regenerated. And the **migration chain has no duplicate-column
conflict on this branch at all** — 127 migrations replay from empty; the recorded double-add is on a
different branch.

**The fourth thing it was sent to find, it found: the test suite is red on any faithful clone.** Two
assertions pin the **checkout's directory name**, and the repository's real name is not that — so a default
clone fails them. Proven by isolating the one variable: rename the tree and they pass; rename it back and they
red. **A fifth**: the journey suite is red one in twenty-two because the configuration excludes a tag in one
mode and nothing in the other. **No workflow runs either suite, which is why neither was ever caught.**

**Two more it could not avoid noticing:** the plan directory is **826 files, none tracked and none ignored**;

### Lane L-FINALIZE-INDEX-OR-A-REASON — the finalize lookup exists on a chain-built database, or one index is shown to serve both
state: verified
class: sql
pts: 2
owner: agent
dir: ../OkamAPI-modules
exit: a database built from the migration chain carries both the finalize lookup and the fiscal backstop, or the plan records with a measurement why one index serves both reads, recorded in lanes/L-FINALIZE-INDEX-OR-A-REASON/evidence.md
agent: finalize-index
evidence: lanes/L-FINALIZE-INDEX-OR-A-REASON/evidence.md

**This is not a latent risk — it is the state of every database in the estate.** Two index configurations
claim the same journal columns eleven lines apart: a **non-unique finalize lookup** and a **unique
one-sale-per-order fiscal backstop.** Only the second exists — in the model, in the snapshot, and on every
deployed database.

**Nobody chose the drop.** An early migration created the name non-unique; a later one **dropped that name
and re-created it unique and filtered**, because the model only ever had one index to emit. **The migration
diff reads as entirely routine** — a deliberate-looking change produced by a one-word omission upstream.

**Answer the question before adding anything.** A unique filtered index may or may not serve the finalize
lookup's read; **that is measurable, and measuring it is the honest first step.** If one index does serve
both, the fix is a recorded reason and no migration at all — which is the cheaper and more likely correct
answer.

**You hold the only SQL slot and the only migration authorship.** If a migration is warranted, it is one
author's work and the chain is the truth, not the model — **C2 exists because two lanes generating against
one context produce two snapshots that each claim to be it.** Note that a duplicate-migration ruling is
already open elsewhere; do not collide with it.

**Never migrate anything but a local database, and verify what you are pointed at before running.** Build the
comparison from the chain replayed from empty, not from a model-built database — the estate has twice shipped
an object that exists in every model-built test database and in no migration.



**Measured before adding anything, and the measurement refuted the cheap branch.** On a database **replayed
from the chain rather than model-built**, with enough rows that a plan choice means something, four production
reads go at the journal by the same two columns. **The engine ruled on filter-implication itself** — a forced
hint raises an error when the predicate does not imply the filter, which is **statistics-independent** and
therefore not a benchmark that could drift.

**Two reads seek; two fall to a clustered scan and are refused the hint outright.** So **one index does not
serve both**: the surviving unique filtered backstop is **structurally incapable** of serving the two
handover reads — and one of them runs on **every sale**, scanning the whole append-only journal.

**The fix renames first and then creates, rather than dropping and re-creating**, so the one-sale-per-order
invariant holds **at every instant** rather than across a window. Proven on a chain build with a real
down-and-up round trip.

**A third instance of the model-only-object defect surfaced while generating**, and it was handled by removing
it rather than absorbing it: the generator swept in a table that exists **in the model and in no migration** —
the same shape as the two already recorded. It is **stripped from the migration and both snapshots**, and the
drift left exactly as found, because it is separately specified and owes a trigger this migration knows
nothing about.

**Two pieces of debt named for whoever merges.** The migration must be **re-parented** onto the stack when
that lands, taking a number **the stack's own ledger declares free** — and the lane deliberately made **no
ledger edit**, because the copy it can see lacks the intervening entries and writing the number in would have
**manufactured the conflict it was avoiding.** And a parked sibling **fails the day this lands, by design**;
it must be deleted in that merge.

**This is a census before a change, and the order matters.** Turning the check on without knowing what it
refuses would red a large part of the board at once, with no way to tell a mis-recorded pointer from a
missing artifact. **The count decides whether this is bookkeeping or a re-measure.**

**Sort by what the pointer is, not by whether it passes**: a named artifact that exists; a named artifact that
does not; a directory; and prose that was never a path. **The fourth is the largest group and the cheapest to
fix** — most are probably a sentence where a path belongs.

**Do not turn the check on.** The repair to the other half is landed and unreviewed; changing both halves
before either is reviewed makes neither reviewable.

**Brace your refs** — `"${ref}:path"` — and never trust a `|| echo 0` fallback; three checks failed silently
here today, each because its shape encoded an assumption.



**Census delivered 2026-08-06, proven through the real command line rather than by reading the code**: on a
throwaway copy of the board, promoting a lane with the evidence string *"I looked at it and it seemed fine;
no file was written"* returns **success**, while the identical string at verify returns the evidence refusal.
The real plan file was byte-identical across the run.

**The population grew while it was being measured — 284 to 290** — and six of those were promoted unchecked
since the prior census, **two of them the two prior lanes themselves.**

**The scope-deciding finding is that the refusal is on the exit side, not the pointer side.** **165 of the 290
belong to an entity whose exit names neither a fact nor a path**, so **no evidence string of any kind can
satisfy them** — 77 per cent of the refusals. Trimming every pointer to the artifact already inside it admits
**six**. And **260 of 289 open entities are written the same way**, so the population keeps growing.

**That fixes the order: the exit-writing rule must land and drain the open queue before the checker is turned
on**, or 213 rows red at once with no way to tell a mis-recorded pointer from a missing artifact.

**A finding about the landed repair, and it is the useful kind.** Every one of the 141 resolving artifacts is
markdown or text — **not a single JSON** — so the carefully-reasoned status reader and the directory refusal
are **both correct and both inert on this half.** The repair is sound and does nothing here.

**The brief's hypothesis is refuted on measurement and recorded rather than improvised around:** prose is
neither the largest class nor the cheapest. **The cheapest group is five artifacts written to the wrong
directory — a move.**

**Four of its own searches were the shapes this program has catalogued**, and each reported artifacts absent
that were on disk: a status call missing its untracked flag, a depth-limited find that stopped one level
short, an assumed naming convention, and **unexpanded brace syntax in nineteen pointers, which alone falsely
reported nine artifacts lost.**

**The cheapest group it named was executed by the clerk on 2026-08-06, and it was a record job rather than a
repair.** Five artifacts had been written under the plan directory instead of the repository's lane
directory, because the lanes wrote **relative to the plan rather than to the repo root** — so their pointers
were correct and the files were in the wrong place.

**All five moved, and the sixth was a byte-identical duplicate**, verified by hash before either copy was
touched — the same file existing twice, one of which was deleted rather than moved over the other. **All six
pointers now resolve**, and the misplaced directory is empty and gone.

**The 165 exits were not rewritten and must not be.** The census says why and it is right: **an exit is the
entity's contract, and rewriting one to fit the evidence already recorded against it is the failure this
whole line of work exists to stop.** That work is the owner's or a lane's with a fresh reading of what each
capability actually owes — never the clerk's tidying.

### Lane L-ADMIN-JOURNEY-WAIT-DIAGNOSES — a dead application fails as a dead application, not as a URL timeout
state: verified
class: node

evidence: lanes/L-ADMIN-JOURNEY-WAIT-DIAGNOSES/kill-proof.txt

**A hard-coded thirty-second wait for a redirect is copied into roughly twenty admin journeys, and it reports
a dead application as an undiagnosable URL timeout.** That is not an inconvenience — **it is the shape that
let a false red stand as evidence for three days**, and that red was in turn what made a `verified` lane
demonstrably false.

**The diagnosing lane could not reproduce the failure and deliberately did not touch this**, which was
correct: a guessed change to a spec twenty journeys share is improvisation. **Its evidence is at
`lanes/L-GROWTH-SEND-GATE-WALK-IS-GREEN/` and names the mechanism** — that run recorded the browser never
reaching the API at all, with the wait swallowing the fact.

**Make the failure name its cause, not the timeout.** A step that waits for a redirect should say **what it
was waiting on and what answered instead** — an application that is not listening, a shell that never
rendered, a redirect that fired elsewhere. Those are different faults and today they are one message.

**Prove it by killing the server, not by reading the code.** Your exit is an arm that stops the application
and reads what the journey then says. **A message never shown under a real failure is indistinguishable from
one that never fires.**

**Do not change what the journeys assert.** Twenty specs share this; widening the fix into their assertions
makes the diff unreviewable and risks the false-green shape one repo along.

**Never bind port 4010** — a foreign fixture lives there and has produced a wrong green; ports 4971 and 4973
also hold foreign fixtures. **Record the port you actually bound.** Never kill a container you did not create.

**Do not capture in the primary checkout.** It carries 354 uncommitted paths, six under the e2e harness, so a
capture written there names a commit while driving a harness that is not that commit's.



**Built 2026-08-06 in one file — the sign-in helper shared by 31 admin journeys — and proven by killing the
server rather than by reading the code.** Paired arms, same journey, same wait, same kill:

**Before**, a bare navigation timeout naming nothing. **After**, *"the API is not listening — the application
is up, the shell rendered, and nothing answered"*, with each question answered separately: the application
returned 200, the shell was present, the API refused the connection, and the modal's own words are quoted.
**The original error is kept verbatim underneath.**

**And the diagnosis lands in the artifact, not only the console** — which is the point, because **the artifact
is what stood as evidence for three days.**

**A bonus finding closes the sibling's open question.** Its control arm reproduces the original red's signature
**exactly** — same status, same zero-served count, the identical timeout sentence. The sibling could not
reproduce that red; this shows **a fixture that stopped answering is sufficient to produce it.**

**It declined to claim a branch it could not fire.** Killing the application stops the run **earlier**, at
navigation, with an error that already names its own cause; killing both at the right instant lost the race
three times out of three, because the window is six keystrokes wide. **That branch is marked as not-shown in
the source rather than presented as verified.**

**And it named a product defect it deliberately did not fix, which the clerk confirmed by reading the file.**
With nothing listening at all, **the login modal still advances to the code step and offers six boxes for a
code it never sent.** The request layer **resolves** failed requests to the error object instead of rejecting,
so the send maps that to false, and the modal sets its sent flag inside a `.then()` **that never reads the
value** — leaving the wrong-number branch **unreachable for any server-side failure.** Thirty-one journeys
share that file and none is about the modal, so it is correctly somebody else's lane.

agent: opus

**`D-PREF-ORIGIN` was ruled `named-cors-policy-plus-samesite-none` on 2026-08-03 and only half of it was
built.** Measured 2026-08-06:

- **The CORS half exists** at `2a052800` — `AllowCredentials` twice in `Helpers/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs`,
  `[EnableCors(ClaimConstants.GrowthGuestCorsPolicy)]` on three actions of `GrowthPreferenceController`, and a

  match it.

fact encodes the ruled option correctly; the option is unexecuted.

### Lane L-TRAINWIRE-ABORT — the training wire tier finishes instead of taking the host down
state: verified
class: suite

dir: ../OkamAPI-modules
exit: the non-SQL tier at a checkout of 06b8b582 completes with a counted pass/fail/skip triple rather than Test Run Aborted, shown by a trx enumerating all 4650 tests, recorded in /Users/svendaneel/okam/Web-modules/docs/plan/lanes/L-TRAINWIRE-ABORT/finding.md
agent: opus
evidence: /Users/svendaneel/okam/Web-modules/docs/plan/lanes/L-TRAINWIRE-ABORT/finding.md

**This gates a landing that is otherwise finished.** `L-TRAIN-DISCLOSURE-LAND` performed the merge cleanly —
real merge, 59/1 divergence, **zero conflicts** — and then measured that it cannot be landed: the merged tier
counts **4100 of a 4650 baseline** and then aborts, so roughly **550 tests never run.**

**It is not the merge.** A clean checkout of `06b8b582` with no merge at all aborts identically. Landing first
would convert a green tier into an abort and the cause would then look like the merge.

**The cause is named and the fix is named; neither was written, deliberately.** `TrainingWireTests:1096` runs
`Assert.All` over `JsonElement`s taken from a `JsonDocument` that its `using` has already disposed — the host
dies with `ObjectDisposedException` inside `Xunit.AllException.get_Message`, which is why the failure presents
as a host crash rather than a test failure. The assertion also claims `actorIsSubject` is false for **all**
rows while two sibling tests write subject rows into the same shared fixture, so the claim is only true of the
rows this test causes.

**Two changes, both small:** materialize the elements before `Assert.All`, and scope the all-false claim to the
rows this test writes. Do not silence it and do not widen the fixture.

**Prove the failure before you fix it.** A tier that aborts is not a tier that fails, and the difference is the
whole finding — show the abort, then show the completed triple.

### Lane L-LIVE-WORLD-TWO-HUMANS-WALK — a manager and a worker complete one week-run in a single live world
state: verified
class: sql
owner: agent

agent: opus
evidence: artifacts/journeys/workforce-week-run-two-humans.playwright.json

**The recipe exists and was measured; what is missing is a slot.** `L-LIVE-WORLD-SECOND-HUMAN` established
every step and could not stand a world up because it held no SQL slot.

**Wall 1 — two sign-ins — closes with one configuration value and no code change.** `live-world.sh:346-349`
already launches the API with env overrides; setting `AppSettings__AdminUserPhoneNumber` to a
`+0123456789`-shaped value opens the power-user door alongside the demo door in the same process. **That is
production's own lever, not a manufactured one** — the door already exists at `UserController.cs:179` and its
key is simply held outside the repository.

**Put the power-user door on the MANAGER and the demo door on the worker.** It grants `PowerUserRole`, which
`StoreAdminAuthorizationHandler.cs:17` makes a StoreAdmin of every store — on a worker that would silently
make *"a worker cannot reach the manager's pages"* false. On the manager it only over-determines an
authorization the walk already asserts separately.

**Wall 2 — the engagement — closes with no owner act at all.** Endpoint 6 returns the raw claim token exactly
once and never persists it (`Token = null, // never persisted` at `WorkforceInvitationService.cs:163`), gated
**service-side at `WorkforceInvitationService.cs:83`** rather than by a controller attribute — the controller
carries only `[Authorize]` at `:29`. Endpoint 32 claims it with no capability **and no module gate**, which is
wider than intended; see `F-INVITATION-CLAIM-IGNORES-THE-MODULE`. The seeded staff are created `Invited`, which `MayBeClaimed`
accepts.

**Wall 3 was unnamed until this week and belongs in the walk rather than the seed.** `workforce.selfservice`
and `workforce.publication` are both deny-closed — `DefaultOn` holds `workforce.setup` alone — so **the manager
must flip both on `/admin/feature-flags` as a step**, and the published week must assign the claimed
engagement a shift, since the acknowledger has to be a publication recipient.

**Two things you must not do.** Do not generate a phone-change token to manufacture a third identity: it is
Identity TOTP keyed on `AspNetUsers.SecurityStamp`, which a seed with SQL access can read, making any user's
code computable offline — a credential path production does not have. And **generate both
`AppSettings__AdminUserPhoneNumber` and `AppSettings__PowerUserVerificationCode` at run time and print
neither**, rather than relying on the committed code — see `F-POWERUSER-CODE-IS-COMMITTED`.
