### Lane L-A-LOGIN-TOKEN-EXPIRES-WITHIN-A-SESSION — the hundred-year token stops being unrevocable by construction
state: verified
class: node
owner: agent
dir: ../OkamAPI-modules
exit: the token /User/login issues expires within an ordinary session lifetime and its SMS companion refuses a caller that asks too often, shown by a wire proof of both that reds against the current behaviour, recorded in lanes/L-A-LOGIN-TOKEN-EXPIRES-WITHIN-A-SESSION/evidence.md
agent: opus
evidence: lanes/L-A-LOGIN-TOKEN-EXPIRES-WITHIN-A-SESSION/evidence.md

**`/User/login` returns a JWT with `AddDays(36500)` — `UserService.cs:547`. A hundred years.**

**And there is no revocation path.** `Helpers/ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:195-204` fails
`OnTokenValidated` **only when the user row no longer exists** — no security stamp, no denylist. So
*"expires in 100 years"* is operationally *"cannot be revoked short of deleting the user"*, and **that
decides the shape of the remediation**: shortening the lifetime is the fix that is actually available,
because a revocation list is a larger change than this lane.

**It is delivered in a body that the wildcard `access-control-allow-origin: *` makes script-readable from
any origin**, so a token that never expires is also a token any page can pick up. That wildcard is
recorded separately and is **not yours to change here** — but it is why the lifetime matters more than it
would elsewhere.

**Its SMS companion is `Controllers/UserController.cs:161-181`** (route attribute at `:162`) and it is
unlimited. **Both halves are in the exit** because a short-lived token that can be re-minted without
limit is not a smaller attack surface, only a busier one.

**Pick the lifetime from evidence and name it.** Read what the clients do — whether anything refreshes,
and what breaks when a token expires mid-session — before choosing a number. **A number that logs
everyone out every hour with no refresh path is a worse product, and saying so with the reason is a
legitimate outcome** that turns this into an owner question rather than a bad guess.

**The module produces its own anti-pattern on the one day a venue is most likely to look.** A venue that
switches Margin on and trades the same day sees **theoretical 0,0 % beside a real actual** — and it heals
overnight, so whoever looks first sees the worst version and nobody who looks later can reproduce it.

**The mechanism is precise.** `MarginPeriodSalesAnalyzer` resolves product links, recipe versions and
prices at `fact.BusinessDate`, which is a calendar date stored at **`00:00:00`**. Anything created
*during* the trading day fails `EffectiveFrom <= instant` against that day's own sales.

**One of the three consequences is escapable through the product and two are not** — the flag records
that links can be backdated via the DTO's `effectiveFrom`, **a field the UI deliberately never sends**,
and that doing so moved coverage from **0 % to 93,41 %**. **Read the flag in full before choosing
where to fix it**: backdating from the UI, comparing against the sale instant rather than midnight, and
resolving at end-of-day are three different products, not three spellings of one fix.

**Say which you chose and what it costs.** Comparing against the sale instant is the answer that matches
what the numbers mean, but it changes what every historical statement would recompute to — **check
whether anything depends on the current behaviour before you assume it is safe.**

C1 is in force: statements are append-only. **Do not repair existing rows** — this lane changes what
future statements compute, not what past ones said.

No migration without saying so first. Never touch `okam-lwtwo-sql` or `okam-lwtwo-redis`, never bind

**Measured at the landed pair, and larger than anyone has said out loud: 313 `lane/*` branches are not
ancestors of their trunk** — **111** frontend against `a63c30f`, **202** backend against `a1c1a6dff`.
Four landing waves carried twelve named branches. The rest has never been sorted.

**Most of it is almost certainly dead, and proving that is as valuable as finding the live ones.** A
prior census found **62 frontend and 112 backend** completed-lane refs whose files matched nothing in
the landing tree. **A row that says "absent, and here is the check" retires a branch permanently**; a row
that says "might be something" retires nothing.

**One is already known to be real and is the reason this lane exists.** `lane/wf-kodeoversikt-ui` at
`f4c355b` carries **four commits** and is not on the trunk — the § 8-5-6 identity-code register button,
whose absence the plan-gap reading named as Workforce's single largest gap. **If one survived four
landing waves unnoticed, others will have.**

**Four buckets, and each needs a different check:**
1. **carries-unlanded-product-work** — commits whose content is on no other ref. `git cherry` plus a
   tree probe, not a branch-name guess.
2. **patch-carried** — the change is already on the trunk under a different commit. `git patch-id` is

HEADs**; under `--single-worktree` two commits turned out to be on no named ref at all.

`getRandomValues`, Node `crypto`, then an explicit named throw. **Eight call sites depend on it**: two
cash-out RETRECs, a drawer movement, a payroll-bearing punch, two invitation claims, and the
`Idempotency-Key` header on **every** Workforce mutation.

**C4 is why this needs a reading rather than a nod.** A repeated key is a replayed money write — the
lane's own citation is that the server dedupes, returns the earlier posting, and **the UI reports success
while the drawer is short by 4 500**. **Check every rung for a path that could return a repeatable
value**, including under concurrent calls in one tick.

   non-CSPRNG**, including the Node path's behaviour when `crypto` resolves but is a stub.

   `Error`, not a bare `ReferenceError`. **Check the message says something actionable.**
3. **The bundler claim is measured, so re-measure it.** The lane reports `__non_webpack_require__` with a
   `module.require` fallback keeps the file at **1,386 → 2,651 minified bytes, 1 → 2 modules, zero
   crypto-polyfill modules**, against **208 modules / 1.36 MB** for a literal `require('crypto')`. **That
   technique is invisible to webpack's parser by design, which is exactly why it deserves a second pair
   of eyes** — confirm it does not break the Node/SSR path it exists to serve.

**One scope correction already established, so you do not re-derive it**: only **two** components were
ever unmountable — `ReturnBuilder` and `RefundModal`, which call `newGuid` from `data()`. The other four

against an `engines` field of `22.x`, and **node 16 has no `crypto` global**. The lane did not
demonstrate a prerendered route reaching `newGuid`. **Say whether the generate step can reach it.**

agent: opus
evidence: docs/plan/lanes/L-A-WORKER-SEES-WHAT-SHE-CONFIRMED/evidence.md

**Found by walking it, which is the only way it could have been found.** The worker presses **Bekreft**
and **is shown nothing at all.**

**The mechanism is a contradiction the code cannot escape**: `acknowledge()` stores the receipt and then
reloads the inbox — but acknowledging implies *seen*, so the item drops out of the unread list and the
entire notice is `v-if`'d away, **taking the receipt with it.** So the fix is not a missing render; it is
that the receipt must outlive the thing that carried it.

notice that never leaves the DOM in the harness — which is precisely the world the defect does not live
in. **Pin it in the week-run journey.**

### Lane L-MAIL-CONNECTS-ON-A-HOST-THAT-CANNOT-CHECK-REVOCATION — one property decides whether any mail leaves at all

exit: a send over the product's own transport completes its TLS connect on a host that cannot complete a certificate-revocation check, shown by a probe that reds against the current bare client, recorded in docs/plan/lanes/L-MAIL-CONNECTS-ON-A-HOST-THAT-CANNOT-CHECK-REVOCATION/DECISION-RECORD.md
agent: opus

**A lane went looking for why Events guest links never arrive and refuted the recorded cause.** The
fourteen failures are **not** the missing `SmtpFromPassword`: the session dies in `ConnectAsync`, **before
`AuthenticateAsync` is ever called** — the world's own log says `after 0 sent … SmtpStatus none`. **A
password that is never offered cannot fail a handshake.**

**The real cause is one unset property.** `MailKitSmtpTransport` does `new SmtpClient()` and sets nothing,
so MailKit's `CheckCertificateRevocation` keeps its default **`true`**, and this host cannot complete that
check. Measured, not argued: same host, same port, same options with revocation **off** connects, brings
TLS up, and the server **advertises AUTH**. One property is the whole difference.

**The blast radius is why this is a blocker and not a test-harness note.** `IEmailService` is the **one
mail seam** for **fourteen callers** — confirmation codes, invoices, POS receipts, payouts, Workforce,
Growth, end-of-day, SAF-T. **On any host with the same constraint, none of them can send.**

**The production host was not measured and you should not assume it.** Whether prod completes revocation
checks is unknown here. **Say what you can establish and what you cannot** — a fix that is right for this
host and wrong for prod is worse than the defect.

**Do not simply flip the flag off and stop.** Revocation checking exists for a reason. **Decide from the
code and say why**: whether it should be off always, off only outside production, or configurable with a
safe default. A dev-only certificate callback is a separate and more dangerous switch — **if you add one,
it must be impossible to reach in production**, and prove that rather than assert it.

**C7 is in force and this is its neighbourhood.** No password, host, token or certificate material into a
config file, a log, a fixture or a commit.

**A successful send prints nothing in this world** — `Logging:LogLevel:WebApi=Warning` suppresses every
`EmailService` information line. **Your evidence must be the transport's own result or a sink capture,
never an API log line.**

**The live API cannot be re-pointed without a restart** — `Program.cs:52` and `EmailService.cs:23-28`
bind `IOptions<AppSettings>` once — and **restarting it is not yours**. A probe against your own build is
the shape that works; a sibling lane proved a loopback sink accepts a message once revocation is off and
a certificate callback is present.

### Lane L-READ-THE-REVOCATION-LEVER — a security check was switched off and someone else has to agree it was the right one
state: verified
class: analysis
owner: agent
dir: ../OkamAPI-modules
exit: a verdict on lane/mail-revocation-lever 69e6ca8af, naming whether unset truly binds to true through the real configuration path, whether anything other than revocation was relaxed, and what a revoked provider certificate would now do, recorded in docs/plan/reviews/L-READ-THE-REVOCATION-LEVER.md
agent: L-READ-THE-REVOCATION-LEVER
evidence: docs/plan/reviews/L-READ-THE-REVOCATION-LEVER.md

**This lane weakened a certificate check to unblock mail, and that is a trade worth a second reader.**
`lane/mail-revocation-lever` @ **`69e6ca8af`** off backend trunk `81d06c10a`. It is the fix for all
fourteen `IEmailService` callers, so if it is wrong it is wrong everywhere at once.

**The load-bearing claim is a language detail, and language details are where this fails.** The lane
says `AppSettings:SmtpCheckCertificateRevocation` is a **`bool?`** where **unset means true**, and that
a plain `bool` would have read `false` from a missing key and **silently disabled revocation checking
estate-wide with no diff to review**. That reasoning is correct in the abstract. **Prove it holds through
the actual binding path this codebase uses** — `IConfiguration` binding, `Configure<>`, options
validation, whatever it really is. **Three cases the claim must survive**: the key **absent**; the key
present but an **empty string**; the key present as the string `"false"` in a different casing. If any
of those lands on `false` when the author expects `true`, that is the finding.

**Then ask what was relaxed besides revocation.** The lane asserts **no `ServerCertificateValidationCallback`
is added on any path in any environment**, and offers the absence as proof. **Grep for it yourself
across the whole backend, not just the diff** — the strength of that claim is exactly its scope, and
scope claims are the easiest to overstate.

**Name the consequence in plain words, because nobody has.** With the switch on, **what happens if the
provider's certificate is genuinely revoked?** The lane's own evidence says the chain's only fault is
`RevocationStatusUnknown` — a host that cannot *reach* the revocation endpoint. **A host that cannot ask
and a certificate that has been withdrawn are indistinguishable once the check is off.** Say whether the
resulting exposure is acceptable and for whom, or say it is not.

**Check the refactor did not change behaviour it was not meant to.** `MailKitSmtpTransport` was moved
**out of `EmailService` into its own file**. Compare old and new for timeout, disposal, authentication
order, and `Connect` overload — **a move is where a silently dropped `using` hides**.

**Only the client half of this defect is fixed, and the wire still tells the lie to everyone else.**
`POST /workforce/pos/clock-events` answers a clock-out with **no open session** as
`200` · `accepted: true` · `clockSessionId: null` · **`sessionState: "Open"`**, because **the field is
derived from `closedUtc` alone** — so an absent session and an open one are indistinguishable.

**What it does to a person, which is why it is a blocker and not a tidy-up.** A register bound to
`sessionState` **flips to "clocked in" at the moment a worker presses *Stemple ut***. She leaves believing
she clocked out; the register carries **no end time**; and the hour that reaches **payroll, the attendance
record and the § 8-5-6 personalliste** is wrong in the same direction.

**The client fix is already in** — `utils/workforce/pos-clock-state.js` makes `clockSessionId`
authoritative. **Do not undo or duplicate it.** Your job is the wire, so that a second client, a partner
integration or a future screen cannot inherit the lie.

**`accepted: true` on an act that accepted nothing is the other half of the defect.** Decide deliberately
whether the endpoint should refuse, or answer truthfully with a state that is not `Open` — **the flag
permits either**. Write which you chose and why. **If you choose to keep `200`, say what a caller is meant
to branch on.**

file, watched failing, reverted. Report the count. **A test that survives every mutation you can think of

`docs/plan/lanes/L-THE-LAST-UNTESTED-MEALS-AND-EVENTS-SCREENS/mutate.js` restores a mutated file with

**Run against uncommitted work — which is every lane mid-flight — it deletes the lane's own edits.**

**It has already fired once.** It did exactly this to `plugins/global-mixin.js`. Nothing was lost, because
that runner's own **verify-after-restore** assertion caught the mismatch and halted — **the guard saved it,
not the restore**. The lane re-applied by hand and wrote its own buffer-based replacement.

**The reason this is a blocker rather than a note: the broken copy is still sitting where the next lane
will find it.** Three lanes this evening copied a sibling's mutation runner as their starting point. The
next one to copy this file gets a tool that silently reverts its work at the first restore, and the only
thing standing between that and lost work is an assertion the copier might strip as noise.

**Do three things.**
1. **Sweep**: grep every `mutate*` script under `docs/plan/lanes/` for `git checkout`, `git restore` and
   `git stash`, and **list every one you find** — the report is half the deliverable, because nobody knows
   how many copies exist.
2. **Replace, do not patch.** The correct implementation reads the original into memory, writes the
   mutation, then restores **from that buffer** and asserts the bytes match. `lane/eleven-wolt-statuses…`
   @ `32518da` carries a working one — **read it rather than writing a third variant.**
3. **Keep the verify-after-restore assertion in every copy**, and say in your return why it must never be
   removed: it is the only reason this defect cost nothing.

**One boundary.** Lane directories are other lanes' evidence. **You may replace a broken tool, but do not
edit any lane's findings, logs or results**, and say exactly which files you touched.

description.

**"Tilbudet er utløpt"**. So a network blip makes a guest phone the venue asking them to reissue an offer
that is **still live**, and the venue has no way to know the offer was fine. **The page must distinguish
"we could not load this" from "this has expired."**

onto `offerProposal` unguarded, so a `200` with an empty body parses to `''` and **blanks the page after the
order is placed** — no confirmation, no error, no way back. **The order exists and the guest cannot tell.**
That ordering is what makes it a blocker: the damage is on the far side of the money.

`RED`**. So the defect is not merely unguarded — it is asserted as the contract, which is why it survived a
hardening pass whose stated purpose was this class of bug.

**The same hole is why it cannot judge a .NET suite** (`F-THE-CANONICAL-MUTATION-RUNNER-CANNOT-JUDGE-A-DOTNET-SUITE`):
the red-name counter reads **jest markers only**, so every xunit run prints `RED (0)` — indistinguishable
from a void run. **One fix should close both, and if you find it cannot, say why.**

4. **Add two void-direction pin arms** — one per exit direction.

`DESTROYED` reproduction arm, the standing tree-wide sweep, anchor repair, and copy-depth resolution via
`package.json`. **The gate confirmed all of these hold.** A previous lane also proved that the zero-test
abort must not be a `process.exit` inside the mutated window — `process.exit` does not run a `finally`, so
aborting after applying a mutation leaves the mutant on disk. **Measure the baseline before a single byte is
written.**

**Two disclosures to preserve rather than quietly resolve.** A sibling lane deliberately changed a self-test
that asserted a crash yields `RED` — *that is the defect, not the contract* — to assert `INVALID`. And

branch is now landable**, since a landing lane is waiting on that answer.

**do not land anything** — build the fix and report.

**A signed-in user can give away a gift card they have never owned, if they can guess or obtain its id.**
Verified by the clerk at trunk `057c390ad`: `Controllers/GiftcardController.cs:232-237` declares
`[HttpPost("transfer/{giftcardId}/{newReceiverPhoneNumber}")]` and calls
`_giftcardService.TransferGiftcard(giftcardId, newReceiverPhoneNumber)` — **the caller's identity never
reaches the service.** The class carries a bare `[Authorize]`, which establishes only that *somebody* is
signed in.

**`CancelPurchase`, directly above it in the same file, IS role-gated.** So this is not a codebase without
the concept — it is one place that was missed, which is why it reads as safe on a skim.

**The lane that found this deliberately did not fix it, and its reasoning is your starting point.** The
service takes **no actor at all**, so the check cannot be expressed without changing the signature and its
callers — **a different change that should not ride inside a money fix.** It was right to hold. **You are
the lane that does it properly.**

**An independent review has since named the same change, without being asked to.** The Fable reading of
the two money fixes ranked this **above both of them**: *"TransferGiftcard moves value with no resolved
caller identity, a standing C4 breach the lane disclosed and did not close."* Its named change is
**resolve the caller, require `giftcard.ReceiverUserId == callerId`, record the actor.** Two independent
readings converging on one change is the strongest signal this program produces — **but implement it
because you verified it, not because two agents agreed.**

**That review also settled what makes this expensive.** `GetBalance` sums `Purchased` minus `Redeemed`
**by `UserId`, never joining the card** — which is why value moved this way is untraceable from the card
itself. A wrongly transferred card is not merely misfiled; **the balance follows the new holder and the old
holder's own record cannot explain it.**

**This is a C4 obligation** — an actor on money writes — so **name what the actor is** in your return:
the authenticated user id, and how it is obtained on this path. **Do not invent a second mechanism if the
estate already has one**; find how other money-path actions establish the caller and follow it.

**Decide and state what a refusal looks like.** A `404` and a `403` say different things to an attacker
probing for valid ids: one conceals whether the card exists, the other confirms it. **Say which you chose
and why.** This is the kind of call that should be visible in the record rather than inferred from a status
code.

**Enumerate every caller of the service method before you change its signature.** A widened signature with
an un-updated call site is precisely the shape that produced a **clean merge that did not compile** in this
program — `git merge` reported success and the tree failed to build, because a test called a method a lane
had widened. **Grep call-site arity after your change.**

ownership check against the pre-fix body means writing a guard around behaviour that is about to change.

**CLERK CORRECTION 2026-08-08 — a `needs:` was removed after one tick, and the mistake was mine.**

This lane returned `blocked` because the host load gate never cleared, and **I told it to name
`F-HOST-VM-EATS-THE-CEILING`** as the blocking entity. That was wrong in a way worth recording: **the lane's
condition was transient (load too high *right now* to add a fourth concurrent tier) and that flag is
standing (this host's VM is undersized for the ceiling).** Pointing a transient block at a standing flag
makes the lane unstartable forever — the flag's `clears_when` names no `fact:` key, so `plan flag clear`
refuses it and only an owner override could ever release the lane.

**The condition is met in substance**: load read **13.34** at the retry, under both the dispatch ceiling of
21 and the in-lane tier gate of 13. Nothing about the host changed to require an owner's judgement.

**So the structural line I authored is removed and the flag is untouched.** No flag was cleared, no decision
ruled, and the standing observation about the VM stands on its own.

**The general lesson, since this is the second `needs:` I have had to remove**: a `needs:` is for a
dependency that will be *satisfied by work*, not for a condition that is merely *true or false right now*.
A lane blocked on transient capacity should return `blocked` with the reason in its log and be re-dispatched
when capacity returns — which is exactly what happened here, minus the self-inflicted gate.

### Lane L-AN-XZ-REPORT-COUNTS-ONLY-MONEY-THAT-ARRIVED — a statutory report claims receipts it never received
state: verified
class: node
owner: agent
dir: ../OkamAPI-modules
exit: no X or Z report includes a receivable in its received total, shown by a test that reds when a company-account sale is counted as received, with the non-SQL tier green at the composed tip, recorded in docs/plan/returns/L-AN-XZ-REPORT-COUNTS-ONLY-MONEY-THAT-ARRIVED-1.md
agent: L-AN-XZ-REPORT-COUNTS-ONLY-MONEY-THAT-ARRIVED
evidence: docs/plan/returns/L-AN-XZ-REPORT-COUNTS-ONLY-MONEY-THAT-ARRIVED-1.md

**An X/Z report is a statutory document, and this one overstates what the venue took.** Company-account
receivables — money **invoiced**, not received — are counted inside **`Sum mottatt`**. A venue reconciling
its day against the till reads a figure that includes sales nobody has paid yet.

**A fix exists at `lane/xz-printed-defects` @ `6c394057e` — and a verification pass measured it INCOMPLETE.
Do not land it as it stands.**

**The defect reproduces at the trunk `1c71ae951`**, verified before the branch was trusted:
`EscPosXZReportBuilder.cs:98` takes **every** `PaymentMeansTotal` with no exclusion, `:102-104` prints them
all under **`MOTTATT BETALING`**, and `:114` sums the same unfiltered list into **`Sum mottatt`**.

**But that branch filters at the PRINTER** — `allMeans.Where(p => !p.PaymentType.IsCompanyAccount())` —
**and the receivable enters upstream of every printer.** `XZReportService.cs:703-721` builds `paymentMeans`
from every `entry.PaymentLines` with no exclusion, **so the model itself carries it**, and **four emitters
read that model**:

| emitter | repaired by `6c394057e`? |
|---|---|
| `EscPosXZReportBuilder.cs` — the printed roll | **yes, only this one** |
| `SaftCashRegisterExportService.Transactions.cs:49,90` — the SAF-T export | no |
| `TripletexPosService.cs:114` — the accounting push | no |
| `XZReportService.cs` — the builder, where it enters | no |

**Landing it alone makes the same day reconcile differently depending on which artifact an inspector
reads.** For a statutory document, **two artifacts disagreeing is worse than one being wrong.**

**Fix at the model, not the printer** — either exclude where `paymentMeans` is built, or make the split a
property of the model every emitter reads. **Then show each of the four emitters agreeing.**

**MEASURED SINCE: only THREE emitters were ever wrong to check, and one of the four was already right.**
`TripletexPosService` books `CompanyAccount` to a **receivables account** and **must** iterate every medium,
because a double-entry voucher that filtered the company line would leave the revenue credit with no
matching debit. **Verified correct as-is — do not change it.** The exit criterion is therefore short by
**one** emitter, `SaftCashRegisterExportService`, and that one is **blocked on
`D-DOES-A-SAFT-PAYMENT-ELEMENT-ADMIT-A-CREDIT-MEDIUM`**, not on work.

**One half of that branch is right and should be kept**: it adds an **unconditional
kontantsalg/kredittsalg split** under § 2-8-2, so the report **distinguishes** rather than silently
excluding — which is the C6 answer, and it means a venue seeing a smaller `Sum mottatt` is told what the
credit sales were rather than assuming the till is broken.

### Decision D-CONFIRM-SIXTH-HEAD — an unreviewed sixth head sits above the merged confirm family
state: ruled

| merge-as-is — take it on the strength of its own receipt ; pro: it carries a measured receipt and is only two test-only commits ; con: unaudited code enters a composed tree that was audited precisely because nobody could see across the family, which is the property the review bought
| leave-it-out — land the reviewed five and let the sixth ride its own lane later ; pro: nothing unreviewed enters, and both merge points already have receipts so either can be taken alone ; con: a head left outside a merged family is how this estate got a nine-deep stack in the first place

Found by the lane that merged the family, **by pairwise ancestry check rather than by reading the log** —
which is why nobody had seen it. A sixth true head sits two test-only commits above one of the five, with
its own measured receipt. **Neither the review nor the brief mentions it.**

**The lane did not merge it, and the restraint is the point.** Unlike the post-merge repair it did take —
which both the review and the brief had named — this one was never reviewed or trial-merged, so pulling it
in unilaterally would put unaudited code into a tree whose whole value is that somebody read across it.

It also left **two separate stopping points, each with its own receipt**, so the reviewed-scope merge can be
taken alone and the repair separately.



**Moot as of 2026-08-05, verified twice.** The sixth head is `lane/crypto-pin-byform` — two test-only commits
above the family head — and **it is already an ancestor of the backend tip**, landed through a different
composition entirely. The clerk confirmed the ancestry directly.

**So `merge-as-is` has already happened de facto, and `leave-it-out` is no longer available.** What remains is
a **retroactive review** of two test-only commits and retiring the superseded family ref. **The plan currently
says the opposite of what the object graph says**, which is the part worth correcting promptly: unreviewed
code is in the tip while the board reports it waiting.

### Decision D-INTEGRATION-FASTFORWARD — whether the integration branch moves onto the merged stack
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: F-MIG-CHAIN-STACKED, F-DETACHED-MIGRATIONS
options:
| fast-forward-now — move `feature/restaurant-modules` onto the merged stack ; pro: the merge is done, the branch is a strict descendant so this is a fast-forward with nothing to resolve, the fast tier was green at every one of the seven merge commits, and it stops the next migration author forking a chain that is nine deep and not an ancestor ; con: it moves the reference under 152 in-flight lane branches, every one of which will find its base has moved
| fast-forward-after-the-walk — hold the ref until the standing worlds are walked and torn down ; pro: fewer lanes in flight to disturb, and the freed memory lets the SQL tier prove the joins first ; con: every hour it waits, more lanes branch from a base that is nine migrations behind the truth
| leave-it-and-land-per-lane — keep the integration branch where it is and merge each lane individually later ; pro: no single disruptive move ; con: it is what produced a nine-deep unmergeable stack in the first place
| author-a-merge-lane — one authored merge of the stack into the integration branch, chain-replayed from empty and tier-rerun at the merge commit ; pro: it is the only option that describes something that can actually happen — the two sides diverge 59 against 34 with neither an ancestor of the other, so no fast-forward exists — and it treats the stack as what it is, a real code merge carrying 126 files outside Migrations ; con: it is a genuine merge with conflicts to resolve, it serialises behind one author, and the duplicate-migration collision lives inside it and must be resolved there rather than before it
default_if_unruled: none
reopen_when: the merge lane finds the two sides cannot be reconciled by a merge either, or the duplicate-migration collision inside it turns out to need resolving before the merge rather than within it
ruled: author-a-merge-lane 2026-08-06 by @sven

Raised by `L-MIG-STACK-LAND`, which did the whole merge and then **stopped at the one act that is not
its own**: `feature/restaurant-modules` is unmoved and nothing was pushed. Its branch is a strict
descendant, so the landing is mechanically trivial — **the question is entirely about timing under 152
in-flight lanes**, which is a judgement about people rather than about git.

The merge itself is proven: all seven links in dependency order, fast tier green at **every** merge commit
rather than only the last, and the model snapshot clean at the tip — which is the check that matters,
since the snapshot auto-merged at three of the links.

**What is not proven is the SQL tier.** 584 tests were discovered at the tip and zero executed; the joins
are unverified on a real catalog. The one that matters is the last link, whose accounting-day index tests
**compile and have never run anywhere.**


**The blocker audit makes this the dominant decision on the board, 2026-08-03.** Its finding: **the root
cause of forty-seven open blockers is merge, not build.** The integration branch has not moved since
2026-08-02; every clearing branch measured is unmerged; 162 of 259 branches sit behind it.

So the queue is not forty-seven things to build. **Most of them are things to land**, and the ref not
moving is what keeps them looking like work.



**Measured 2026-08-04, and it changes what this decision is asking. Verified by the clerk, not taken on
report — a lane reported divergence and the numbers here are my own.**

```
git merge-base feature/restaurant-modules integration/mig-stack-land  ->  3579bbbc
git rev-list --left-right --count  ->  59 ahead / 34 behind
git merge-base --is-ancestor feature/restaurant-modules integration/mig-stack-land  ->  false
```

**The branches have diverged. A fast-forward is not possible.** `integration/mig-stack-land` did not fall
behind the integration branch — it forked at `3579bbbc` and both sides have moved since, the integration
branch by 59 commits (eight merge lanes landed there today) and the stack by 34.

**So the question is no longer "does the integration branch fast-forward onto the stack".** It is whether
those 34 commits — which carry the whole W5 timesheet family and MIG-25/MIG-26 — are **merged into** the
integration branch, with everything a merge here implies: the seven hazards this program has catalogued,
a chain replay across a migration stack, and a tier re-run at the merge commit rather than inherited.

**Sharpened 2026-08-04 by `L-MEALS-IDEMPOTENCY-REFUSAL`, which measured what the 34 commits actually
contain rather than only how many there are:** they touch **only `Migrations/**`** — zero
`Services/Meals/**` files differ between the two branches.

That narrows the question usefully. The fork is not two divergent bodies of product code; it is a
**migration stack** on one side and 59 commits of merged module work on the other. So the risk in
reconciling is concentrated where this estate has been burned before — chain replay, an index that exists
in the model and not the chain, and the `AccountingSummaries` shape — rather than spread across the
services.

**Two lanes have already chosen the stack as their base** (`L-WF-TIMESHEET-RACE`, and its killed
predecessor independently) because it carries the family the integration branch does not. So work is
accumulating on **both** sides of a fork that nothing has yet reconciled.

This is not a recommendation — the ruling is Sven's. It is the measurement the ruling needs, and the
option names in this decision no longer describe the choice available.

**The premise under this decision's first option no longer holds, measured 2026-08-05, and the clerk verified
it independently.** This block says the branch is *"a strict descendant, so this is a fast-forward with nothing
to resolve"*. It is not. `integration/mig-stack-land` and `feature/restaurant-modules` have **diverged: 34
commits on the stack side, 59 on the integration side**, and `--is-ancestor` fails in **both** directions.
Confirmed a second way: `GrowthAuditWriter.cs` exists on the integration branch and is absent from the stack.

**This is not a stale-ref artefact.** The integration branch last moved at 2026-08-04T12:00:29, roughly fourteen
hours before the document that described the relationship was written.

**So `fast-forward-now` is not available as written.** Landing the stack is a **hand merge across a 739-line
ledger divergence with the MIG-22 collision inside it** — a different act, with a different risk, from the one
this option describes. The other two options are unaffected; what has changed is that the cheap one is not
cheap.

**The clerk passed the false version to Sven in a status report.** Recorded here rather than quietly amended,
because a decision offered with a wrong `pro` is worse than a decision not yet offered.


**Fable-reviewed 2026-08-05, and none of the three options survives measurement.** At the backend refs the
merge-base is `3579bbbc` with a **59/34 divergence and `--is-ancestor` false in both directions** — so
`fast-forward-now` and `fast-forward-after-the-walk` **describe an act that does not exist**, and
`leave-it-and-land-per-lane` is the pathology that built the stack in the first place. The reviewer's
recommendation is to re-author this as a **single authored merge lane, chain-replayed from empty and
tier-rerun at the merge commit.**

**A second falsehood sits inside this block, and the clerk verified it independently.** The 2026-08-04
sharpening says the 34 stack commits *"touch only `Migrations/**`"*. Measured at the same refs, the stack side
carries **126 files outside `Migrations/`** — the Workforce timesheet family, Margin waste, Tripletex,
accounting summaries, plus entities, enums and tests. **This is a real code merge, not a chain replay with
trimmings**, and only the narrower claim — no `Services/Meals/**` on the stack side — holds.

**It interlocks with the duplicate-MIG-21 decision**, whose collision lives *inside* this merge and has to be
resolved within it rather than before it.

### Decision D-MRG-CURATION-CONTENT — the ingredient list itself, in the file that is waiting for it
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MRG-STARTER-150
options:
| fill-the-csv — edit `Services/Margin/margin-starter-ingredients.csv` in place and set its two counters ; pro: the form is the file, it opens in Excel, its own header explains every column and both enforced rules, and the mechanism around it is built and mutation-proven — an evening's work with no question to ask anybody ; con: it is your evening, and the yield column will validate but not yet cost anything
| ship-the-sixteen — leave the curation at sixteen and revisit after a pilot ; pro: nothing to do, and the mechanism serves whatever is present ; con: onboarding is this module's own stated kill risk and sixteen ingredients is not a library a venue did not have to type
| seed-from-invoices — build the library from a real venue's supplier lines instead ; pro: names, units and pack sizes are already true for that venue ; con: it needs the invoice ingest, which is itself waiting on `D-EHF-INVOICE-ACCESS`
default_if_unruled: none
reopen_when: the EHF spike returns SHIP and a pilot venue is connected, making that venue's own supplier lines the better first library
ruled: fill-the-csv 2026-08-05 by @sven

Raised by `L-MRG-STARTER-150`, which built the mechanism and **refused to invent the content**, exactly as
`author-the-list` intended. Five semicolon columns: `name;base_unit;yield;packs;notes`.

**Its most useful design choice is a guard against the one failure a 150-line paste makes easy and
expensive: a tail that never arrived.** The file declares its own row and yield counts, and the pins hold
the parsed list to them — because a truncated list has **no wrong row in it**, there are simply fewer of
them, and a blank yield column is legal, so neither can be caught by validating rows one at a time.

**A refused line is dropped, never served**, so a bad edit can neither put a wrong factor in front of a
venue nor take the ingredients endpoint down for one.

### Flag F-MRG-YIELD-NOWHERE — a curated yield has nowhere to land and would cost nothing
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: an ingredient carries a default yield that reaches the recipe lines using it, or the curation stops collecting yields

Found by the lane preparing the curation, and it changes what the curation is worth. **A yield factor
exists on exactly one thing in this product — a recipe line — and not on the ingredient.** So a curated
yield cannot follow an ingredient into the recipes that use it, and the field appears **nowhere in the
frontend**: today every recipe line is costed **at no loss whatever the curation says.**

The lane captured and validated yields anyway but **deliberately does not silently cost them**, and says so
in the file to the person filling it in — rather than leaving a column that looks load-bearing and is not.

Making them count needs a default yield on the ingredient — a migration — plus a recipe-line control that
pre-fills from it. Worth knowing **before** an evening is spent authoring 150 of them.

### Decision D-TRAIN-RETENTION-BASIS — two questions the horizon needs answered, not one number
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MIG-TRAIN-DISPLAY-SNAPSHOT
options:
| counsel-first — get a period and its authority confirmed by counsel before any column ships ; pro: it is what the module's own spec §13.5 demands in writing, and it is the only route that lets the pack name a duration without inventing one ; con: it is external and slow, and the frozen-name defect stands until it returns
| product-policy-no-statute — set a documented product retention with expiry that DELETES, stated as policy and never as a legal duration ; pro: §13.5 explicitly permits a documented product policy, so this is inside the spec rather than around it, and it gives the data a real end ; con: the sweep must remove rows that GuardAppendOnly and two triggers protect, so it needs an explicit C1 exception written as an exception rather than smuggled in
| lock-only-and-say-so — freeze the name, set a keep-until lock with no deletion, and state on the pack that these records are retained indefinitely ; pro: it is what the personalliste actually does today, so it is honest about the estate's real behaviour and needs no new mechanism ; con: it does not close the erasure gap at all — it documents it, which is a different thing from curing it
default_if_unruled: none
reopen_when: counsel returns with an actual statutory retention duty, which sets the period by that authority and may forbid deletion entirely
ruled: product-policy-no-statute 2026-08-05 by @sven

Raised by `L-MIG-TRAIN-DISPLAY-SNAPSHOT`, which **refused to build rather than pick a number because one
was needed.** The brief made the retention period the gate and named three permitted groundings; the lane
measured all three and all three fail.

**Two things must be ruled here, not one.** First, **what period on what authority**, given §13.5 forbids
asserting a statutory duration without counsel. Second, **what the horizon does at expiry** — lock, in
which case the defect stands and is merely dated; or delete, which needs a C1 exception written openly,
because the sweep must remove rows that the append-only guard and two triggers exist to protect.

The lane re-proved the underlying defect by execution rather than inheriting it: a completion written
under one name, the roster renamed, the pack re-read — **identical apart from the subject line, and the
old name survives nowhere in the reprint.**

### Decision D-TRAIN-ERASURE — a frozen name in an append-only table that no erasure request can reach
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MIG-TRAIN-DISPLAY-SNAPSHOT
options:
| snapshot-with-horizon — pro: the pack is stable and the personal data dies on a schedule, which is the answer the personalliste already gives one module over ; con: needs a retention period nobody has ruled, and a sweep deleting from an append-only table is a new exception to C1 rather than an application of it
| no-snapshot-print-current — pro: creates no new personal data, leaves C1 untouched, and has no erasure problem to solve ; con: the internkontroll spec requires the snapshot in two places, and an inspector reading a reprinted pack cannot tell what the record said on the day it was written
| snapshot-opaque-reference-only — pro: satisfies the spec's opaque-identity-reference half and keeps names out of the append-only rows entirely ; con: does not satisfy the display-snapshot half, so the pack still reprints a live-resolved name and the defect survives under a different description
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: snapshot-with-horizon 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: a retention period is named and an inspector asks for a pack older than it, or the append-only sweep the horizon needs is refused

Raised by `L-TRAIN-DISPLAY-SNAPSHOT` on hand-back, and it is the reason that lane returned blocked rather
than building. The module's **only** erasure mechanism is the spec's sentence permitting personal
free-text in deviations to be anonymized in place on request. That cannot run on training completions:
the deny-trigger and the append-only guard both refuse an in-place edit.

So the column would create personal data **with no permitted erasure path** and — unlike the
personalliste, which does this exact shape in Workforce — **no retention horizon** after which the
question stops being asked.

This is a fork rather than a lane because all three answers are defensible and they trade different
things: the first spends a C1 exception, the second spends a stated statutory requirement, the third
spends the requirement's other half.

**Correction, 2026-08-03 — the pro recorded against the chosen option was false, and I wrote it.**
`snapshot-with-horizon` was offered on the grounds that the data "dies on a schedule, which is the answer
the personalliste already gives one module over." **It does not.** Measured by the lane sent to build it:

- `RetainUntilUtc` is a **keep-until lock, not a deletion deadline.** Its own test is named *the retention
  horizon is set and cannot be shortened*, and asserts a trigger **refuses** shortening it.
- **There is no sweep.** The field is referenced by four non-test files, all writers and projections.
  **Nothing deletes.** The participant display name is never erased.

So copying that shape would have shipped the defect **with a date next to it**: a frozen name, no erasure
path, and a column that looks like it closed this decision without closing it. The lane built nothing for
exactly that reason.

It also measured the other two groundings and both fail. The Training spec's own §13.5 says retention is
*a documented product policy, not a marketed legal duration — the module never claims a specific statutory
retention period it has not confirmed with counsel*, which is **a written refusal rather than a gap to
fill.** And the personalliste's three-year-six-month period is grounded in bokføringsforskriften § 8-5-6,
the bookkeeping regulation governing the personalliste **as a bookkeeping document** — Training records
are IK-mat, IK-alkohol and HMS, so carrying that period across would invent a duration and attribute it to
a statute that does not say it.

The ruling stands as Sven's; what it was ruled *on* did not survive measurement. See
`D-TRAIN-RETENTION-BASIS`.

owner: @sven
blocks: F-PROBE-ROOT-WRONG-WORLD
options:

Raised 2026-08-02 while installing the world guards. `../ConsumerWeb` is on `feature/swiss` and one probe
reads it. Writing `feature/swiss` into its `world.config` would have made the guard report conformance —
**by defining conformance as wherever the checkout happened to be sitting.** That is the guard passing by
definition rather than by measurement, so the expected value is left empty and the fact reads `unknown`.

`unknown` is deliberately not `false` here. The checkout has not failed a check; it has never been given
one, and those two states must not render the same.


### Decision D-MAIL — which provider Growth's mail actually leaves through
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-GROWTH-MAIL
options:
| postmark — pro: deliverability and template API, named first in the spec shortlist; con: no EU data hosting, which makes it a subprocessor problem for Norwegian guest data
| brevo — pro: EU hosting, full bulk capability set; con: template tooling and suppression export are ours to integrate
| mailjet — pro: EU hosting, the third shortlisted option; con: same integration cost as brevo with less familiarity
| smtp-promote — pro: a one-line factory swap to an adapter that already exists; con: it answers only submit, so lookup, suppression export and webhook verification fail closed; cost: every uncertain delivery parks for review instead of resolving
| stay-fake — pro: nothing leaves the process, the correct posture while there is no pilot; con: Growth cannot be demonstrated to a venue at all
recommend: smtp-promote — It is the only option that costs nothing to reverse: the adapter exists, the swap is one line, and it makes Growth demonstrable before a venue is named. The postmark/brevo/mailjet fork is a subprocessor and data-residency choice, and this plan holds no venue to make it for; rule that one when a pilot signs.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: postmark 2026-07-31 by @sven
reopen_when: Postmark's hosting region or data-processing terms change, or a venue's DPA refuses a non-EU subprocessor for guest contact data

- The bound provider today is the in-memory fake, which is what `F-GROWTH-FAKE-MAIL` records.
- Nothing about the choice is reversible-in-name-only: the three hosted providers differ in where
  Norwegian guest data lands, which is a data-processing decision, not a technical one.
- `L-GROWTH-MAIL` cannot start until this is ruled, and Growth cannot be shown to anyone until
  that lane lands.

### Decision D-PAYROLL — the column layout of the Workforce timesheet export
state: ruled
owner: @sven
options:
| pilot-accountant-map — pro: the first venue's accountant imports it without hand-mapping; con: nobody is named yet, so it cannot be executed today
| neutral-okam-csv — pro: the byte-deterministic hours export already exists and works; con: the accountant maps columns by hand every month
| provider-boundary-first — pro: builds the export provider seam with today's CSV as provider one, so a vendor format is additive later; con: the timesheet tables it hangs off do not exist
recommend: neutral-okam-csv — It is the only option that can be executed today. The accountant-specific map needs an accountant nobody has named, and the provider seam needs timesheet tables that are not built; both stay available afterwards, because a neutral CSV is what provider one would have been anyway.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: neutral-okam-csv 2026-07-31 by @sven
reopen_when: a pilot venue names its accountant and that accountant states an import format the neutral CSV does not satisfy

- An hours export already exists, is byte-deterministic, is gated on the payroll approver and
  carries no money.
- What is unbuilt is the persisted timesheet batch behind it — the export provider interface is
  spec text with no C# type.
- Tripletex and Visma appear in the estate only as accounting adapters, explicitly out of
  Workforce v1; SAF-T here is cash register only; Huldt&Lillevik appears nowhere.

### Decision D-GROWTH-RETENTION — retention against Growth's own deny-triggers
state: ruled
owner: @sven
options:
| amend-13 — pro: no migration and no weakened control; the append-only receipts are kept for the life of the controller relationship; con: the spec's stated retention windows stop being true and have to be rewritten
| dated-carve-out — pro: honours the spec as written; con: each trigger has to admit DELETE past a horizon, a materially weaker control needing its own tamper tests
| aggregate-reduce — pro: keeps the evidential value while shrinking the row count; con: a new summary table plus the same carve-out on the source rows
| shred-is-retention — pro: matches what the code already does, since erasure is a crypto-shred on the contact point rather than a delete; con: receipt volume grows without bound, and it now grows with mail volume
recommend: amend-13 — The disagreement is between a spec sentence and a schema control, and the sentence is the cheaper of the two to correct. Every other option teaches a deny-trigger to admit DELETE, which is the control C1 exists to keep; a document can be rewritten without weakening anything.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: amend-13 2026-07-31 by @sven
reopen_when: a controller or supervisory authority requires time-limited purging of the append-only receipt tables, or erasure stops being a crypto-shred on the contact point

- Erasure is **not** blocked. Five Growth tables carry append-only triggers, but the contact-point
  table does not, and erasure nulls the encrypted address there.
- What the triggers block is time-limited retention purging — a contradiction between the spec and
  the schema, not a rights problem.
- Whatever is ruled, C1 is the constraint it has to survive: an append-only table is never purged
  in place.

### Decision D-MEALS-EMPREF — the Meals employee reference, before the first invitation
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MEALS-EMPREF
options:
| nullable-copied-at-claim — pro: additive, no FK, no index, and the statement falls back to the id when absent; con: an invitation issued without one still produces an unreferenced membership
| required-on-invitation — pro: no unlabelled membership can exist at the pilot; con: the company must have the reference ready before anyone is invited
| post-claim-backfill — pro: dissolves the deadline by letting a company admin set it later; con: it is the thing R4 in intent.md rejects, because a claimed membership cannot acquire the value afterwards and statement lines freeze on finalization
| ship-guids — pro: nothing to build; con: the pilot's first statement is permanently unreadable to the company that pays it
recommend: nullable-copied-at-claim — It is additive, it lands before the deadline without asking a company for data it may not have on day one, and the statement degrades to the id rather than to nothing. required-on-invitation is the same column plus a gate that can be added later; post-claim-backfill is already rejected in intent.md as R4.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: nullable-copied-at-claim 2026-07-31 by @sven
reopen_when: a company requires that no membership exist without a reference, or a finalized statement proves unreadable because the id fallback was used

- The deadline is not a date — it is the first invitation. A membership claimed without the column
  can never acquire it, and statement lines freeze on finalization.
- The frontend already blocks the issue button behind an explicit acknowledgement of exactly that.
- `F-MEALS-INVITE` is the flag holding this open, and `L-MEALS-EMPREF` is the lane that clears it.

### Decision D-MEALS-SPLIT — whether a company pays part of a lunch and the guest pays the rest
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: nothing yet
options:
| cap-only — the company funds up to its cap and an order above it is refused before the guest commits ; pro: it is what is built and proven today, the refusal is legible, and no money is ever split across two tenders ; con: an employee who wants a 210-kr lunch on a 188-kr allowance cannot simply pay 22 kr — they order something else or nothing
| split-tender — the company pays its share and the guest pays the remainder on their own card ; pro: it is what a person expects from an allowance, and it removes the most likely daily friction ; con: the cart carries one payment type, completion takes one token, and the quote reserves a cap rather than splitting one — this is a new endpoint and a second tender on one order, in the module whose money path is the most carefully guarded in the estate
| topup-wallet — the employee pre-loads their own balance and the company reimburses ; pro: keeps one tender per order ; con: invents a wallet, and Norwegian tax treatment of a reimbursed balance is a different question from a subsidised meal
recommend: cap-only for the pilot, and rule split-tender only if a venue asks. The refusal is honest and arrives before the guest commits, which is the failure mode that matters; a second tender on a funded order touches the reservation guard, the journal and the statement at once. Written by @claude from what the lane found buildable, not from any venue's experience.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: cap-only 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: a pilot venue reports employees abandoning orders at the cap rather than reordering

Surfaced by the lane that built the funded checkout. Its objective said the company pays its share and
the guest the remainder; that is not buildable — above the cap the reservation is denied outright, and
nothing in the cart, the completion route or the quote reserves a partial amount. The lane reported it
rather than inventing a shape.

### Decision D-CORE-PIN — how a shared-client fix reaches the clients that ship
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-CORE-ORE-LABEL
options:
| bump-all-four — land the fix on each Core branch and bump the pin in every client repo ; pro: the defect is actually gone everywhere a guest can see it, which is the only version of "fixed" that means anything ; con: four repos, three Core branches, and two of them are divergent local histories carrying commits with identical subjects under different hashes — this is a day of careful work before anything is better
| consumer-only — fix the two clients that show the defect and leave the others pinned ; pro: it is where a guest actually sees a price, and it is already done and proven ; con: the estate keeps four Cores that disagree about how money is printed, and the next person to read one of them learns the wrong rule
| converge-core — reconcile the Core branches onto one history first, then fix once ; pro: it removes the class rather than the instance, and the class has now produced two lane-blocking findings in two days ; con: a reconciliation nobody has scoped, on submodules that have drifted for months, before a one-line rendering fix
recommend: consumer-only now, converge-core as its own scoped piece of work. The defect only renders in the two consumer clients — the three admin surfaces overwrite the suffix at startup — so the reachable harm is already closed, and pretending a four-repo bump is a rendering fix would hide how much the divergence actually costs. Written by @claude from the lane's pin map, not from any judgement about how the submodules came to differ.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: consumer-only 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: a defect appears in a client that was left pinned, or the four Core histories are converged for another reason

`core` is a git submodule and five checkouts hold **four distinct pins across three Core branches**.
ConsumerApp's pin is not even an object in ConsumerWeb's copy, and both carry commits with identical
subjects under different hashes. No single Core commit reaches every client.

The lane established this before changing anything and stopped rather than fixing one copy and
declaring the defect closed — which is the trap that turned a plan fact green over an absent capability
two days ago.

### Decision D-MEALS-STATEMENT-LEVER — may a venue's own admin arm its billing surface
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MEALS-REACHABLE
options:
| catalogue-the-flags — put meals.statements, ordering and projection in the operator catalog so a venue switches its own module on ; pro: the venue is self-serve, and "enabled" stops meaning nothing ; con: the flag-setting endpoint authorizes on store-admin, so this hands a pilot venue's own admin the switch that arms issuance of billing documents the module already records as un-withdrawable
| tell-the-truth — leave them as deployment configuration and have the operator surface say "disabled at deployment" instead of reporting effective ; pro: a venue is told the truth rather than shown a switch that lies, and nobody can arm billing by accident ; con: it costs a shared platform field for a non-toggleable flag plus a frontend change — the lane checked and disagreed that this is the cheap option
| leave-it — keep the opaque 404 and rely on the runbook ; pro: nothing to build ; con: a venue that enabled Meals through the only control it has gets an opaque 404 across 25 of 29 routes, indistinguishable from the module not existing
recommend: tell-the-truth — on the merits rather than on cost. Arming irreversible billing issuance is not a switch a pilot venue's own admin should hold before the fiscal floor is met, and an operator surface that reports a module effective while it is dead is the advertised-but-ungating flag failure this estate has already shipped once. Written by @claude from the lane's wire measurement, not from any venue's experience.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: tell-the-truth 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: billing documents stop being un-withdrawable, or a venue needs to arm the module without an operator

The lane proved the state rather than describing it: on a host at the shipped configuration, setting
`meals.module` returns effective **true** and all five statement routes still answer 404. The cause is a
conjunction of two host-configuration flags. It covers 25 of 29 routes, not five — `meals.ordering` and
`meals.projection` sit in the same position.

It returned blocked rather than picking, because the lane's own exit and the flag's clearing condition
point in opposite directions, and choosing between them is a product decision about who may arm
billing.

### Decision D-DOCKER-VM — how the SQL tier gets a machine to run on again
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MRG-WASTE
options:
| reset-docker-vm — factory-reset Docker Desktop, which discards its 66 GB disk image and every cached image and stopped container ; pro: it gives a clean VM in minutes ; con: it destroys eight pre-existing stopped containers and every cached image, none created by any lane here — and measurement since shows the image is not what is filling the volume, so it buys 66 GB once and the host fills again
| reclaim-build-output — delete the 516 obj and bin trees across the estate's worktrees, then restart Docker ; pro: it touches no container and no source, and the estate's own notes say it reclaims tens of gigabytes in minutes ; con: a worktree a lane is compiling in loses its build mid-run, and the same sweep has silently gutted node_modules binaries here before, which needs a forced reinstall to repair
| defer-sql — keep building on the fast tier and accept that nothing touching a trigger, a rowversion or a filtered index is proven until a machine exists ; pro: nothing is destroyed and lanes keep landing ; con: three migrations and every immutability guard authored today are proven at the application layer only, and that is precisely the gap that has twice let a dropped SQL guard ship
recommend: reclaim-build-output — run in a quiet window when no lane holds a worktree, excluding anything under node_modules. It is the only option that costs nothing you cannot rebuild. If it does not free enough, reset-docker-vm is yours to authorise — I will not remove containers I did not create. Written by @claude from the volume state and the lane's own account.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: reset-docker-vm 2026-08-01 by @sven
reopen_when: the VM fills again, or a reset is needed a second time — at which point the question is not how to recover but why this host cannot hold the estate's working set

**Recovered without the reset, 2026-08-01.** The agent spent three minutes booting the VM before
discarding anything, on the theory that ext4 would replay its journal now the host had space. It did.
Everything came back readable, and the ruled option was not needed.

That call mattered: a factory reset would have destroyed **nine locally-built images with no registry to
pull them from** — including the harness and stage0 API images — plus five named volumes holding
**seeded harness databases**. Given the known migration-replay bug that breaks a fresh harness bring-up,
rebuilding those was not obviously cheap.

Reclaimed instead: 40.1 GB of build cache, two crash-orphaned test containers and nine anonymous volumes
from the run that died. Docker's image went 66 GB to 35 GB, host free went 53 to 103 GiB, nothing a lane
needs was lost.

**Proven, not assumed:** 18 of 18 SQL-traited tests green across four fixtures and four real containers,
each migrating the full chain from empty. The three migrations authored on 2026-07-31 that had never met
a real database have now run against one four times, and one fixture additionally proved the down-and-up
round trip. The remaining 520 are untested-since, not known-red.
reopen_when: the VM fills again, or a reset is needed a second time — at which point the question is not how to recover but why this host cannot hold the estate's working set

**Corrected 2026-08-01, and the correction changes the remedy.** The lane first attributed this to
Docker's image growing until the host was exhausted. Measured an hour later with that lane idle, the
image had **not grown a byte since the VM died** — and the host kept losing space anyway, swinging
between 30 GiB and 9 GiB free as other lanes build and test. Docker's 66 GB is a *symptom*.

The working set is the estate itself: roughly 122 GB under `~/okam`, 34 GB of system temp, 28 GB of
application support and 23 GB in `/private/tmp`, on a volume all but full. So **resetting Docker reclaims
66 GB once and this host fills again** — it is the wrong remedy, and the option below that says so is
the one to weigh.

**Docker's virtual machine is down and will not come back.** A lane's SQL run died seven minutes in
with every test reporting a terminated connection, after the VM's filesystem logged an aborted journal
and remounted **read-only**. Its sparse disk image had grown to fill a volume with almost nothing left.

So the SQL tier is unavailable estate-wide. Everything authored today that depends on a trigger, a
rowversion or a filtered index — three migrations among them — is proven at the application layer only.

The reclaim is not mine to run: every option either destroys containers I did not create or removes
build output from under a lane that may be mid-compile.

**One measured lead, 2026-08-01, and it is not ours.** Ten gigabytes of the twelve now free sit in
Claude Code session scratch for a *different* project — `raiis-saladin-web` at 5.2 GB and
`raiis-saladin-core` at 4.9 GB under `/private/tmp/claude-501/`. This estate's own session scratch is
241 MB.

If no session is live on that project those directories are dead and removing them nearly doubles the
free space in one command, without touching a container, a worktree or a build. I have not removed
them: I did not create them and cannot tell from here whether a session still holds them.

### Decision D-MRG-CURATION — which ingredients a Norwegian venue starts with
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MRG-STARTER-150
options:
| author-the-list — you name the ~150 ingredients with their units and yields, once ; pro: the mechanism is finished and reachable, so the list is the only thing between a venue and a library it did not type; and a yield is an arithmetic input to every plate cost, so it wants a person who knows food ; con: it is your evening, not an agent's hour
| seed-from-invoices — build the library from a real venue's own supplier lines instead of a curated list ; pro: the names, units and pack sizes are already true for that venue, and the e-invoicing mandate makes structured lines routine from January ; con: it needs the invoice ingest lane, which is itself gated on the unpark ruling, and it gives a venue its own catalogue rather than a starting point
| stay-at-sixteen — accept a short library and let venues type ; pro: nothing to decide ; con: the module's own spec names onboarding as its kill risk, and a competitive review ranked the empty library its first deal-loser, surfacing in the first hour
recommend: author-the-list for the pilot and seed-from-invoices afterwards — they compose rather than compete. The lane deliberately added zero ingredients, because a wrong yield propagates silently into a food-cost figure an owner makes decisions from, and a hundred and thirty-four invented rows would be worse than sixteen real ones. Written by @claude from the lane's finding, not from any knowledge of Norwegian kitchens.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: author-the-list 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: a venue rejects the authored list, or supplier invoice ingest lands and can seed a better one

The lane confirmed the mechanism is complete end to end — library, read, and the chips on both admin
pages that copy a candidate into a real ingredient with its conversions. **Nothing is missing but rows.**

### Decision D-BUILDER-PRUNE — how the build cache stops eating the machine again
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: nothing yet
options:
| scheduled-prune — a periodic `docker builder prune -af --filter until=48h`, by cron or once per wave ; pro: it is the fix that would actually have bitten, and it costs a cold first build per lane after each prune — minutes, against the hours a dead VM cost today ; con: something has to own the schedule, and a prune landing mid-build slows whichever lane is unlucky
| lower-the-cap — drop the builder's keep-storage from 20 GB to 10 GB in the daemon config ; pro: one token ; con: the cap is **already set at 20 GB and the cache still reached 40.1 GB**, so the setting is configured and demonstrably not holding at this build rate — and it only applies on restart
| accept-and-watch — leave it, and reclaim by hand when the volume gets tight ; pro: nothing to build or own ; con: today that meant a read-only VM, a dead tier, a stalled lane and several hours
recommend: scheduled-prune — the agent applied neither option deliberately and was right to: a malformed daemon config bricks Docker for every queued lane, and a restart would have killed a live container. Written by @claude from the agent's measurements, not from any judgement about how this machine is normally used.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: scheduled-prune 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: a prune lands mid-build often enough to cost more than the cache did, or nobody owns the schedule

**A disk cap would not have helped.** The sparse image fails when the *host* runs out, whatever its
declared maximum — Docker was the victim rather than the cause, exactly as the corrected diagnosis said.
What actually filled the volume was 40.1 GB of build cache accumulating under a policy that is switched
on and not holding.

### Decision D-EV-VAT — how an Events deposit is treated for VAT
state: ruled
owner: @sven
options:
| on-account-liability — pro: the deposit is a customer prepayment on account with no VAT column at all, which is what an accountant expects; con: five follow-on sub-decisions about rendering, sign and forfeiture
| taxable-advance-composite — pro: one number, taxed at the accepted proposal's composite rate; con: a composite rate is a fiction when the proposal mixes rates
| taxable-advance-configured — pro: the venue states one rate; con: needs a schema column and a prompt that does not exist
| keep-withholding — pro: shipped and honest, since the statement's VAT total is null whenever a deposit line is present; con: every realistic pilot settlement therefore shows no VAT total at all
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: on-account-liability 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: any of the five follow-on questions about rendering, sign or forfeiture cannot be answered on account

- No recommendation is recorded, and that is deliberate: this turns on how a Norwegian accountant
  treats an advance for a mixed-rate proposal, which is a fact about the outside world that this
  plan does not hold. Ask the accountant, then rule.
- What the plan can say: the shipped behaviour is `keep-withholding`, and it is honest rather than
  wrong — the VAT total goes null rather than guessing.
- C6 applies to whatever is chosen: the product may not print a VAT treatment it cannot produce
  the document for.

### Decision D-EV-DINTERO — where a Dintero deposit's money lands
state: ruled
owner: @sven
options:
| no-commission-full-split — pro: a synthesized single split routes the whole deposit to the venue; con: Okam earns nothing on deposits; cost: the split is invented rather than derived from a cart line
| commission-at-store-rate — pro: consistent with every other payment on the platform; con: a deposit has no order line to compute a split from

default_if_unruled: none
ruled: own-credentials-only 2026-07-31 by @sven

- Two of the three Dintero blockers are plain engineering: payment creation reloads a cart by user
  and store, and the callback resolves a merchant reference a deposit never writes.
- Only the money routing needs a ruling, and C4 binds it — every money-path write names the actor
  that caused it.

### Decision D-IDCODE — the personalliste identity-code register
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-WF-IDREG
options:
| venue-procedure-template — pro: cheapest; Okam ships a kodeoversikt template and an on-screen instruction and the venue keeps the register; con: the statute treats the register as part of the personalliste with the same retention, so a venue spreadsheet is weaker than the rest of the family
| in-product-register — pro: the register is producible on demand and retention-locked like its siblings; con: Okam starts collecting fødselsnummer, contradicting the module's own privacy stance and dragging a new class of personal data into scope
| print-national-id — pro: lawful under the paragraph's first branch with no register at all; con: the wire bans raw national identifiers today and a test actively scans for them
| no-claim — pro: nothing to build; con: this is the status quo the audit calls a missing field; cost: it carries the only priced legal consequence in the programme
recommend: venue-procedure-template — C6 rules out no-claim, because the product already prints the § 8-5-6 claim on screen and cannot produce the register behind it. Of the three that keep the claim printable, this is the only one that neither collects fødselsnummer nor prints a raw national id the wire currently bans. It is the weakest of the three legally, so rule it knowingly — and it is a legal posture, not an engineering one, so reject it freely.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: venue-procedure-template 2026-07-31 by @sven
reopen_when: a venue cannot operate the template register, or an inspection demands the kodeoversikt and the template proves insufficient

- `F-WF-NOREG` records the gap: personalliste codes have no register, and the register is what
  makes the substitution lawful.
- The claim is already on screen, which is what makes this urgent under C6 rather than merely
  desirable.

### Decision D-ACCT-TIMING — fix the missing unique index now, or at the chain squash
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-ACCT-UIDX
options:
| hand-author-now — pro: the accounting day stops being able to post twice on any database built from the chain; con: takes the single migration-author slot; cost: needs a duplicate sweep before the index can be created
| defer-to-squash — pro: the squash re-emits model-versus-chain drift in one pass; con: two live documents disagree about whether it does, and one says the operations must be hand-authored either way
recommend: hand-author-now — The defect is live on every database built from the chain, and the case for deferring rests on two documents that disagree about whether the squash would even emit it. One of them says the operations have to be hand-authored either way, which makes deferring a delay rather than a saving.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: hand-author-now 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: the duplicate sweep the index needs cannot be run against a real database, or the squash is shown to emit the operations after all

- `F-ACCT-DUP` is a blocker flag, not a warning: the accounting day can post twice today on any
  database built from the migration chain.
- R3 in intent.md is the reason the model-built tier cannot answer this — it agrees with the model
  and never with the database a customer would get.
- Whatever is ruled, C2 binds it: one migration author at a time, and the chain is the truth.

**Settled by measurement 2026-08-03, and it settles the deferral argument outright.** The lane ran
`ef migrations add` against the current model: it produced an **empty `Up` and `Down` and left the snapshot
unmodified.** The snapshot had been regenerated after the model gained the index, so the differ has nothing
left to emit — **the squash could never have emitted these operations.** The two documents that disagreed
about whether it would are now moot; the migration had to be hand-authored, exactly as `hand-author-now`
assumed.

Three further findings from that lane, each worth keeping:

**The generated rollback could never have run.** A typed column alteration resolves its indexes-to-preserve
from the *target* model, so the generated `Down` dropped the unique index twice and re-created it on the
widened column — unique over an unbounded string, which SQL Server refuses outright. **Found by reading the
generated script rather than the C#**, which is the only place it was visible.

**It refuses; it does not repair.** The migration counts duplicate groups and stops. It deletes nothing,
because both duplicates may have reached the webhook and **which claim is real is an accounting decision,
not a schema one.** The sweep queries are recorded as an owner action.

**The catch this makes live was over-broad**, and that mattered the moment the index existed: a bare update
exception would have reported **any** write failure as a safely-skipped duplicate, and the accounting day
would have silently never posted. Narrowed to the unique-violation test.

It also kept the migration number the ledger had already named this change, rather than minting a fresh
one — two entries for one migration is the failure the renumbering convention exists to prevent.

### Decision D-PREF-ORIGIN — how the preference centre becomes same-site
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-GROWTH-PREFCENTRE
options:
| named-cors-policy-plus-samesite-none — pro: keeps the API where it is, with a named policy carrying explicit origins and credentials on the preference controller plus a cross-site cookie; con: adding credentials to the default policy would throw at startup, so the scoping has to be exactly right; cost: a cross-site cookie is a weaker posture than same-site
| same-origin-proxy — pro: dissolves both halves at once with no policy or cookie change; con: the proxy in this repo targets a loopback address and describes itself as a preview tool, so this is a deployment decision about hostnames rather than a code change
recommend: named-cors-policy-plus-samesite-none — It is the option this branch can actually execute; the proxy route is a hostname decision that belongs to whoever owns the deployment, and it is strictly better if that person can give the preference centre a same-origin hostname. Rule this one to unblock the lane, and reopen it if the deployment answer arrives.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: named-cors-policy-plus-samesite-none 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: the API moves to the same registrable domain, at which point the named policy and the cross-site cookie are both unnecessary

- `F-PREF-UNREACHABLE` records the symptom: the preference centre cannot open a session from the
  deployed origins, so a guest cannot take themselves out of a mailing list.
- That withdrawal path is named in the objective, which is why this is not a cosmetic fork.

**Correction, 2026-08-03 — the brief this was ruled against contained a false "or", and I wrote it.** It
said both the CORS policy and the cookie have to move, *or* the API has to be served same-site. **That
"or" is wrong.** `api.okam.no` and `okam.no` are the same *site* but a different *origin*, so CORS still
applies and the wildcard is still refused. **The named CORS policy is required under both rulings.**

Anyone who read that sentence and shipped only the subdomain move would have shipped a still-broken page.

The lane implemented `api-subdomain` plus the **named-CORS half** of this ruling, and left the cookie at
`Strict`. Its finding on the other half: `samesite-none` would permanently give up the browser's own
cross-site protection, leaving the CSRF token as the sole defence, **to buy what the subdomain gives
free** — and it would still need the same CORS policy. Strictly more change, strictly less protection.

Both can technically stand; usefully they cannot, and the lane recommends retiring the `samesite-none`
half rather than leaving two live instructions. **That is yours to retire, not mine.**

| delete — pro: removes a class that has never executed, and the sweep entry that tracks it; con: whatever motivated it in 2025 goes with it
