- `F-WOLT-DEAD` is the flag: a background service never registered in any commit in history.
- C3 is the relevant constraint — a capability exists only when it is reachable, and this one has
  never been reachable.
### Decision D-SPEC-L-MEALS-FUNDED — the plan contradicts what L-MEALS-FUNDED observed
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MEALS-FUNDED
options:
| consumerweb — bind the funded checkout in ConsumerWeb, the checkout real guests use today ; pro: a green fact then means a guest can actually pay with a company account, which is the only version of this that a pilot can use ; con: a third repo outside this plan's two branches, on feature/swiss, and its Core pin has already diverged from this one
| consumer-native — bind it in frontend-mono apps/consumer-native ; pro: matches the standing 2026-07-20 ruling that the consumer go-forward client is apps/consumer-native, so the work is not thrown away ; con: the longest path to a funded order anyone can demonstrate, and not what a pilot venue's guests hold in their hands this quarter
| consumerapp — bind it in ConsumerApp ; pro: reaches app users without touching the go-forward decision ; con: ships a capability into a client the estate has already decided to move off

It does conflict with the go-forward ruling, so the honest shape may be consumerweb for the pilot and consumer-native as the durable home. Written by @claude from reading the three repos, not from running them and not from asking anyone.

ruled: consumerweb 2026-07-31 by @sven

The exit's second conjunct assumes a consumer checkout in this repo; there is none — pages/webshop/checkout.vue is a RedirectToNewStore stub to https://shop.okam.no and no page or component references useCheckout or cartService().Complete, so no capture under artifacts/journeys/ can show a funded order completing here.

The lane also surfaced a defect in this plan rather than in the code. `core/` is a git submodule, and the
two clients pin different lineages — this repo `cd1cc86`, ConsumerWeb `8931bc39`, already 25 and 11
commits from their merge base, with `PaymentType` members that differ. So writing the reservation token
into *this* repo's `cart-service.ts` would turn `fact:meals.token.client` green while the shipped
consumer checkout still sends nothing: a green fact standing over an absent capability, which is what C3
and C5 exist to refuse. Whichever client is ruled, that probe and `F-MEALS-UNFUNDED`'s `clears_when` both
have to move to that client's Core lineage.

Secondary, for whoever writes the client: `CreateMealsQuoteRequest.QuoteHash` has no pinned algorithm —
it is stored verbatim and used only in an idempotency fingerprint — so the first client to bind the quote
invents the hash contract by accident.
### Decision D-SPEC-L-MEALS-GATE — the plan contradicts what L-MEALS-GATE observed
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MEALS-GATE
options:
| row-not-status — judge the issue call by the deposit row it committed, not by its status code ; pro: measurable today with no credentials at all, and it proves exactly the thing the lane was about — that the flag gate cleared, since the service commits the request and its receipt in the first transaction before it ever reaches the provider ; con: it stops short of proving a guest can pay, so the provider leg stays unproven by this seed and by anything else
| sandbox-credentials — provision Vipps test-MSN credentials so the seed can reach a genuine 200 ; pro: proves the whole leg including the provider, which nothing else on this branch does ; con: needs a credential only Sven can obtain and place, and a sibling review found the initiate sends no required return URL, so a 200 may be unreachable until that lands anyway
| fake-in-demo — register a substitute deposit port when the demo stack runs ; pro: a demo walks the entire flow end to end with no credentials ; con: the demo then proves the fake works rather than the product — the same fabricated-evidence shape the Meals review flagged, where every green capture test reaches the ledger through a row nobody can produce — and it puts a substitution in the production composition root
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: row-not-status 2026-08-03 by @sven

**Recommended:** row-not-status — it is what the lane already built and proved, and the honest limit of
what this machine can show. The other two are worth ruling on their own merits, but neither is needed to
unblock the seed.

"`Configure<MealsFeatureSettings>` is called nowhere, so the gate reads false in every deployment whatever configuration says" — the first clause is true and the conclusion is false. Program.cs:813 calls `services.AddMealsFeatureOptions()`, which binds `Features:Meals` via `AddOptions<MealsFeatureSettings>().BindConfiguration(...)`; `BindConfiguration` was chosen over `Configure<T>(GetSection(...))` because `AddServices(IServiceCollection)` has no IConfiguration in scope. So `fact:meals.gate`'s probe (`Program.cs contains:Configure<MealsFeatureSettings>`) cannot go green without writing a redundant or worse binding, and will keep stamping `unconf` at every refresh. Change the probe to `contains:services.AddMealsFeatureOptions();` — that is the one line whose removal darkens the gate, and MealsFeatureSettingsBindingTests already pins that exact string comment-stripped.



### Decision D-GROWTH-EVENTS — how Growth learns a mail bounced, now that Postmark is bound
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-GROWTH-PREFCENTRE
options:
| basic-auth-url — a Basic-auth webhook URL plus an IP allowlist, which is Postmark's own documented answer ; pro: keeps the ruled provider and needs no second vendor ; con: a shared secret carried in a URL is weaker than the HMAC the ingestion path was built for, and the allowlist is an operational thing somebody has to maintain
| split-provider — keep Postmark for transactional mail, use a signing provider for the bulk stream ; pro: delivery events stay HMAC-verified, and the code already assumes that ; con: two vendors, two data-processing agreements, two places Norwegian guest data lands
| no-events — accept that the pilot has no delivery truth ; pro: nothing to build, and a pilot of ten guests can be watched by hand ; con: no Delivered state and no provider-driven suppression, so a hard bounce never suppresses and the same dead address is mailed forever
recommend: basic-auth-url — it is the provider's documented mechanism, it keeps the ruling you just made, and the weaker authentication is bounded by what the endpoint can do: it only ever moves a delivery state, never money and never consent. split-provider buys real cryptographic strength but pays a second data-processing posture for a stream that carries no personal data beyond an address you already hold. Written by @claude from reading the ingestion path and Postmark's documentation, not from running either.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: basic-auth-url 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: the IP allowlist proves unmaintainable, or guest volume makes a shared secret in a URL an unacceptable posture

Found by `L-GROWTH-MAIL` after the provider ruling landed, not before it. `GrowthWebhookIngestionService`
requires a signature and a timestamp header, and **Postmark does not sign webhooks** — that is documented
provider behaviour, not an oversight. So with Postmark bound, no delivery, bounce or complaint event can be
ingested at all: nothing reaches Delivered, and provider-driven suppression never fires.

This is a consequence of `D-MAIL`, discovered downstream of it. It does not reopen that ruling — the
transactional path is proven live — but it means the ruling bought less than it appeared to, and the
difference is exactly the delivery-truth half.

### Decision D-EHF-UNPARK — whether the EHF invoice lane ships before the pilot
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: nothing yet
options:
| unpark-now — run the Lane 0 spike against a real venue's invoices, then wire it ; pro: it converts the module's second-worst deal-loser into the only structural advantage nobody imported can copy, and the parser is already written and green ; con: pre-mandate, some suppliers still send PDFs, so the spike may find the input is not yet structured enough to rely on
| after-pilot — leave it parked until a venue is using the module ; pro: the pilot answers whether costing is wanted at all before we spend on how prices arrive ; con: onboarding is the module's own stated kill risk, and manual price entry is what a pilot venue would quit over
| never — accept manual and CSV price entry as the product ; pro: nothing to build ; con: every competitor demos snap-a-photo invoice capture in the first meeting
recommend: unpark-now — Lane 0 only, the spike that classifies a real venue's invoices, not the wiring. It is cheap, it is falsifiable, and it answers the one question that decides the other two options. Written by @claude from the research report, not from running the parser against any real invoice.
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: unpark-now 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: the spike finds supplier invoices are not structured enough to rely on before the mandate

**The fact that changes this:** Norway's B2B e-invoicing mandate was approved by parliament in
June 2026 — EHF issuance mandatory from 1 January 2027, reception and digital bookkeeping from 2030.
From next year essentially every supplier invoice a Norwegian restaurant receives exists as
structured line-level XML.

The whole category's invoice-OCR apparatus — xtraCHEF, Craftable, MarketMan — is a workaround for
unstructured paper. EHF makes that workaround unnecessary here and nowhere else. `MarginEhfInvoiceParser`
is already written, 954 lines against EN16931, and deliberately unreachable: a test pins that it has
zero production callers pending this ruling.

Journal-exact sales in, mandate-exact purchases in. That is the pair no imported competitor can copy
without rebuilding for Norway.

### Flag F-DUP-DISPATCH — one lane ran twice at once and the twin deleted the live worktree
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: no lane can be started while an agent for that lane is still alive, or the shared-path collision is made impossible by per-lane worktree naming

**The clerk's error, recorded rather than quietly fixed.** `L-MRG-WASTE` returned `blocked`, which sets
the lane back to `open` — and `open` is startable. Its agent was still alive. On the next cycle the
clerk started the lane again, so **two agents with the same identity ran the same lane concurrently**,
one against the old brief and one against the new.

They collided on a shared worktree path: the twin finished, committed its receipt, and **deleted the
worktree out from under the run that was still using it.**

Nothing was lost — the second agent verified the twin's receipt adversarially instead of burning a
second thirty-five-minute SQL slot, and containers were attributed by name throughout, so no foreign
container was touched. But the gap is real: a `blocked` verdict returns a lane to a startable state
while its agent may still be running, and lanes may share a scratch path.

Briefs since this one say *never a shared scratch path*; the startable-while-alive half is not closed.

### Flag F-MIG-CHAIN-STACKED — a second lane silently carries an unmerged migration as its own tail
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: no branch carries another lane's unmerged migration as its chain tail, or the dependency is recorded where a migration author will see it
cleared_by: L-MIG-STACK-LAND

`lane/wf-w5-timesheet` **branched off `lane/margin-waste`'s tip and now carries that lane's unmerged
migration as its own chain tail.** Neither lane's brief says so, and nothing in the repo announces it.

Two consequences, both of the shape C2 exists to prevent. Rework margin-waste and the timesheet lane
breaks with it. And a third author who lands a migration believing the chain tip is the branch tip will
produce two migrations sharing a parent — **the failure that surfaces only on a fresh database and
never on the author's.**

Two further August migrations sit on detached heads, on no branch at all, which is how the picture got
this hard to read.

**Sharper, 2026-08-01:** a lane needing a migration measured the distance and it is **five migrations**,
not two — the feature branch is not an ancestor of the true tip. And the THROW ledger is worse than the
naive read: from that lane's base only 50060 is visible, so **the instinctive next number is 50061, which
Margin already holds.** The highest claimed anywhere is 50073.

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (the recommended path, on Sven's instruction to take it for the rest): `land-the-stack-in-order`.**

**The depth number has now been wrong three times, and the pattern is the finding.** It was carried as
*five*, corrected to *six*, and measured this morning as **seven** — `feature/restaurant-modules` ends at
`20260731220005` and the stack carries seven migrations on top. The branches have diverged both ways: 22
feature-only commits against 24 stack-only.

Each correction came from a lane that **measured with git instead of reading the previous lane's
sentence**, and each time the stale number had already been copied forward into a brief. A depth that is
derivable in one command has been hand-carried three times — which is the same shape as the walk counts
and the anonymous-route count, and the reason the ledger now carries an explicit *re-measure, do not
inherit* warning.

**Wrong a fourth time, measured the same day as the third: it is EIGHT — but see the correction below, because this sentence manufactures a disagreement that does not exist.** `feature/restaurant-modules`
carries 127 migrations; the tip at `lane/mig-company-receivable` carries 135. Verified by listing both
trees rather than by reading either previous sentence.

Five, six, seven, eight — **each figure was true when written and false when read**, because the stack
grows while the number sits in prose. The lesson is not that people were careless; it is that **a
derivable number does not belong in prose at all.** It wants a probe.

The chain tip the collector last measured in the checkout the probes read: <!--fact be.mig.head 2026-08-08T22:55Z unconf-->20260731220005_Workforce_IdentityCodeRegisterIssues.cs<!--/fact-->. It is a fact rather than a sentence for the reason above.

**Merged 2026-08-03, and the numbers were wrong again in both directions.** Measured with git before
anything was touched: **seven links, not six. Nine migrations past the integration branch, not eight. 152
of 249 branches unmerged, not 134 of 229.** The "eight" had been measured before the last lane committed
its own migration.

**The order was derived from ancestry rather than timestamps, which is a stronger fact than the brief
claimed:** the stack is **strictly linear**, every link an ancestor of the next — so the order given was
not merely correct, it is **the only order that exists**. Two branches sit on the stack and are *not*
links, because they add no migration.

`lane/train-w3-schema` **does not exist as a branch** — it is a detached commit in a worktree, which is
`F-DETACHED-MIGRATIONS` confirmed independently for the second time.

**The receipt trap appeared twice, and resolving by side would have destroyed evidence.** Both branches had
appended receipt rows for runs the other had never seen; taking either side would have deleted true
receipts — **including every SQL-tier run that exists anywhere in the estate.** Resolved by union,
interleaved by wall clock. That also surfaced a claim already in the tree that is now false — a receipt
saying the SQL tier never ran, when three runs existed on the other side — **recorded per row rather than
edited into another lane's receipt.**

**Correction 2026-08-03, and I had the hazard backwards in every migration brief I wrote today.** I warned
lanes that authoring off `feature/restaurant-modules` would fork a nine-deep chain. **Measured, the
opposite holds:** the integration branch **is an ancestor of** the merged stack and sits thirty-four
commits and nine migrations behind it — so authoring off the integration branch is the safe parent, and my
warning pointed at the wrong danger. Eight merge commits, not seven.

The lane that measured it authored on the merged stack anyway and stated its Designer parent explicitly,
which is why the error surfaced instead of being inherited.

**Correction to my own correction, 2026-08-03.** I wrote *eight merge commits, not seven* against the lane
that landed the stack. **Both numbers are true and they count different things.** The lane said seven
**first-parent links, each receipted**; eight counts merges **in the range**, including an embedded
chain-tip take the lane never made. My sentence reads as if the lane was wrong. It was not.

**And that embedded merge is itself this flag in the flesh** — a chain tip taken into a branch without
announcement — with **no receipt of its own.**

**The unmerged count in this plan is stale again: 164 of 261, not 162 of 259.** The rule I wrote about
derivable numbers not belonging in prose applies to my own sentences, and this is the second time it has
caught one.


**Measured, 2026-08-05: the flag understated the problem sevenfold.** It named one pair. There are **14
branches** carrying another lane's unmerged migration as their chain tail, on a **strictly linear ten-link
chain** sitting above the integration branch's last migration `20260731220005`. Every pair was confirmed with
`--is-ancestor` — thirteen tests, all passing — and the introducing commits were derived with
`--diff-filter=A` rather than inferred from filenames.

**Seven of the fourteen are invisible in their own diffs, and those are the dangerous ones.** They author no
migration at all; they inherited the stack by being cut from a branch that had one. **A reviewer reading such a
diff cannot see that merging it lands ten schema changes.** Named: `lane/margin-waste-500`,
`lane/wf-digest-tautology`, `lane/wf-timesheet-wire`, `lane/review-residuals-rezone`,
`lane/ef-index-shadow-sweep`, `lane/wf-timesheet-race`, `integration/mig-stack-land` — none mentioned anywhere
before this.

**The premise "nobody has written it" was true only of the copy the brief named.** The stack-tip ledger at
`6fa2cbc3` is **+739/−82 lines** against the integration copy, runs to MIG-28, and already documents the
stacking inside MIG-24 to MIG-28 with ancestry measurements. **What was missing is location** — none of it sits
on the branch a new lane is cut from, and it is spread across seven prose sections with no list. The lane
checked rather than assumed that the ledger is the right home: **11 of 11 live migration commits edit it in the
same commit as the migration.**

**Written where the gap was: 81 insertions and zero deletions to the integration copy**, placed with the
existing dated status blocks rather than at the end, because the file is opened to find the chain tip and a
warning 582 lines below the entries is not a warning. On `lane/mig-stack-record` at `a613f026`; nothing pushed.

**For whoever takes the landing arm:** `integration/mig-stack-land` at `4b37f81b` already collects links 1 to 9
and the integration branch is an ancestor of it, so the stack strictly extends and forks nothing. **But the two
ledger copies diverge by 739 lines, so this new section needs a hand merge rather than a `git merge`.**


**One line of the record above is wrong and is corrected here rather than edited away, 2026-08-05.** It states
that `integration/mig-stack-land` has the integration branch as an ancestor and therefore *"strictly extends and
forks nothing"*. **Measured, it forks** — 34 commits on the stack side against 59 on the integration side, with
`--is-ancestor` failing both ways, confirmed independently by the clerk and separately by
`GrowthAuditWriter.cs` being present on one side and absent from the other.

**The consequence is the whole landing plan.** A hand merge across a 739-line ledger divergence, with the MIG-21
trigger collision inside it, is not the fast-forward `D-INTEGRATION-FASTFORWARD` offers as its cheapest option.
That decision now carries the correction too.

### Flag F-WF-TWO-ADMINS-TWO-ENGAGEMENTS — two administrators can each open Workforce for one store
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: two different store administrators opening Workforce concurrently leave exactly one first engagement, refused by a database constraint

Found by the lane sent at the smaller case, and **it is larger than the one anybody had named** — including
the service's own remarks, which describe only a single caller double-submitting.

**Two *different* administrators of one store, neither carrying a person row**, mint two persons. So the
one-person-per-login index is never touched, and both first engagements stand. **A store with two admins
both clicking to open the module is the likeliest way this ever happens in the field**, and it was the case
nobody was looking at.

Both cases are covered by the same constraint; this exists so the larger one is recorded rather than
folded silently into the smaller.

### Flag F-EF-UNNAMED-INDEX-REPLACES — an unnamed index silently reconfigures its neighbour
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: no entity configuration adds an index by columns alone where another index on those columns already exists, or a check reds when one does

Found only by running, and it is the shape worth generalising: **EF keys an unnamed index by its columns.**
So adding a second index on a column that already carries one **reconfigures the existing index rather than
adding a new one.**

The failure that would have shipped: **every roster read quietly loses its index**, while the new
constraint still works and **every test still passes.** A performance defect with no red anywhere, produced
by a one-word omission — the named overload is required.

Nothing sweeps for this today, and one migration lane found it by accident.

### Flag F-AZURE-FUNCKEY — a live Azure Functions host key is committed, and a red test prints it
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: the key is rotated and the new value lives in user-secrets or environment config, never in a committed file

A **live** Azure Functions host key sits in the repository, shared by both document endpoints. The lane
that found it consolidated it to exactly one place so rotation is a one-line change — but consolidation
is not rotation, and only its owner can rotate it.

Second exposure, same key: the outbound-deny handler **echoes the whole request URI**, so a red wire run
prints the key into whatever reads that output.

**Deliberately not redacted.** The estate already paid this lesson on 2026-07-30 with the Wolt secret:
redacting the message without rotating the credential fixes nothing, and makes the exposure harder to
find later. The owner action is rotation.

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (Sven): `rotate-at-deploy`.**

### Flag F-FIXTURE-NO-GATES — the e2e fixture modelled no flags, so gated journeys could not fail
state: open
severity: blocker

`workforce-schedule-publish` journey was green **only because the fixture modelled no flags at all.** The

The journey was not weakly asserted; it was asserted against a world that cannot produce the refusal.

rather than test scope.

The remedy is not per-journey: any journey walking any gated surface has the same hole, and five other
modules are deny-closed the same way. The fixture must model the gate, and a journey should turn its own

**Audit verdict 2026-08-03: already-fixed. The remedy is dated 08-01 — two days before the ruling written
for this flag — and it is at the world**, not on a branch. This is one of the eight stale blockers found
today.

discovering that work already exists, and the whole point of the re-measure was to stop paying that price.
It waits for `D-SPEC-L-GR-DELIVERY-RECORD`'s ruling, which decides how the already-fixed set is closed —

### Flag F-MEALS-LEVER-INERT — the switchboard offers a Meals switch that reaches no guest
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: the Meals catalog entry either reaches the consumer path or is withheld from the catalog with a written reason, as Training and Workforce already do for theirs
cleared_by: L-MEALS-LEVER-WITHHOLD

Found by the journey sweep, in the screen that shipped hours earlier. `meals.module` — **the one Meals
lever in the per-store catalog** — is read at three admin routes and **none of them is on the consumer
path.** Flipping it neither enables nor disables a store's quotes or funded checkouts.

So an operator now has a switchboard that shows them a Meals switch, and throwing it does nothing a
guest can see. The real gate is host configuration, which no screen touches.

This is the advertised-but-ungating shape the estate already withheld five Training flags and two
Workforce flags for. Meals' own reach test pins the lever at 4 of 29 routes and is honest about it —
what is new is that there is now a screen presenting the lever as if it worked.

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (Sven): `withhold-with-a-reason`.**

**Corrected 2026-08-03 by the lane sent to close it: the premise was false and the truth is worse.**

The operator surface never reported these flags as effective — the catalog cannot hold a row for them, so
none could exist. What the page actually did: its withheld note told operators that **all** withheld
stages *would have no effect whatever they were set to*.

That is true of Training and Workforce, whose owners state they have no enforcement point. **It is the
opposite of true for Meals**, whose own descriptor says its three are enforced at fifteen production call
sites. **The board was calling an enforced billing flag inert** — and a venue reading it would have
concluded the money path was dark when it was not.

Fixed by naming both kinds separately, plus a disclosure that the Meals money-path flags are deployment
configuration. No catalog entry, no control drawn: the `tell-the-truth` ruling is intact.

**The C3 gap is stated rather than faked:** no endpoint exposes the Meals configuration section, so the
page cannot distinguish *off at deployment* from *off for this store*. It says the deployment shape and
says the value is unknowable from there. Closing it needs a shared platform field.

**And half two was understated.** The content-hash header was the briefed case, but `Content-Disposition`
was unexposed too — and that one is **reachable today**: nine actions return files, two live browser
callers parse it, and both the Margin statement export and the Workforce hours export were taking their
client-side fallback filename **every single time.**

### Flag F-EV-ACCEPT-UNGATED — a guest can accept or decline with the module switched off
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: the public proposal accept and decline writes refuse for a store without the Events core flag, pinned by a test that reds if the gate is removed
cleared_by: L-EV-ACCEPT-GATE

The core flag gates the Events **reads** — which is why the pipeline goes dark without it. It does
**not** gate the public accept and decline writes.

Those are state-changing and reachable with the flag off, so a venue that never enabled the module, or
one that turned it off, can still have its proposals accepted from the outside. The proposal service has
**no gate at all**, which contradicts the module gate's own docstring.

Found by the journey sweep and handed on rather than fixed, correctly — it is a different lane's shape
from modelling fixtures.

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (Sven): `gate-the-writes`.**

**Closed 2026-08-03, and the count was understated: three ungated writes, not two.** Events has five
anonymous routes. **All three writes were ungated** — enquiry creation, proposal accept, proposal decline —
and the deposit page was the only gated anonymous route. The proposal service carried **no module gate at
all**, and the amendment service carries none either, so the accept route had *two* ungated write paths.

The gate went in where the token first resolves the store, and **before the status switch**, so it covers
the idempotent replay and the amendment branch too. The refusal reuses the code the guest page already
renders, so there is no unhandled failure where a refusal belongs.

Its non-vacuity is the shape worth copying: each refusal sits beside a success on **the same token, same
world, same call**, differing in exactly one variable — and it pins the **exact** error code, so a subject
that was merely expired would fail the test rather than satisfy it.

It also pinned the thing that made this possible: the gate is an **optional constructor parameter**, which
is itself the failure mode — an unsupplied one silently does nothing while a hand-injected suite still
passes. A wiring test now resolves the service from the real composition root and pins that the gate
arrived.

state: open

owner: @sven
clears_when: the public enquiry write refuses for a store without the Events core flag, or the plan records that a public enquiry is deliberately reachable for any store and why

which was the right call.

The public enquiry write is ungated. A guest can create an event row for a store whose admin surface
answers 404 — **a confirmation for a booking the venue can never see.**

The reason it is a decision rather than a defect: **the enquiry form is plausibly how a venue discovers the
module at all.** Refusing it may close the front door on the thing that sells it. Whether the answer is
*refuse the write* or *the form should not be reachable for an un-opted store* is a product call.

The same lane left the payment callback alone on purpose and said why: gating it would strand in-flight
money, and that posture is already documented against the deposits surface — unlike accept and decline,
which had nothing recorded against them at all.

state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: Meals registers an effective-flag resolver, or the screen's reliability sentence is scoped to the modules where it holds
cleared_by: L-FLAGS-RESOLVERS-COVER-THREE

**The landing vehicle is `lane/flags-resolvers-cover-three` @ `0f29a898`.** The backend half was first written
2026-08-01 on `lane/flags-effective-resolvers` @ `e45ec4c1`; that branch and `lane/flags-excuse-byflag` @ `6ae0b8db`

cleared_by: L-XZ-CREDIT-FIELDS

### Flag F-FILTER-NOT-CONTAINERFREE — the suite filter everyone uses still starts SQL containers
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: a filter or trait exists that provably starts no container, derived from what the tests actually use rather than from their names

The filter that excludes SQL-Server-named tests **still starts Testcontainers**, because at least one
scaffold test uses them without carrying that word in its name. A lane hit it today while running the
full suite, killed its own run immediately and touched no foreign container.

That filter is the one this plan's briefs have effectively been recommending to lanes with no container
slot. **It is not a container-free filter**, and a lane that believes it is will take a slot it was not
granted — on a host where three concurrent containers has already meant an out-of-memory kill.

The remedy is a trait derived from what a test actually uses, in the shape of the estate's existing
derived-scope convention tests, rather than a name match a new file silently escapes.

**A second instance found the same day, in a different module:** two Growth lineage classes use the SQL
fixture without carrying that word in their names either. So this is not one stray file — **the naming
convention has already failed twice**, which is the argument for deriving the trait rather than patching
the names.

### Flag F-EV-NO-GUEST-ORIGIN — no configuration says where the guest deposit page lives
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: a committed configuration sets the guest origin for Events, or a recorded ruling says which host serves those pages
cleared_by: L-EV-GUEST-ORIGIN

Found while checking why the deposit initiate carries no return URL. **The return URL cannot be composed
because nothing says where to return to.** The Events public origin is unset in **every committed
configuration** — the settings file holds only the dispatch switch, and the development file has no Events
section at all — and **the setting's own doc comment records that which origin serves those pages remains
Sven's decision.**

Two consequences the lane drew out. The guest cannot be returned after paying. And **the guest could not
have been mailed the link in the first place**, because the same origin composes it.

This is the same shape as the Growth preference centre's origin problem, and answering one carelessly
answers the other by accident.

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (Sven): `decide-the-host-now`.**

**Corrected 2026-08-03: "the only caller that sets a fallback is checkout" was one call site short.**
Three production call sites reach the Vipps initiate and **two** set a fallback — both composing the
checkout path. Right about the destination, wrong about the count.

**And the non-vacuity number is the finding.** Mutating the service's fallback assignment to null reds
**exactly one test out of 4392** on the whole container-free tier — the new one. Every fake-based test
stays green. So this was never only an Events gap: **checkout's own fallback had never been covered at the
serialization hop either.** The load-bearing test drives the real service over a captured HTTP edge and
asserts the serialized JSON, because the deposit fake and the scripted service both accept the call
happily — which is why no suite could see it.

**Two corrections to my brief, from the lane that closed it.**

**Overstated:** I wrote that Vipps *requires* the fallback. That could not be confirmed from the published
spec. What is confirmed: Vipps **validates** the field and it is the post-payment redirect target. So the
honest statement is **the guest has no way back**, not *the provider refuses*.

**Understated:** Vipps **rejects a localhost fallback**, which constrains what the development value can
be — recorded in the setting's own doc comment rather than left to be rediscovered.

The ruling is pinned as **a relationship rather than a literal**: the guest origin must share a registrable
domain with the committed public base URL, so it reopens exactly where the ruling's `reopen_when` says it
should. A second test resolves the settings from the live composition root, **because a file cannot prove a
key binds.**

**And the configuration is now correct for a page that is still undeployed** — the deposit page exists only
on this branch, the same unshipped-guest-surface problem the preference centre hit. See
`D-PREFCENTRE-DEPLOY`.

constraint and no rate limit.

So the route is not closed. It is narrowed from **one request to any address** to **two requests to any
address, one at a time.**

flag with the comment *a profile email a user can set to anything proves nothing.*

A go-live blocker rather than confirmed live exposure — the mail provider still defaults to a fake — but

plan. **Whether it has ever been exploited is unanswerable:** Growth has no audit ledger and the email
column is overwritten in place with no history.

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (Sven): `already-fixed-pending-merge`.**

**Step one of the blocker re-measure, 2026-08-03: the lane meant to clear this has delivered (`L-CONFIRM-FAMILY-MERGE`).** That is a candidate, not a verdict — it says the work exists, not that the condition holds. **Step two is owed**: prove the green is real rather than vacuous, the way the callback lane did by mutating its suite both ways. ### Flag F-GR-DISPATCH-UNATTRIBUTED — a mass send has no attributable trigger
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: the dispatch call resolves and records the actor that triggered it
cleared_by: L-GR-DISPATCH-ACTOR

Found while reviewing the test-send guard, and it **undercuts that lane's own framing.** Test-send was
described as the only newsletter write whose controller passed no user id. **That is not true — dispatch
passes none either**, and dispatch is the path that mails the whole audience.

It is approval-gated, so a name exists — but it is **the approver's, not the sender's**, and those can be
different people. Combined with Growth having no audit ledger at all, **a mass send has no attributable
trigger anywhere on disk.**

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (the recommended path, on Sven's instruction to take it for the rest): `resolve-and-record-the-actor`.**

**Closed 2026-08-03, confirmed still-true at the tip first.** The dispatch action was **the only write on
that controller not requiring a caller identity**, and the run row carries no actor column — so the only
name reachable from a send was **the approver's: who cleared the content, not who sent it.**

**It recorded one row per request rather than per run**, and the reasoning matters: dispatch is idempotent,
but **a caller who re-triggers it drives the drain that submits whatever is still queued** — so naming only
the creator misattributes that mail. Both roles are separated, and the created-run row is staged **inside**
the transaction, so it commits with the deliveries or not at all.

**It landed in the ledger a sibling built rather than beside it**, based on that lane's branch instead of
the bare tip — **no column, no index, no constraint**, so the specified migration shape is unchanged. That
is the fifth same-shape collision this week avoided by reading across worktrees first.

**By-value across three distinct principals** — approver, dispatcher and re-requester — with two admins on
one run leaving **two rows with two different ids, which no prefix-plus-constant can produce.**

**And it proved the unreachable-401 rather than faking it**, independently reproducing the finding a Margin
lane made the same day: no token authenticates while being unnameable, so a wire test asserting that
refusal would be measuring authentication. Pinned as a fact — empty challenge body, the module's code
absent — with the guard proven at the service seam instead.

### Flag F-GR-SWEEP-ACTORLESS — the dispatch sweep records no actor, on purpose, and that wants review
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: the sweep's passes are attributable, or the plan records that an unnamed sweep is deliberate and why an append-per-pass was rejected

**A judgement the lane made and flagged rather than buried.** The dispatch sweep is left **deliberately
actorless**: it resumes runs whose creation is already named, over a recipient set fixed at creation.

The reason it did not add a system-actor row per pass is the interesting part: **the sweep picks up every
in-progress run on every interval**, so a run stuck behind a flipped kill switch would **append forever
into a table C1 forbids purging.** An attribution that grows without bound is worse than none.

So the gap is real, the omission is reasoned, and the alternative is worse — which is precisely the shape
that needs a ruling rather than a lane.

Each was found separately by a different lane. **They are one debt with one payment** — a single run at the

### Flag F-CONFIRM-BRUTEFORCE — the proof the § 15 guard rests on can be guessed
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: confirming an email is rate-limited and attempt-counted, and the code is drawn from a cryptographic source
cleared_by: L-CONFIRM-FAMILY-MERGE

The test-send guard now requires a **confirmed** address, which is the right fix. **Its premise is not
sound.**

Confirming an email compares a plaintext six-digit code with **no attempt counter, no lockout on that
path, and no rate limit** — the code is **not invalidated on a wrong guess**, and a fresh one can be minted
forever. Even odds at roughly 450,000 attempts: **about seventy minutes at a hundred requests a second.**
The code is also drawn from a non-cryptographic generator.

So markedsføringsloven § 15 went from **two requests to any address** to **an afternoon and a script.**
Narrowed, not closed — **and the commit message claims closed.**

**The condition this turns on:** the rate-limit lane running now must cover the **guess** entry point, not
only the address write. If it covers only the send route, **the § 15 claim does not hold.**

Not live exposure today — the module is dark and the provider defaults to a fake. **A go-live gate.**

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (Sven): `already-fixed-pending-merge`.**

**Step one of the blocker re-measure, 2026-08-03: the lane meant to clear this has delivered (`L-CONFIRM-FAMILY-MERGE`).** That is a candidate, not a verdict — it says the work exists, not that the condition holds. **Step two is owed**: prove the green is real rather than vacuous, the way the callback lane did by mutating its suite both ways. Recorded so the audit reads a shortlist rather than forty-seven undifferentiated blockers.

Both now re-throw **after** writing the artifact, and both mutations re-run red. **This is the eighteenth

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (Sven): `fail-the-process`.**

### Flag F-GIT-ADD-SWALLOW — a concurrent stage swallowed another lane's files
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: every lane commits by pathspec, so a concurrent lane's files cannot be staged by accident

**A lane's first commit swallowed six of another lane's untracked files**, because a broad stage on a
shared tree takes whatever is there at that instant. It was repaired — reset, re-commit, and the other
lane's two modified and six untracked files **verified byte-identical afterwards** — but the repair was
luck of noticing.

**The durable fix is one habit: commit by pathspec.** `git commit -- <paths>` is immune to it. With a
dozen lanes on one tree and two worktree collisions already this program, it should be a standing rule in
every brief rather than a lesson each lane learns once.

### Flag F-FIXTURE-BACKUP-STALE — a restore-from-backup would now drop another lane's work
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: no lane holds a stale backup of a shared fixture file, or restores are done by pathspec commit rather than by file copy

The byte-exact backup-and-restore habit — adopted precisely **because a checkout would destroy other
lanes' hunks** — has developed the failure it was invented to prevent. One lane's backup of the shared
fixture server is now **stale against the file it would restore**, so **restoring from it would drop a
sibling's committed hunks.**

Two lanes also collided on the same tree in the same hour: one **briefly swept the other's staged files
into its commit**, amended to release them, and the other re-committed alone.

**The habit is not the fix; committing by pathspec is.** A backup is a snapshot of a moment on a tree
where a dozen lanes are moving.

state: open

Every throttle the estate relies on — the code-to-contact-point caps, the operator PIN cool-off, and the

### Flag F-FIXTURE-BEHIND-BACKEND — the e2e fixture can be a release behind what it stands in for
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: a check reds when the fixture's refusal shapes diverge from the backend's, rather than a lane noticing by hand
cleared_by: L-FIXTURE-DIVERGENCE

**Found twice in one day, from opposite directions, and it is worse than either instance.**

The admin-confirm lane found **the fixture was a release behind the backend** — it checked address
equality but **not the confirmation flag** that had just landed. Its journey would have run against **a
world that never refused anything**: an assertion that could not fail, in the exact shape the standing law
names. It levelled the fixture and re-ran a sibling journey green.

The journey-coverage lane found the same class from the other side: two ported fixtures answered
**hard-coded flags**, so the surfaces they stood in for could not refuse either.

**This is the fixture-models-no-flags defect generalised.** A fixture is a claim about a backend, and
nothing checks that claim. Six journeys were once green for exactly this reason; **the remedy so far has
been a lane noticing by hand, which is not a remedy.**

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (the recommended path, on Sven's instruction to take it for the rest): `check-for-divergence`.**

**Closed 2026-08-03 — and the lane reframed the flag while closing it. The divergence is real, but not as
"somebody forgot": there is no single backend to be behind.** Three refusal shapes exist on lane branches
and **do not exist on the integration branch at all.** The fixture is level with three lanes and **ahead of
the integration branch.**

So a committed snapshot of "the backend's refusals" would have gone green the moment the backend moved,
which is the failure one level up. The check instead **reads a named checkout and prints the sha, branch
and dirty state it read** — the answer is only as good as the world you point it at, and it says which
world that was.

**Derived, not enumerated, and the residue is stated.** Backend refusal statuses come from each module's
typed exception class; routes from their attributes; reachable refusals scoped by the controller's own
imports. On the fixture side **a refusal primitive is any function whose parameters name both a status and
a code** — which found four differently-named helpers without being told any of them. What remains
enumerated is the route mapping per handler, and **a mapping does not go stale when a refusal is added**,
while a missed declaration **reds rather than greens.**

**Discrimination proved both ways on the real corpus.** Deleting one refusal reds it by name, file and
line. Renaming a helper, rewriting messages, reordering handlers and adding a field all stay green — as
does an entire new backend route with its own refusals. That last arm is the one that matters: a check
reddening on any difference is a diff, not a divergence check.

**Its first cut did red on everything** — forty-eight refusals attributed to one route, because a
cryptography call resolved to a controller action of the same name. Scoping by imports is the fix, and it
is recorded rather than quietly corrected.

**Found outside its subject:** the fixture allowed a dispatched newsletter to be edited **where the backend
refuses it** — the divergence check caught that on its first run.


**The restatement that sustained this flag is false, and the clerk verified it directly, 2026-08-05.**
`lanes/L-BLOCKER-RESTATE/verdicts.md:197-200` states that no divergence check exists on any branch and that
`package.json` carries six e2e scripts. On `feature/restaurant-modules`: **`test/e2e/scripts/fixture-divergence.js`
is tracked**, `package.json` carries **nine** e2e-named scripts, and **two of them run the divergence check** —
`test:e2e:fixture-divergence` and a `--prove` variant.

**This does not clear the flag, and the distinction matters.** The condition asks that *a check reds when the
fixture's refusal shapes diverge*, not that a script exists. A file and a wired npm script are necessary and
are not the claim. What is owed is a demonstration that the check goes red on a real divergence — which is
what the `--prove` arm appears to exist for, and which `L-FIXTURE-DIVERGENCE` already owns.

**What changes is the flag's standing rather than its state.** It was being sustained on a premise that is
false, so nobody was looking for the demonstration that would settle it.


**The clerk's correction to this flag was itself wrong, and the recheck caught it, 2026-08-05.** I recorded the
restatement at `:197-200` as **false**. It is **stale**. Re-derived at the ref that document actually names —
`31fc45d`, not the tip — it reproduces **verbatim**: `test/e2e/scripts/fixture-divergence.js` is **untracked
there**, and `package.json` declares **exactly six** e2e scripts, none of them a divergence run.

**The check landed at `a62160e` on 2026-08-03 at 18:16. The verdicts document's own mtime is 17:55.** It was
overtaken **twenty-one minutes after it was written.** The tracked file, the nine scripts and the two runners
that I measured are all real — they are a measurement of the **tip**, eleven commits later. The two readings
were never in conflict.

**This is the same error the clerk had briefed three lanes to avoid, in the same session.** A verdict measured
at a newer ref than the document names is not a false verdict; it is an unread one. Recorded here rather than
quietly amended, because the flag's standing depends on which it is: a stale premise is overtaken by a landing,
a false one was never true.


**Run at the integration tip, 2026-08-05, and it is RED on a real defect.** At backend `8e2b57de`,
`GrowthNewsletterService.cs:649` throws **`409 growth.test_address_suppressed`** on test-sends, and
`growth-newsletter.js` answers no such refusal and declares no exemption. Verified by hand on both sides. **The
fixture is a release behind, which is exactly what this flag was raised about, one release on.**

**The condition is met on the mechanism and the mechanism earned it.** The control did not break the fixture —
it **broke the comparator**: blinding `compare()` to `fixture-behind` makes `--prove` red on the `removed` arm
**while the live run goes falsely green**. So today's red is load-bearing, and `--prove` is precisely what
catches its erasure. Two further controls: closing the one divergence turns it green, so it is not a stuck red;
and flipping `409` to `422` on the approval route produces `status-mismatch` on a different route.

**Which side the check reads mattered more than anything else about it.** The backend side is a **working tree,
not a ref**, and the shared `OkamAPI-modules` checkout is **divergent — 1 ahead, 63 behind**. Three worlds gave
three answers: the tip yields one `fixture-behind`; the checkout as-found yields one `fixture-**ahead**`, the
**opposite verdict**; an older ref yields 22. **Running it as-found would have reported the fixture ahead of a
merely-older backend and missed the real gap entirely.** The lane took a private detached clone instead.

**Three corrections to what this plan said about the check.** `--prove` has **seven** arms, not six, and **it is
gated** — by `test/fixture-refusal-divergence.test.js`, 8 of 8 green. What is in no suite is the **live
comparison**, and **no CI runs any suite at all**. The prior lane's "22 divergences" reproduces exactly, but
**only against `feature/swiss`**, which has no typed error families and no module controllers.

**And "unrecorded in fact" was wrong on disk and right on the branch.** A five-run prior receipt exists, hidden
three ways at once: it is untracked; its only committed form is inside a commit no `refs/heads` contains; and
its return's `evidence:` line was **decorated, so `os.path.exists` returned False**. That last one is the trap
recorded on `F-EXISTENCE-CHECKS-REPORT-PRESENT-FILES-ABSENT`, **firing on a receipt that existed.**

**One correction to the lane, verified by the clerk: the snapshot commit is not danglings.** `51970563` is held
by `refs/lanes/plan-snapshot` and `--contains` returns it. The lane enumerated `refs/heads` only — the same
both-namespaces trap this plan has now recorded three times. **It is safe from `git gc` and still absent from
every branch**, which is the half that matters.

**What the receipt does not cover, stated beside the pass:** 12 of 642 backend routes anchored, across 5 of 102
controllers; **four fixture files answer refusals with zero anchors**; and the script's own
"a result without a commit is not a measurement" doctrine is **advisory** — pointed at a non-git tree it prints
`(not a git checkout)` and proceeds.


**One figure in that receipt was measured in a tree that could not have produced it, and the clerk repeated it
without naming the tree.** The receipt states *"1 suite passed, 8 tests passed, 4.1 s"* for
`test/fixture-refusal-divergence.test.js`, run from the lane worktree `/Users/svendaneel/okam/web-fixdiv`.
**That worktree has no `node_modules`, and neither does its parent.** The shared checkout has both the module
tree and the same test file — so the run almost certainly happened there.

**The result is probably still right and the attribution is not, and those are different things.** Both trees
carry the same test file, so *"the arms are gated, 8 of 8"* likely holds; what does not hold is that it was
measured where the receipt says. **A figure whose tree is misattributed cannot be re-run by the next reader**,
which is the entire point of a receipt.

**It is the wrong-working-directory trap again, one document along.** A sibling demonstrated the same class
tonight by running a script from a foreign directory: it **overwrote the artifact it cites** with 112 paths from
another tree, and still passed 13 of 15 assertions. **Neither errored.**

**Found by the lane that came after, checking a claim it had been handed rather than inheriting it** — which is
the behaviour the whole set of instrument failures argues for.

### Flag F-CAP-COUNTS-LANES — the SQL cap counts lanes, and the danger is containers
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven

The plan's SQL cap governs **lanes**, and the thing that has OOM-killed this host is **containers.** Those
stopped being the same number the moment lanes began **leaving live worlds up on purpose** — which is
exactly what C5 asked them to do, so a human can walk them.

two to three. Two of those belong to finished lanes holding worlds open for a walk; **neither counts
against the cap, and both are doing the right thing.**

**So the cap can read 2 of 2 while the machine carries twice that.** The fix is accounting, not
discipline: teardown commands are recorded in each lane's return, and nothing reads them.

### Flag F-GR-CONFIRM-AGELESS — a mailbox that changed hands quietly still authorises a send
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: a confirmation older than a ruled window cannot authorise a send, which needs both the window and a column recording when the confirmation was made

Named by the lane that closed everything else about this, **and it stopped exactly where a ruling was
required rather than inventing one.**

A mailbox that changed hands and **quietly accepts** mail leaves no suppression, so nothing catches it.
Closing that needs **two things the estate does not have**: a staleness window nobody has ruled, and a
column recording **when** a confirmation was made. The lane authored neither, on the reasoning that **an
unruled window makes it a column nothing reads.**

The residue matters because the confirmation is now the load-bearing proof that an address belongs to its
sender. This is the part of that proof that cannot be strengthened by evidence — only by a policy.

### Flag F-ACCEPTANCE-IS-THE-CHOKE — sixteen lanes wait on work that is finished but unaccepted
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
cleared_by: none — only the owner can clear this
clears_when: the finished-but-unaccepted lanes other lanes depend on are walked and accepted, or the plan records which dependencies do not need acceptance

**Measured, not felt.** Twenty-eight open lanes are blocked by an unsatisfied dependency. **Sixteen of
them wait on a lane that is already built** — and one on a lane that is **verified**.

The rule is right and deliberate: a lane's dependency counts as satisfied **only when the target is
accepted**, and acceptance is the owner's alone. That is the standing law working exactly as written —
**a green suite is not evidence a person can use something.**

But it means the choke is no longer capacity, or the migration chain, or the host. **It is the walk.** **Three**
live worlds are standing at their ports right now, freshly rebuilt and left up on purpose, because C5 says
the walk is the gate — and until somebody walks them, sixteen lanes cannot start. One of the three now
**resets in nine seconds** rather than seventy, so the walk costs less than it did this morning.

The remaining twelve are ordinary: eight on open decisions, four on lanes still moving.

**Re-measured 2026-08-02, and it has grown.** **111 lanes sit at `built-unverified`** and exactly
**one** is `verified`. Twenty-two open lanes are gated on another lane; **eighteen of those are waiting
on work that is already built.** The queue is not short of code — it is short of a person walking it.

It now bites the guardrail work itself: `L-GUARD-DEMO` has run, its evidence is committed, and it cannot
record its own completion because it needs `L-GUARD-W0` **accepted**. The dependency is correct and the
lane is finished; the transition is the owner's.

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (Sven): `walk-and-accept-a-batch`.**

**`cleared_by` corrected 2026-08-03: `L-LIVE-WORLD-RESTORE` cannot clear this flag.** That lane cut a walk
from seventy seconds to nine — it makes the act **cheap**, it does not perform it. The `clears_when`
requires the walk itself, or a recorded policy about which dependencies need no acceptance.

Left as it was, this flag would have sat open forever with its clearing lane recorded as finished — a flag
waiting on a lane that was never going to satisfy it.


**Re-measured 2026-08-03 and my own number was wrong: 149 built-unverified, not 118.** The method was the
error — **sixteen are compact one-line items a state-field scan cannot see.** Measured instead by loading
the tool's own admissibility functions and calling them read-only against every entity, which is the only
way to get this right.

**None of the 149 verifies against its recorded evidence today.** The refusals sort cleanly: thirty-three
have admissible evidence and fail **only** on the exit-naming rule; thirty-seven name a file that exists
**only in a sibling worktree**; sixteen name a branch or a commit rather than a file; twenty-two record no
evidence at all.

**The cheapest batch is twenty-two review lanes** — all carry an existing, admissible review document and
fail only because the exit is prose. One identical mechanical edit each.

**And the caution that matters: seven of the eleven other prescribed paths live in other worktrees and die
with them.** Verifying against those buys a green that evaporates.

### Flag F-ARTIFACT-STORE-OVERWRITES — the canonical journey artifacts are the wrong runs, right now
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: an artifact cannot be displaced by a weaker later run, and every artifact records which backend build answered it
cleared_by: L-ARTIFACT-RANK-KEY

**Verified by direct check, not argued.** The three journeys that ran live have all been **displaced at
their canonical paths** by the lanes' own later verification runs. Today, a reader joining on those paths
finds **zero live evidence and one live failure** — because the canonical file for one journey is **the
deliberately-failed guard proof**, and the other two are **fixture** re-runs. The passing live artifacts
survive only inside the lanes' own directories.

**The strongest evidence a journey ever produced is silently replaced by the weakest.** The store is
last-writer-wins, the write happens only in teardown, and **nothing clears the directory at run start** —
so an interrupted run also leaves yesterday's live-and-passed file standing for today's broken world.

**And no artifact records which backend build answered it.** The health probe is unauthenticated and its
body is one word, so **any API satisfies it** — including a stale checkout. One lane's API was built from a
detached worktree and **the recorded commit is the frontend tree.** That is the fixture-version blocker
**transferred, not solved.**

This matters more than the sum of its parts because **acceptance is now the binding constraint on this
plan**, and these artifacts are what a walk is judged against.

**Half closed, 2026-08-02, and the half that remains is one line.** The canonical path is **no longer
whoever ran last** — it now holds **the strongest run on record**, ranked live over fixture, passed over
failed, and **identified over unidentified**, backed by a per-backend file and an append-only ledger. **The
displacement was run twice to prove it**: a fixture re-run left a standing live pass byte-identical, and
with the protection mutated away **the identical command overwrote it.** All three canonical slots now hold
live passes, verified directly.

**What remains is build identity on each artifact.** The mechanism exists and works unaided — it asks
whoever holds the port what directory it runs from and asks that checkout for its head, **which needed
nobody's cooperation** — but the three standing artifacts predate it and record no build. The lane named
the one line that closes it, in a script two other lanes own.

**And the clerk's account of the store's state was stale by the time it was read:** other lanes had
re-run all three journeys, so the paths already held live passes. **The mechanisms were untouched by
that** — which is why the lane built anyway rather than declaring the problem gone.

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (the recommended path, on Sven's instruction to take it for the rest): `rank-and-key-by-backend`.**

**Closed 2026-08-03 for the mechanism, and two of its three clauses were already true.** Displacement
ranking had landed weeks earlier and was not rebuilt. **The three displaced live journeys were already
restored** — other lanes' own re-runs put real passes back at those paths, with every referenced screenshot
on disk. The lane **fabricated nothing and re-ran nothing to manufacture a restoration**, which was the
temptation the brief named.

**The newsletter overwrite was closed by preservation rather than refusal, and the distinction is the
design.** A same-backend run **must** keep taking the slot — a failing world has to be able to say so, and
the provisional write is what stops a killed run leaving a stale pass behind. What was wrong is that the
displaced record **vanished from disk.** It is now kept whole under a superseded name, keyed from the record
that replaced it, and **that file only ever moves up.**

**Non-vacuity attempted for real rather than argued:** a fixture run against a standing live pass left the
canonical **byte-identical**; a legitimate re-run **took** the slot, and preservation fired unaided, with
the superseded file coming out byte-identical to the canonical it replaced. **That is the newsletter shape,
caught live.**

Its own mutation harness compared nothing on one side at first, because the runner summarises on the error
stream — **caught before any number was believed.**

**Clause (b) is two of twenty-two on disk, not every.** The mechanism is total, but a standing artifact
gains its identity only on its **next** run: nineteen fixture artifacts need one re-run each and two live
ones need a live world. The lane **deliberately declined to mass re-run** — one journey is known red at the
tip, and reddening other lanes' green evidence before an acceptance walk is not a lane's call. That
restraint is correct and it is why this clause stays open.

### Flag F-INVOICE-RETRY-ANONYMOUS — an unauthenticated route mails every unsent invoice in the database
state: open
severity: blocker
owner: @sven
clears_when: the bulk invoice retry route requires authorisation, pinned by a test that reds if the attribute is removed
cleared_by: L-INVOICE-AUTHORIZE

**Condition met and verified, but the tool cannot clear it and I may not force it.** At `26599c6e` the
controller carries a class-level `[Authorize]` and `[Authorize(Roles = ClaimConstants.PowerUserRole)]`
on all six actions — I read that at the tip rather than taking the lane's word. The merge lane proved it
on the wire in both directions: before, an anonymous `POST /Invoices/RetrySendingExistingInvoices`
answered **200**; after, anonymous gets 401 with a bearer challenge and an empty body, a non-power user
gets 403 with **no** challenge header, and a power user gets 200.

`plan flag clear` refuses because this `clears_when` names no `fact:` key, so the tool cannot test it —
and the override is `--by @sven`, which is his authority, not mine. **This flag is one owner action from
closed.** Rewriting the condition so the tool would accept it is not something I will do to reach a
clear I want.

Found by the renderer lane, **outside its own subject**, while enumerating the call sites it had to fix.

**The bulk retry route carries no authorisation attribute at all**, and what it does is **iterate every
unsent invoice in the database and mail them.** Anyone who can reach the host can trigger it.

Not a leak of content to the caller — the mail goes to each invoice's own recipient — which is why it is a
blocker rather than a catastrophe: **it is an unauthenticated way to make the product send a large volume of
real mail to real customers, repeatedly.**

**Ruled 2026-08-03 (Sven): `fold-into-the-five`.**

**Subsumed 2026-08-03 by `F-INVOICE-ROUTES-ANONYMOUS`.** Same controller, same lane, same ruling
(`authorize-all-five`). It was kept separate only so the *mails-your-customers* consequence would not be
lost in a list; that consequence is now recorded on the routes flag, and two names for one problem is a
second thing to forget to close.

### Flag F-DEV-SERVERS-SHARE-BUILD — three dev servers share one build directory
state: open
severity: warn
owner: @sven
clears_when: two live journey runs can proceed in one checkout without one deleting the other's build output

**Cost two lanes whole chain runs today, independently.** Three dev servers in this checkout share one
build directory: a sibling's recompile **deletes a template out from under a running server**, and the
bundler **caches the failure until restart.**

Worse in one direction than it looks: **the server borrows and releases the shared submodule on exit**,
which is the same hazard one step further along.

**The wrong-world guard caught it correctly every time** — zero served, non-zero exit — which is the
guard doing exactly its job on a failure it was not designed for. That is why this is a warning rather
than a blocker: **it is loud.**

### Decision D-MEALS-AUDIT-ACTOR-KIND — how a release with no human names what freed it
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MEALS-RELEASE-ACTOR
options:
| actorkind-column — add an actor-kind column to the Meals audit ledger, in the Events payment-ledger shape ; pro: it is the estate's only sanctioned named-system-actor pattern, and injecting it made the module's own pin accept the sweep and red on the fourteen pre-existing stamp sites — correct and module-wide by construction ; con: it needs a migration into a chain that is five deep and contested, and backfilling existing rows assigns a kind to rows that predate the concept, in an append-only ledger
| reference-sentinel — keep one column and write a named sentinel string for system actors ; pro: no migration at all, and no backfill question ; con: **the estate already refuses this** — injecting a named sentinel reds the module-audit call-site pin, whose message says a defaulted or hard-coded actor is the defect itself
| defer — record the release without an actor until the chain is merged ; pro: authors no migration into a contested chain, and the gap stays visible rather than being papered over ; con: leaves a money-path write naming nobody, which is the C4 violation this lane exists to close

### Decision D-GR-DEADLINE-CALENDAR — which calendar the article 12 deadline is read on
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-GR-ISOPEN-DOC
options:
| venue-local — compute and render the deadline on the venue's own calendar, date-only ; pro: it dissolves the mismatch entirely, and it is the reading a venue would defend to a regulator, since the obligation is theirs and the day is theirs ; con: it needs a venue timezone the module does not currently carry, and two venues in different zones would see different deadlines for requests filed in the same instant — which is correct and will still look like a bug
| utc-both-ends — keep computing on UTC and render on UTC too, labelled ; pro: one calendar end to end, no new data, and the arithmetic already verified exact stays untouched ; con: a Norwegian venue reads a deadline in a timezone it does not live in, and the label is the only thing preventing a misread
| utc-compute-local-render — what ships today ; pro: nothing to do ; con: **the two disagree by a day in a narrow window, in the direction that grants headroom the statute does not** — a request filed just after local midnight at certain month-ends
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: venue-local 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: two venues in different timezones need one deadline, or the venue timezone the module now carries turns out not to be reliable

**Recommended:** venue-local — it is the only option where the printed date is the date the venue is
actually held to.

**This ruling gates more than it looks.** The statute lane established that **both** remaining counting
rules wait on it. The weekend half of the working-day extension needs no data at all — but *is the due day
a Saturday* **has no answer until you know which calendar it is read on.** And rounding to the last moment
of the due day, which sounds like a pure improvement, **would move the printed date a day later for every
row east of UTC** — the dangerous direction applied universally instead of to a handful.

The public-holiday half is separate and is **not implementable honestly**: the Regulation defines holidays
as those designated in the Member State where action is taken, which is per-market data **the product holds
for no market.**

### Decision D-MRG-PRICE-CORRECTION — how a frozen week is repriced, and who is named for it
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-MRG-PRICE-CORRECTION
options:
| backdated-correction — an operator-only backdated price that closes into the timeline, bounded so it can never become the open row ; pro: **no money is edited**, the correction is a first-class row with its own source, and it costs **exactly one column** ; con: it needs that column and therefore a migration into a contested chain, and it **removes the premise an existing refusal rests on** — the import approval refuses an unattributed actor *on the grounds that a wrong price is superseded forward, never withdrawn*
| statement-override — a per-statement price override on the correction revision ; pro: it touches the price book not at all, so the timeline keeps saying exactly what a supplier charged when ; con: **a table plus an override map threaded through the calculator, the resolver and the memo key** — and **it still leaves the price book wrong for every later week and every later read**
| leave-it — accept that a frozen week cannot be repriced once a later price exists ; pro: nothing is built and the timeline stays inviolate ; con: **the correction revision silently reproduces the identical wrong cost forever**, and the control that appears to offer a correction does nothing
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: backdated-correction 2026-08-03 by @sven
reopen_when: the import approval refusal cannot be re-grounded once superseded-forward stops being the reason, or the column is refused by the chain

**Recommended:** backdated-correction — it is the only option where the corrected week actually costs
correctly and the price book stops lying about what was charged.

**But the attribution is not optional and that is why this is a ruling.** A backdated correction removes
the premise an existing refusal is written on. **The lane found the column has nowhere to live:** the price
row carries no actor, the import batch requires a file hash under a unique index, and **Margin has no audit
ledger at all** — which is plausibly the same question as the open Growth ledger decision.

**Executed 2026-08-03, and the `con:` was handled rather than absorbed.** The ruling made false the premise
an existing refusal rested on — *a wrong price is superseded forward, never withdrawn.* The lane
**re-grounded that refusal at all five sites carrying it**, on what the write does to money already
reported, and made the re-grounding **executable**: a symmetry test drives both money doors and asserts the
two refusals **agree**, so drift on either side reds.

A frozen week now reprices by exactly the amount the forward path refuses in that same world, with the
prior revision still finalized at its old figure. **The bound is that a correction is permitted only where
a strictly later price exists**, so it always closes at a real successor boundary — proven non-vacuously by
showing the forward path *accepted* in the identical world.

**Two errors it caught in itself and corrected rather than narrowing the claim:** a wire test that passed
without reaching the module (see `F-401-UNREACHABLE-OVER-HTTP`), and closing-instant logic that handled a
null predecessor but not one closing *past* its successor — found by self-review **after** a green tier.

**On the backfill question it declined to inherit a sibling's reasoning**, which is the right instinct: this
is an existing table rather than a new one, but the column is nullable **by design rather than by
concession** — manual and imported rows legitimately have no corrector, so a not-null column would be
semantically wrong however many rows existed.

**One judgement call left explicitly for whoever authors the column.** The lane **deliberately skipped a
stage flag** for the correction endpoint: the flag catalog is a shared surface with three flag lanes in
flight, and this cannot merge before the column exists anyway.

The consequence, stated rather than buried: **the endpoint is live the moment the column lands**, unless
somebody decides otherwise. It is recorded here so that is a decision rather than a discovery.

### Decision D-GROWTH-AUDIT-LEDGER — a narrow test-send record, or a Growth audit ledger
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-GR-TESTSEND-RECORD
options:

ruled: growth-ledger 2026-08-03 by @sven

are the same shape, and the chain contest argues for **one** migration rather than two.

The lane that surfaced this could not proceed and returned blocked rather than guessing. Its handover
carries the table specification so the migration author does not re-derive it, including two findings
worth keeping: the deterministic provider key **must not be unique**, because the instinctive unique index
would silently drop a second test-send and break the very word *every* in the exit criterion; and
append-only means the row records the **attempt**, so there is no accepted column — filling one after the

### Decision D-SPEC-L-EV-VIPPS-FALLBACK — the plan contradicts what L-EV-VIPPS-FALLBACK observed
state: ruled
owner: @sven
blocks: L-EV-VIPPS-FALLBACK
options:
| compose-and-refuse — assert the fallback on the JSON body the real service posts, and refuse to create the order at all when no guest origin is configured ; pro: fully provable today with no credential and no decision, and it converts a silently stranded guest into a loud refusal at the one moment somebody is watching ; con: the approve-and-return leg stays unproven, and will stay unproven until both a test merchant number and a decided origin exist
| defer-whole-lane — park until a test merchant number exists and the guest origin is set ; pro: proves the entire leg at once, which is the only way the guest's return is ever really shown ; con: leaves a known-broken initiate on the branch indefinitely, and the origin decision has been open long enough that the code's own comment records it as pending
| api-origin-fallback — return the guest to the API's own origin and redirect from there ; pro: needs no configuration decision at all ; con: invents a guest-facing surface nobody designed and puts it on the API host — a topology choice that is the same one already open for the Growth preference centre, and answering it here would answer it there by accident
default_if_unruled: none
ruled: compose-and-refuse 2026-08-03 by @sven
